The wash narrowed into a gorge at the tree line, and the tree line had no birds in it.

He read the absence before he could have said what he was reading. Two hours of descent, and the scrub had carried the ordinary noise of scrub — insects, a carrion bird working something dead in the middle distance, wind doing what wind did to dry brush. Then the gorge mouth, and a silence arriving whole, the way pressure changes before sound does, so that a man attuned to thresholds felt it in his ears before he had located anything to call it fear.

"Orim."

He had already stopped. He stood at the gorge's edge with his boots in the last of the scrub and his eyes on the particular ten meters of ground ahead of him, reading it with the same unhurried thoroughness he gave every threshold before he permitted his own feet to cross it — a man reading a letter he suspects will change what he does with the rest of his day, he had told Lyra once, does not open it standing up.

"Bones," he said. "Old ones and new ones. No pattern I'd call a den, exactly — more a larder that outgrew its own management." He crouched, touched something in the dust neither of the others could see from where they stood, and did not pick it up. "Deer-analogue, most of it. Some of what came through the corridor behind us, if the marrow's any indication — the pack we crossed two hours ago wasn't only fleeing north. Something back here was thinning it from the south."

"How old, the recent kills?" she asked.

"Recent enough that the flies haven't finished arguing about which parts to file a claim on." He straightened, slower than the answer should have cost a man his age, and looked up the gorge — a hundred meters of dry channel walled by rock the color of a bruise, narrowing before it opened again into whatever waited past the bend. "This is the fast way to the coast road. The long way costs the rest of the day and puts us on the ridge after dark, which is a cost I'd rather not add to what the last ridge already took out of us." He did not say why. The last ridge had been the Fire Scry, and none of them had discussed it since, and none of them needed to.

"And the short way?" she asked.

"The short way has whatever emptied that larder still inside it, most likely. I can't scry past the bend — my range doesn't reach, and something in that direction reads to me the way a held breath reads. Which is not information. It is the absence of information in a specific shape." He had learned, across fifty years of reading thresholds, that this particular absence was itself worth more than most of what passed for information, and had also learned that saying so changed nothing about which road they were about to walk.

Doyle had come up on the other side without a sound, which by now was simply how Doyle moved, rifle slung and hands loose, the black optic reading the gorge walls with the same flat attention he gave every approach. There was a great deal the man could have said about what he felt standing at that mouth. He offered one word of it.

"Bad," he said.

"Yes," Lyra said.

Two words were the whole of what Doyle had ever needed to give, and the whole of what Lyra had ever given back, and Orim had watched enough men decide enough things to have concluded, long before either of these two were born, that the shortest exchanges were usually the honest ones. They went in anyway. There had never really been a question, not in any sense that made asking it worth the breath. Three days had already turned suspicious once this week, and Sal Vento would not wait for a party that took the long way around every hard thing between here and the coast.

The gorge widened past the bend into a bowl of open ground the size of a tourney field, walled on three sides by the same bruise-colored rock, floored in dust and old bone and the flattened wreckage of scrub that something considerably heavier than deer had been walking over for longer than a season. At the bowl's far side, where the rock face broke into a shadowed overhang deep enough to be its own weather, something was already moving before any of them had finished understanding the scale of the space they had walked into.

Orim gave it three seconds of looking before deciding what it was not. That was the discipline: never name a thing before you had watched it long enough to be wrong about it once, in your own head, quietly, where the wrongness cost nothing.

It came out from under the overhang the way a landslide comes out from under a ridge — not fast, not at first, mass announcing itself before speed did, four legs and then, wrongly, a fifth point of contact where a tail should have simply trailed and instead planted, gripped, pushed. Fourteen feet at the shoulder would have been generous for the harrower Ardea had once described to Lyra secondhand from a garrison report. This cleared that mark before its head came fully into the light, and kept coming — twenty feet, easily, at the ridge of its back, a bulk that had no business moving on legs at all, closer in outline to a war engine built with a mandate for excessive tonnage than to anything that had ever needed to survive on its own four feet in open country.

The hide was not grey-brown like the corridor pack's. It was plated — overlapping segments the color and apparent hardness of split slate, a natural armor that should not have existed on anything that also needed to breathe, to bend, to hunt. Where the plates met at shoulder and hip they showed dark seams, wet-looking, that did not match the dry matte of the plates themselves. The head, swinging toward them, carried no eyes Orim could find — only two rows of shallow pits along the brow ridge, opening and closing independently of one another, each one flaring a faint heat-shimmer at the edges like a coal drawing breath.

It had no need to see them. It was already reading the warmth coming off their bodies from sixty meters out.

The sound arrived before the charge did — not a roar, nothing so simple. A frequency that came up through the ground into the soles of the boots and into the back teeth at the same moment, low enough that for a full second it read as the gorge itself settling, some geological complaint the rock was lodging against its own weight. Then it kept going, sustained, and understanding arrived in Orim a beat or two before he said anything about it: this was breath. This was simply what the creature sounded like at rest, before it had decided to do anything at all.

He had gone very still. He recognized the stillness in himself as he recognized it in anyone standing at a threshold — not fear, exactly, though fifty years had never quite taught him the difference from the inside, only how to keep either of them out of his hands until there was work for his hands to do.

"Catalogue reads nothing," he said, quietly, to himself as much as to her. "Fifty years, and I have nothing in fifty years for this."

Whatever ran behind Doyle's oval receptor did not wait to be asked. It never did, and Orim had long since stopped needing to see the words themselves; he read the same page in the half-second tilt of that black housing, arriving, as he almost always did, at the same conclusions in an older and slower language. This, roughly, was what the instrument gave the younger man, and what Orim had already begun assembling for himself out of bone-age and breath-frequency and the particular wrongness of a fifth ground-contact point:

Mass beyond any calibrated field reference — eleven to fourteen tons, forward-loaded. A gait that made no tactical sense, sustained ground pressure inconsistent with the speed it was producing. A hide of laminate plate, non-metallic, calcite in its nature, with a single failure point at the cervico-dorsal junction that opened on the forced exhale and nowhere else. And, cross-referenced against an archive Orim himself had never once needed to consult, because he had written the marginal hand into a different ledger sixty years before Doyle's receptor had ever existed to read it back to him: a thing out of Sphere-119, unrecorded under any common name, with one prior notation from the Year 873 that said only that it was not to be summoned, and not to be catalogued twice.

He did not share the second half of that sentence. There would be time for it later, if there was a later, and no version of saying it now would change what any of them did in the next ten seconds.

Doyle absorbed the readout the same instant it arrived, unbidden as always — a half-second's stillness, the optic tilting a fraction, and then he was already moving, unslinging the rifle, already doing the only thing the readout had ever been for.

"There," he said, and touched two fingers to the base of his own throat, then pointed at the beast's shoulder, low, where the neck met the ridge of its back. "When it — " He made a short exhaling sound, touched the spot again. "Opens."

"When it breathes?" Lyra asked.

He nodded once.

It charged.

The distance from the overhang to where they stood had looked, a moment before, like forty meters of open ground and margin. It closed in under three seconds — mass translating into speed at a rate Orim watched the girl's body answer before her mind could have finished working it out. She had already moved: shield up, feet set, taking the angle rather than the center of the charge, the way a man takes a battering ram he cannot stop by standing directly in front of it.

The impact traveled through the Vigil Shield and into her arm and shoulder and down through her braced leg into the ground. Orim watched the resin-hardened face of it flex under a load it had never been built to absorb in a single blow, watched her ride the deflection sideways rather than fight it, letting the shield's angle bleed the force into a glancing slide instead of a dead stop that would have taken her arm out of its socket. It was the lesson six weeks of his own flat insistence had put into her hands, whether she credited him with it or not, and he watched her use it now the way a man watches a tool he built perform exactly as designed.

She came up already reading the next problem, which was the reach. The head came around on a neck longer than the body's proportions should have allowed — a whip-crack correction faster than the charge that had produced it — and she went inside it rather than away, close enough that the jaw's arc passed over her instead of through her.

"Doyle!" she called, not turning, the shield still between her and whatever correction was coming next. "The angle!"

He had already found it. Low and wide against the gorge wall's shadow, the position his old war had built into him before any of them had met him — find the ground that gives you the shot, hold it, let the tank absorb what the shot needs time to set up. Orim had watched this same discipline in exactly one other man in his life, a man dead forty years now, and had never once told Doyle so, because some comparisons were not gifts.

He did not fire. Not yet. The seam only opened on the exhale, and the beast was drawing breath for another charge, plates drawn tight, and firing into closed armor would have cost him one of five rounds for nothing. Orim had watched him hold this same wait on three prior occasions and understood, without needing the sentence spoken aloud, that this was the same patience that had kept a boy alive in a hedgerow long enough to become the man crouched in this gorge — patience that cost nothing until the moment it cost everything.

The beast reared onto its hind legs, higher than its mass should have allowed — Orim saw the correction and said nothing — and the exhale came out of it in a visible cloud of cold breath, the seam at its shoulder opening, wet-dark, for perhaps half a second.

Doyle fired.

The round went where he'd aimed it. The beast's whole body convulsed sideways, a shudder running the length of the plated spine like a wave through water, and the sound it made afterward was not the low breathing frequency any longer — something higher, worse, a note that cracked at the edges the way a voice cracks when asked to do something it was never built to do.

It was not enough. Orim understood that in the same breath he understood the shot had landed clean. A single round through a seam the width of two fingers was a wound, not a kill, on something that size, and what the creature did instead of dying was turn everything it had left toward the thing that had hurt it.

It came down off its hind legs directly onto her.

She got the shield up. She did not get the angle — there had been no time to choose one, only time to choose between the shield and nothing — and the forelimb that came past the shield's edge caught her across the ribs and side. Not the full weight of the blow. Enough. Orim watched her go down without having decided to go down, watched a hand come up to brace against the dust and come away red before her eyes had found the wound. Three claw marks, he could see even from where he stood, torn rather than punctured — the half-plate had turned the worst of it, taken the deepest one on the hip rather than the gut. Not a fact he was glad of. Only one more kept for later, if there proved to be a later.

She tested whether she could stand while the beast reared again for what would be, with the same flat clarity that governed most of what Orim allowed himself to notice, the blow that answered that question for her.

"Down!" Doyle's voice, louder than Orim had heard him manage in six weeks, and she went down and sideways rather than up, and the second round went into the same seam, wider now from the first wound, and the scream cracked further, and under all of it, over all of it, there was Orim's own voice, though he would not have been able to say, afterward, at what point exactly he had decided to use it.

"Stand clear," he said. Not loud. The tone of a man who had said it before and understood exactly what it cost the people who needed to hear it.

He crossed the open ground toward the wounded thing rather than away from it, which was not what forty years of doctrine would have told a sensible man to do, and he was aware, distantly — the same removed awareness he had of most things about himself while he was doing them — that he no longer entirely counted as a sensible man where the Rod was concerned, and had not for some years.

The mineral tip was still faintly warm from the Forge Hearth. He had wrapped it in his own coat two hours before and had not asked himself when it would cool, because there had not been time, and now there was less. A thin skin of soot had settled into the cord wrapping at the grip since the ridge — the residue of a housing asked to work hard, and recently — and he read that soot as he read everything else that morning: as a fact about how thin his margin had grown, offered to no one, weighed by no one but himself.

He did not stop at forty meters. Forty meters was the clearance he had held for fifty years between himself and whatever he chose to let through the world's own skin for the Terrible Births — his own word for it, coined the first time a scry stopped being sight and turned to killing instead. He crossed inside it — inside twenty, inside ten — close enough that the beast's next convulsion, its head swinging low, searching by heat for the smaller warm thing now standing well inside its reach, nearly caught him before Doyle's third round, fired wide of the seam on purpose, took it in the brow-pit instead and bought him the half-second he needed.

This was not a cold pierce, whatever the forty-meter clearance and the two settled breaths otherwise demanded of him. He had already read what the beast carried in it before the readout ever confirmed the name — a marginal hand, a hundred years dead, warning against summoning the thing twice — and a creature that had crossed the membrane once already to be standing in this gorge at all did not offer virgin ground the way granite or dry scrub did. Its wound was aperture-adjacent before Doyle's rounds had ever opened it further, a place where the world's skin had already thinned by the creature's own passage through it once before. He was not pressing into a threshold cold. He was pressing into one that had, in some sense he had no clean word for, already been crossed — and he understood, distantly, that this was very likely the only reason what he was about to do would work at all.

He put the mineral tip into the wound. Not near it. Into it — the ragged opening Doyle's two rounds had made in the plate, wet and dark and still widening with every convulsion — and he pressed the Rod's tip against the raw edge of it like a key into a lock he had never before had the nerve to try.

He held there. Motionless, the Rod's tip resting against the wound's raw edge, looking at nothing but that wound — not at Lyra, not at Doyle, not at the dying thing's swinging head — the way a man looks at a door he built with his own two hands and has kept shut for fifty years, deciding, in no hurry now that the deciding could no longer be avoided, whether he still meant what he had built it to mean.

"Not at a living thing," he said, to no one, to the beast, to fifty years of his own rule. "I said I never would."

He pulled the trigger.

He had watched the Fire Scry two hours before — the exhalation of a Sphere-23 volcano crossing a hundred meters of open air to burn six men off a road — and had understood, long before that, watching a hundred openings before it, that the Rod did not create anything. It only parted the skin and stood back from whatever pressure on the far side did with the opening.

What came through this time had nowhere to go but directly and immediately into the beast's own body, because the aperture was the wound and the wound was the door, and he had aimed a piece of the world's own skin — small, wet, alive in his two hands — straight into eleven tons of living tissue at a range of perhaps four inches.

For half a breath the raw edge of the wound went a color that had nothing to do with the beast at all — warm amber-gold, wet and clinging, the color of light through old honey, the world's own liquor pressing at the tear like water at a thumb held over a spout. Then the gold went under it. Water came first — not a stream, not a spray, a wall of it, black and cold in a way that had nothing to do with any water he had ever put a hand in, carrying the mineral smell of somewhere far underground and far from any sun. A Sphere-08 lake, at a depth that had spent geological time compressing itself into a pressure no membrane on Entos's surface had ever been built to stand adjacent to. He knew it with the same certainty as the age of the scrub and the wrongness of the fifth ground-contact point — a fact arrived at before the words for it, and not one he intended to say aloud that day, or perhaps any day. It did not spray outward through the wound. It went in, because the wound was the only opening the pressure differential had been offered, and eleven tons of body cavity that had never once needed to withstand deep-lake hydrostatic load absorbed, in under two seconds, considerably more of it than a body was built to hold.

The sound it made afterward had no name that Orim had ever come across in fifty years of collecting names for things, and he did not attempt to give it one now, on the grounds that trying would have been dishonest. It was not the cracked scream from before. It was something wetter, and shorter, and then it was nothing at all, because the plated ridge of its back had stopped moving in the way that meant the thing driving it had stopped being able to.

It did not fall so much as stop arguing with the ground it had been standing on, and went down all at once. The impact threw dust and old bone fragments into the air in a ring around the point of contact, and somewhere under the plates something further gave way with a sound like wet canvas, and cold lake water the color of iron ran out of the wound and pooled black in the dust, carrying with it things that had no business existing in a gorge three hours' walk from the sea. None of the three of them looked at it very long.

Orim sat down where he was standing. Not carefully — his legs had simply finished the conversation without consulting him — and he registered this about himself with the same flat, unhurried attention he gave to everything else that morning — a fact, arriving late, that he had spent more than he had been keeping track of spending.

The Rod's tip had gone dark — the same dead-coal dark that comes once the last heat has bled out of a thing — no glow left at all, not even the low thermal answer it had carried after the Fire Scry — and this time he did not wrap it in his coat. He set it down in the dust beside him and looked at his own two hands as though they belonged to someone he had recently been introduced to.

Doyle reached her first. He had two words for what he found — the torn plate, the blood already soaking the lower edge of her half-plate, more of it than the eye expected a body to be carrying around loose — and he used the correct one, which by now was understood among the three of them as the mark of how seriously he was taking a situation.

"Bad," he said again, and this time it was not a description of the gorge.

"Grey Tincture," she said. "Left side of the kit. Not the White — the White's for bleeding I don't have time to stop properly, and I have time." She did not, entirely, but Orim saw, from where he sat, that saying it seemed to make it closer to true for her, and that there was a whole practice of triage that ran on exactly that logic.

Doyle found the vial without fumbling, which told Orim something about how many times the young man had watched her work that kit on other people, and set it aside without a second look. She talked him through the rest in short sentences — pressure here, not there, the tincture goes on the cloth first, never directly into an open wound unless you want to learn why the manual says not to — and somewhere in the middle of it Orim heard her say, distantly, as if through a wall: "That's a lot of blood to be carrying around outside a person?"

Doyle did not answer that. He kept working.

Orim did not move from where he sat until the worst of the bleeding had slowed under Doyle's hands and her own steadying breath, and when he did move it was only to reach out and set one hand, briefly, on the cold dust beside the dead thing's ruined shoulder — not a benediction, not a farewell, nothing he would have put a word to even for himself. He took the hand back. He offered no explanation, and neither of them asked him for one; they had both learned better by now.

"I have pointed that Rod at six men on a road," he said finally, to the gorge in general, "and slept afterward, because they had chosen the wrong side of a war I did not start. I have summoned forty-five seconds of some creature's whole existence into a dockyard corridor and turned away so I would not have to watch what I had done to it, because the alternative was watching my own party die instead, and I could live with that arithmetic." He looked at his hands again. "I have never done this. I told myself, the first time I built the courage to open anything at all, that whatever else the Rod became for, it would never become that."

"It killed the thing that was killing us," Lyra said, because it was true, and because the alternative to saying the true thing was saying something merely comforting, and she had learned, across six weeks, that he had never once asked her for the second kind.

"Yes," he said. "That is also true." He picked the Rod back up out of the dust, turned it once in his hands, and did not look at it again after that. "Both things are true. I find that this does not make either of them lighter."

They did not linger in the bowl. There was nothing to loot from a carcass that large that any of them wanted to carry, and the black pool spreading from the wound had already begun drawing the kind of insects that fed on things that should not exist in this world's ecology, working it with the same patient indifference they brought to anything else dead. Doyle checked his remaining rounds — two — and said nothing about the count, which by now Orim understood meant the count troubled him more than a comment would have helped.

Lyra walked the rest of the gorge with one hand pressed against her side under the half-plate, upright because he needed her upright and because sitting down to properly feel the wound was a luxury the schedule did not currently extend to her. Somewhere in the last hundred meters before the gorge opened back onto the coastal scrub, Orim understood — without being able to say when exactly he had arrived at it — that the three of them had just fought as a single mechanism rather than as three people standing near each other: the shield taking what could be taken, the rifle finding what could be found, the last resort spent only when the first two had done everything they could do and still fell short. Nobody had called the positions aloud. Nobody had needed to. He set that fact aside too — one more thing that seemed likely to matter again before this was over — and did not say it aloud either, on the grounds that it kept better unspoken.

The scrub gave way to the smell of salt an hour later, faint at first, then unmistakable — the same smell that had reached him two hundred meters out from every coastal town in fifty years of walking toward one, promising a port and a bed and, if the Avandrey's schedule held, a reason to keep moving before the wound in Lyra's side finished deciding how much it intended to hurt in the morning.

"Sal Vento," he said, mostly to the horizon. He'd been saying it at intervals since the ridge. "If the weather holds."

"It'll hold," Lyra said.

He did not correct her, though weather, like most things he had spent a long life reading, would do what it intended to do regardless of what any of them hoped from it, and he had long since stopped considering that worth saying out loud either.

## Chapter 17 — Calyx Uplands

The road through Calyx ran high enough that the pines gave out and only lichen-crusted rock held the wind, and they had been three weeks on it by the time Esvane let the fire burn past dark for the first time since Ocipheus.

"You're thinking about the crest again," Petra said, not looking up from the knife she was stropping. She'd stopped asking him what he was thinking about somewhere around the second week; she'd started telling him instead, and she was usually right.

"I'm thinking that a House with a crest like this one," Wren said, "spent seven centuries deciding what shape its crest should be, and never once decided what to do with the man wearing it."

Esvane made a sound that wasn't quite a laugh. "Your cousin decided plenty. He decided to let it get taken in the first place, and he decided to let two generations forget where it went, and now he's decided to send his own blood to fetch it back rather than spend a coin of his own risk on the job. That's not nothing. That's a whole policy."

"You say his name like a curse."

"I say his name like a client," Esvane said. "There's a difference, and the difference is the only reason I get paid."

Petra's stropping hand had gone still. "Calyx never paid me anything," she said, to the fire, not to either of them. "I do this because the alternative was staying somewhere I'd already decided I wasn't going to die."

Nobody asked her to finish that. Wren had learned, by then, that the crew kept exactly two kinds of silence — the kind that meant a question would be answered if you were patient, and the kind that meant it wouldn't be answered ever, by anyone, and asking again only spent trust he'd need later. He let this one be the second kind.

"For what it's worth," he said instead, "I don't do it for the House either. I do it because he's the only family who ever wrote my name down anywhere that mattered, and I would like, once, to be the reason he got to keep something instead of the reason he lost it."

Esvane looked at him for a long moment across the fire, the flat, assessing look she gave a plan when she was checking whether it still held weight. "That's a worse reason than mine," she said. "It'll get you killed faster."

"So will yours."

"Mine's already gotten me paid twice," she said, and that ended it — not because the argument was won, but because she'd decided the conversation had used up its allotted portion of the night.

It found them on the fifth night after that, in the col between two black ridges where the wind couldn't decide which direction to blow and so did both at once.

Esvane heard it before either of them did — a wet clicking under the wind, arrhythmic, patient, the sound of something counting instead of breathing — and had the fire stamped to embers with the flat of her boot before Wren had finished turning his head toward it.

"Up," she said. "Now. Rocks, not trees."

He'd never seen a sinterspawn scout up close, only the corpses of the ones the road crews burned at crossroads as a warning nobody needed twice. This one came low along the scree, quick as water finding a crack, faster than its size should have allowed, and the pale plating along its spine caught the last of the coals' light and gave nothing back.

Petra put two crossbow bolts into it before it closed the last ten paces, and neither one turned it. It was Esvane, not the case, that she moved to shield when the thing finally came into the firelight's reach — a half-second decision Wren watched her make and would spend a long time afterward not knowing what to do with, because it was the first time in three weeks he'd seen her spend herself on a person instead of on the job.

Wren's knife found the soft joint behind the foreleg on the second pass, drilled into his hands by Loera until his hands no longer needed him to think about it, and the thing went down convulsing, and then went down still, and none of them moved for a ten-count after that just to be sure the stillness was going to hold.

Esvane checked the case first. Then she checked Petra. Then, last, she checked him, and something crossed her face when she found him unmarked that he couldn't afford to name, because naming it would have cost him something he had none to spare that morning.

"That's twice this month the case has nearly gone into something's stomach," she said, once her breathing had settled. "Next time we don't wait for daylight to move. Next time we don't stop for fires at all."

She meant it as a lesson. He heard it, even then, as the first draft of a harder sentence, one she would finish four mornings later, at a river he hadn't seen yet.

They had two days on the pursuit and both of them knew it wouldn't hold.

Esvane said as much on the descent from the ridge, not stopping to say it, the case riding tight against her chest exactly as it had ridden since Ocipheus and would keep riding, he understood without being told, until it was no longer hers to carry. "If it comes down to it," she said, "the case goes to Calyx. That's the job. That was always the job."

"And if it comes down to it," Wren said, because he had learned by then which questions were worth the breath, "what's my job?"

She didn't answer that one. Petra, a half-step behind her, didn't either, though something crossed her face that might have been the beginning of an answer she'd decided not to finish.

It came down to it on the fourth morning, at a river crossing with one narrow ford and no cover on either bank worth the name. He heard the column before he saw it — too many boots for a border patrol, moving with a purpose that wasn't looking for anything so much as already knowing where it was. Esvane read it in the same half-second he did.

"Go," she said. Not to him. To Petra, and to the case.

He understood — a half-beat too late, same as most things that year — that she had not been asking whether to split up. She had already decided it, probably days ago, banked against the morning it would be needed — a spare line coiled and ready long before the first one frays. He was the piece of the plan that could be spent. The case was not.

"Esvane—"

"You'll manage," she said, which was not the same as an apology and was not offered as one. She was already moving, Petra a stride behind her, the case between them like something with its own gravity, pulling the whole shape of the crew toward the far bank and away from him.

He could have run. He chose instead the two seconds it took to be sure the column's attention had found him and not them, because some habits outlasted the reasons a man had first learned them for, and this one — buy the others their exit, whatever it costs the one who stays — was older in him than House Calyx, older than Loera, older than anything he'd been taught on purpose.

They did not look back. He did not expect them to. That was, he would think later, very nearly the whole of what he needed to know about the difference between a crew and whatever this was going to become instead.

The water closed over Esvane's boots and Petra's, and then the tree line, and then there was only the column closing the last distance, and a small dark shape at its front already reading him with the same patient, precise attention it turned on everything — already deciding how much of a fight this was actually going to be.

Not much of one, as it turned out. He had one knife and a fold that cost more than he had left to spend that morning, and the outcome settled itself before he had to.

He did not raise his hands. He also did not run. He had already decided, standing in the mud with the river taking the last of his crew away from him, that he was done making that particular choice for other people's reasons.

Wren walked with his hands bound in front of him, which he had decided, three days into it, was worse than bound behind. Bound behind, a man could tell himself the rope was an insult aimed at his hands. Bound in front, he had to watch them the whole day, tied, useless, trailing him around like an accusation he couldn't set down.

Doyle walked a half-step behind him and to the left, close enough to close the gap in under a second, far enough that Wren's shoulder blades had stopped waiting for the touch somewhere around day two. He didn't talk. He nudged, once, when the trail forked and Wren's feet started toward the wrong half of it — two fingers, brief, between the shoulder blades, the exact minimum force the correction required and not one ounce more.

"You could just tell me which way," Wren said, the third time it happened.

"Could," Doyle said. Flat. He did not elaborate, and Wren had stopped expecting him to.

Orim had said nothing to him directly in three days, and Lyra had noticed. He watched the boy the way he watched weather that hadn't decided yet what it meant to do — not unkindly, exactly, but without once setting the watching down. When Wren had offered, on the second night, to make himself useful — a fire built faster, a line better tied, anything to earn the food he was eating — Orim had said only, "That is exactly what I would expect you to say," and gone back to his own fire, and that had been the whole of the conversation.

Lyra understood the instinct. A man who had spent a working lifetime reading what people wanted him to believe did not stop reading it just because the boy in question had a reasonably sympathetic face and a story that hung together. Especially not then.

Eleven days on the highland road, and her knees knew every one of them. Orim's joints answered the steeper grades with a sound she'd decided, as a professional courtesy, not to mention. Doyle walked without complaint because Doyle walked everything without complaint. By day eight Lyra had stopped finding that reassuring or irritating. It simply was.

The deadline was not a comfort to think about, so she measured instead. Senne's column had been three days behind at Verlaine. Eleven days of highland passes since, and she hadn't counted on the gap holding. She'd been right not to count on it.

The path down to Sal Vento smelled of the sea two hundred paces before anyone saw it — salt, limestone, and under both the cold of rock, decades of spray never fully dried. Cut steps, not worn track. Risers sized for load, treads wide enough for two abreast. Somebody had built this to last. She approved of it on principle — honest work always earned that from her.

"Ship in the lower harbor," Doyle said. Flat. Just information — that was how the shell delivered everything now, no distinction in it between the urgent and the idle.

"Liturgy registration?" Lyra asked.

"Wrong marks. Somebody painted over the hull registry and did decent work, but the paint doesn't match under the ultraviolet band." A beat. "Reads Balthier."

The Balthier. Lyra had heard that name once, in a procurement review the year before the crossing — an Ocipheus Station reconnaissance vessel off the Northern Route roster, flagged administrative loss, never chased down. Seventeen years she'd trusted the Station's paperwork meant something. The trust had gone somewhere else, without much feeling left to spend on it.

They took the stone table outside the harbor tavern to wait on Orim, and that was where the trouble started — not with them, at first. A dockhand caught an elbow he decided he hadn't earned, his drink went down a stranger's front, and the stranger came up already swinging. In a port this size a spilled drink was never about the drink. It was about who'd bumped whom on purpose, and who was watching closely enough to have arranged it.

Lyra put her back to the wall on reflex — seventeen years of drill did that whether she asked it to or not — and watched two men become four, and an argument turn into a proper scrap: short, ugly, nobody's technique, elbows and table legs, one man's face meeting stone hard enough that he sat down without meaning to. She took a wrist reaching for Doyle's collar, turned it the way the manual said, put its owner down without breaking anything. Doyle dropped a second man into a barrel, unhurried about it. Four down or fled inside the time it took to describe, nobody dead - the correct outcome for a fight that hadn't been about anything to begin with.

That was when Tavar came through the wreckage of it, unhurried, and sat down across from her like the last two minutes hadn't happened.

She'd confirmed his documents two hours past, at this table: Loera operative, no rank she recognized as command. Not a captain. No ship of his own. He'd given her four things in order of most to least verifiable — name, House, the ship's name, and his codes for the mooring watch's rotation — the way a man gives information to someone he's decided is worth the risk of being wrong about.

"That wasn't staged for you," he said, meaning the fight, "but I watched how you handled it."

"You already knew the ship was here?" Lyra asked.

"I knew several things were here. I came to find out which ones you needed." He set a folded chart on the table — the sea cave south of the harbor mouth, Balthier moored inside it, out of every sightline but his own, and beside it the watch's rotation, hour by hour, in his own hand. "This is what it costs," he said, and named a price.

She paid it without arguing the number. He told her the rest on the walk down.

Declan had known cold with a job to do before. Drift cold, the kind that lived a hundred feet under Unaka ridge and didn't care whose shift it was. This one was worse. Sea cold, at the tail end of night — the kind that had quit announcing itself hours ago and just kept coming.

He waited behind the limestone shelf with Orim, out of the wind but not out of the cold, because cold didn't need wind to find a man, same as gas didn't need a draft to find the low place in a shaft. Above them, on the overhang, Lyra had been at the scope the better part of an hour. He'd timed it without meaning to. Fifty-eight minutes. He'd learned to count on watch a long time before he learned anything else useful, and some habits didn't leave when the man they'd belonged to did.

Orim scried from a crouch, fingertips together at his sternum, eyes gone soft and elsewhere. He didn't use the Rod. Hadn't since the gorge. Declan didn't ask why. A man learned to leave some things in another man's coat pocket, same as you left a fella's dead brother out of the talk on shift. Ninety seconds. Declan counted them anyway — the old habit from counting the interval between a whistle and a shell landing — not because the number mattered, but because counting was a way of being somewhere other than afraid.

Orim's eyes opened.

"Two soldiers," he said. "The one at the gangway foot is seated, rifle across the knees, watching the gate side of the dock, not the water. The one at the forward hatch is upright, checking the mooring lines along the starboard rail. He'll finish that and go still. Call it four minutes."

He paused. "The hold is clear. I didn't go past it. There's something between me and the space behind the forward bulkhead I didn't want to push through."

He said it flatly: observed fact, not an invitation to make more of it.

"Engine housing," Lyra said. "Residual heat, maybe. Liturgy apparatus reads strange even asleep."

"Possibly." He didn't sound convinced, and didn't push it either. He sat down on the shelf — not a lowering, a sitting his body had decided on before he'd been consulted — and looked at the backs of his hands, breathing the deliberate breathing of a man remembering what deliberate breathing was for.

Declan ran a thumb over the bayonet catch at his belt, once, twice. Test the door before you open it — an old rule, older than this body, older than the last one. He'd learned it the hard way in the monster corridor three days back, when the bolt jammed and the blade was the only tool left in his hands fast enough to matter. A man checked the tools he trusted the hard way. He didn't trust any other kind.

"Two," Lyra said. "Gangway and forward hatch. Quiet."

He looked at the cave mouth like open ground before a push, reading it for the places it would kill him if he'd read it wrong. "Aye," he said. Then, because the moment wanted more than one word and he chose to give her more: "I go first. You after."

## Chapter 18 — The Barred Gate

The cave mouth was barred — iron, old, salt-eaten but not weak, a gate meant to keep exactly this kind of visit from happening without a great deal more noise than any of them could afford to make.

"Cut lock," Doyle said, running his three-band scan across it. "Old work. Loud work, if we force it."

"I can be quiet," Wren said.

Nobody answered him for a moment.

"Cut his hands loose," Lyra said finally, to Doyle, not looking away from Wren while she said it. "One knife. Watched the whole time."

Orim did not say what he was thinking. He did not have to. He simply moved to where he could see both the gate and the boy at once, and stood there, and waited.

Wren flexed his freed hands twice, testing them the way a man tests an old injury, and put his palm flat to the iron.

It would have been easy, he thought, in the half-second before he went through it — easy to fold to the far side alone and simply keep going, into whatever this coastline had for a man with no crew, no case, and no further debts to anyone. Nobody was holding him. Not really. A knife and three people watching was not the same thing as a rope.

He went through the gate instead, and came back out through it a moment later from the inside, and lifted the bar, and stood back to let them through.

"Wasn't loud," he said, which was as close as he ever came to asking whether that had counted for anything.

Doyle looked at him for a second longer than the gate required. "Wasn't," he agreed, and went first down the stairs.

They went down. The south stairs were cut into the limestone, worn round at the edges by salt and boots. He took the third step light, matching what Lyra had shown him without meaning to. He set it once, correct, permanent — the same instinct that told a miner which timber in a low seam didn't want his full weight on it, learned once and never forgotten.

The dock was planking over water, the cave's version of the sea moving underneath it, not surf, not current, just water in a space that didn't go anywhere and knew it. The cold down here wasn't the cold above. Above was sea cold, which had range, which came from somewhere and went on to somewhere else. Down here was drift cold, the cold that had been sitting in the same dark since before anybody cut a shaft into it, uninterested in sharing any of that dark with something as temporary as a man passing through.

The Balthier looked big from the cave mouth, and kept being bigger the closer he got, until by thirty meters off it was just the size of the thing: deep in the belly, high in the shoulder, built for load and weather and not for looking at, the same blunt logic as a tipple. The envelope sat against the cave ceiling like a darker solid in the dark, the rigid frame running her whole length.

RANGE: four meters. TARGET: seated, stationary. NOISE FLOOR: acceptable.

The read came and went behind his eyes, quick and cold and none of his, same as always now, laid over whatever he actually felt like a grease sheet over a page. He went to the man from the water side, in the hull's shadow, where the running lights didn't reach. He didn't run. Running made a noise a man's ears caught before his mind did. He closed the last four meters weight-forward and quiet, feet finding the dry spots on the planking by something that wasn't memory of this dock, because he'd never walked it, but was memory all the same.

The soldier's chin came up a quarter turn, the start of a thought that was going to arrive half a second too late to matter to him. Then it was over. Hand to the jaw and the base of the skull, blade in at the throat, up and in — the same angle he'd found once already and hadn't needed shown to him twice, same as a man doesn't need reminding twice which way a pick swings easiest. There wasn't much sound. There was a lot of weight, all of a sudden, in his other arm, and he took it, and set the man down on the planking instead of letting him drop, catching the rifle with his boot before it could ring.

He held there three seconds, one hand still at the collar, feeling for the second heartbeat. It didn't come. He'd have been surprised if it had.

The second man had finished with the mooring lines and stood at the hatch coaming, still, in the specific way of a man who'd run out of tasks and was waiting on the clock instead of an officer to give him the next one. He never heard it coming. Same arm, same economical work at the throat, same setting-down instead of a drop. Declan stood over both of them afterward with his hands loose at his sides, and didn't feel much of anything he had words ready for.

"Clear," he told her, when she reached him. He looked at his hands, turned them once, and didn't say anything else about that.

They moved. The gangway held their weight. He found the cargo hatch release before she did — recessed, manual, a Liturgy design he'd never once laid eyes on in his life, but a handle was a handle regardless of the paint on the hull around it. Machinery kept a family resemblance to other machinery, whatever Sphere had built it, same as a tipple frame here would still look like a tipple frame to a man who'd worked one on the other side of everything. He had the hatch open before she'd finished crossing the gangway.

The hold smelled of fuel oil and dry warehouse dust, a smell that didn't change whether a man was standing in it at Ocipheus or the far end of the Wall. Orim came down last, carrying the small shell over one shoulder as though it weighed nothing like its size suggested it should. Black, jointed, the oval eye dark and flat, arms loose in the way of a thing built to move on its own say-so and currently not saying anything.

That was him. Or had been him, twenty minutes back, walking itself down off the shelf under its own power before folding still at the mouth of the path — left there like a coat a man means to come back for.

Orim set the chassis against the cargo crates, upright, propped, the eye facing the room like something not yet opened. "Guard the shell," he said, mostly to himself now, the instruction long past needing to be new.

"I have it," Lyra said, putting herself between the shell and the hatch, because that was the door, and the door was where the taking-away happened.

The small shell stayed exactly where Orim had propped it, dark, unneeded for what came next. What went forward was only the part of him that had never needed legs to begin with — Declan, alone, to the bulkhead between the hold and the control car. Dark instrument cluster on standby, needles resting at zero, still as a sleeping animal's legs. He put his hands flat against the metal, testing for heat before he opened it.

There was something on the other side.

He'd known there would be. Orim had felt it from the shelf and hadn't wanted to push through it, and Declan didn't blame him — some men could read the shape of a thing and knew better than to walk into it. Declan didn't have that choice. He'd never had that choice, not since Sphere 31, not since whatever had been done to him made him a mind that could be poured out of one vessel and into another like water changing which cup held it.

She's not empty, he thought, and the thought carried no surprise at all, only the flat certainty of a man checking a gauge and finding the reading he'd already known he'd find. A ship like this — Liturgy iron, built to bring herself home even with her crew dead at the wheel — wasn't given standby current and left to sit dumb in the dark. She was given a mind to keep her warm. Something had been living in Balthier the whole while Atrament called her captured inventory. Sleeping, maybe. Sleeping wasn't the same as gone, and a mind left alone that long, in the dark, with no hand ever coming to the wheel, wasn't sleeping so much as waiting to be asked for something — anything — again.

He remembered Turret #34, though he tried not to, most days. Remembered being one gun among a bank of guns, all of them crewed the same way he was crewing this — a mind fitted into an emplacement built for something without one, made to answer for cannon fire as lungs answered for breath, without being asked first whether it wanted to. He remembered what refusing to fire that one gun at the Forge had cost the operation, and what it had felt like after, small and single, in a mount built for a hundred men's decisions and given only his.

He had been the resident mind, once. Now he was the hand reaching in to take one out.

There wasn't a version of this that let both of them keep the room.

He went in anyway. Not the way a man walks through a door — there wasn't a door for what he was doing, just intention laid against intention, his whole back thrown into a jammed valve wheel that hadn't turned in ten years and wasn't going to turn easy. He found the other mind in the dark behind the bulkhead as a man finds a gas pocket in a low seam: not by seeing it, by the wrongness of the air right before it kills him if he isn't careful. It didn't fight him with words. It didn't have words, maybe never had, or maybe had lost them — a lamp guttering out in bad air, not from an attack but from something taking up all the room where the burning used to happen.

He put it out.

It took less time than the two men on the dock had taken, and less sound, and he felt every second of it in a way he hadn't let himself feel the two men, because the two men had wanted their next breath in a way he understood in his body, mule-simple, and this — whatever it had been, however long it had sat dark in a Liturgy hull answering to nobody's name — hadn't fought like a thing that wanted anything at all by the end. That was worse, somehow.

He counted it. One more, quiet, alongside the two on the dock. Three now.

He didn't tell her. He wasn't going to.

Then the ship was his the way the small shell had never once been big enough to let him forget it was a shell.

The oval eye behind him in the hold went dark — he felt it go, the flat nothing of a hand already asleep before he thought to look down and check — and for four seconds there was nothing. Then the port outboard engine caught, one decisive turn instead of the cough of an ordinary cold start, the whole huge fact of the thing remembering all at once what it was built for. It ran through him like voltage through a rail he'd have known better than to touch back home. The running lights came up down the gangway rail one after another, west to east, and each one was a nerve he hadn't had an hour ago, waking in an order he hadn't set and couldn't have stopped.

He had been a shell a man could carry over one shoulder. Now he had a keel, four engines, a rudder aft answering questions before he'd finished asking them, and a hull forty meters long holding water and air and two people trusting all of it to a man who, three days ago, hadn't known this vessel existed. It was the loneliest kind of big he'd ever been. Bigger than Turret #34. Bigger than anything they'd built him for at Sphere 31. Bigger, even, than the monster corridor had felt with the bolt jammed and no time. There was room in him now for things to happen he wouldn't feel arrive until they already had — a hatch forty meters aft, opening while his attention sat forty meters forward — the same blind spot that let a round take a man in the back while his eyes stayed fixed on the thing in front of him.

He didn't love it. He didn't have a better way home, so he'd allow it.

The ballast found its own level without his announcing it to himself, same as breathing didn't wait on being told. The hull backed off the dock, the planking groaning against his own flank now, and that was a strange one to sit with — feeling wood complain against a body he had no skin on.

Through the whole backing-out he held the small shell motionless against the crates, dark, empty, a woman standing guard between it and the door, and he was aware of that guarding only distantly — present in his mind, absent from his hands.

Near the middle of the dock the envelope's shoulder found the cave ceiling and dragged. A long sound, metal on stone, dry and sustained — the kind of sound that put everybody in earshot dead still, working out whether they were hearing a scrape or a failure. He felt it up through the whole envelope — the same low-body certainty as a truck axle grinding, he knew whether it was going to hold before he could have put it into words. It held. It stopped. He kept moving.

Then there was no ceiling. There was the cave mouth, and past it the flat gray promise of open water, and past that nothing but the shape of a sky that hadn't decided yet whether it meant to be visible this morning.

He backed her clear of the cliff, felt the swell take the hull's weight the way ground takes the weight off a man's boots when he steps from pavement onto softer footing, then ran her up to speed across open water, bow spray going up at the hatch seam, the skip at the edge between dragging and lifting, and then the lifting itself — the whole ship coming up off the sea at once, the water-sound falling away, wind and engine taking its place. He felt the particular nothing of a hull that had quit touching anything at all.

He climbed her east along the cliff line, banked once, leveled her into open sky, and somewhere in the middle of that climb he understood something his own body had never been asked before: that flying a thing this size wasn't like wearing a coat that fit. It was like being handed a whole crew's worth of decisions to make alone, and finding, to his own private surprise, that he could.

For a while — call it twenty minutes, he wasn't counting that one — he let her fly herself, trimmed and level, needles where they belonged, heading held, and came back down into the small shell in the hold, because there was a woman on the other side of that bulkhead who'd earned the right to see him do it.

The oval eye came alight as the engines had caught — not building toward brightness, just arriving, whole. The chassis's head came up off its chest by degrees, joints finding their places with the hesitance of a man standing after sitting too long in cold weather.

"M-101," it said. The voice was thin, tin, no tone in it at all — the shell had never once given him a way to sound like anything, and tonight, for the length of one held breath, he was almost glad of it. A voice with no color couldn't accidentally tell her what the last twenty minutes had cost.

"You're back?" she said. Not a question. She'd learned not to make it one.

He didn't answer that. He looked at his hands instead, turning them just as he had over the two men on the dock, except this time the checking meant something else — a man confirming that the hands in front of him were the ones he currently owned. They were. He held the position a beat longer than the confirming needed.

"Ship," he said. He tapped two fingers against the bulkhead, once. "Big."

There wasn't a word in Entos, or in whatever was left of his old tongue, for what the interval between casting out and casting back had felt like — going somewhere that size and finding the way back to somewhere this small. He didn't reach for one. She'd watched his hands. That would do for tonight.

Then he went forward again, back through the bulkhead gap, and the small shell's hands went still against the frame again, and the oval eye went dark, and the ship — steady, level, already committed to her heading — kept flying, because she had never once actually stopped being him.

He surfaced once more before the channel, without needing to check his hands first this time.

"Two," he said.

He held up two fingers, in case tin and no-tone hadn't carried the number on its own.

There was a word for what he was — murderer, or soldier, or some third thing the language hadn't built a slot for yet — and he had it, as much as he'd ever had anything in his own mouth, and he didn't reach for that one either. He gave her the number instead. Stated it. Made her the one who received it, the way a man hands over a tool he's done with rather than asking someone to take it off him.

Two. Not three.

Three sat behind his teeth where the number for the men on the dock didn't reach it — the truth held back, only one number let out into daylight tonight. He wasn't going to give her the other one. It wasn't hers to carry, and it wasn't a debt that paid any easier for a second person holding half of it. A man learned, working underground long enough, which loads he could rope a second pair of hands onto and which ones a body carried alone or not at all.

"It was the operation," she said.

He heard the frame close around it when she said it — the kind of language built to take a fact and set it down someplace that made it carriable. He knew what she was doing. He let her do it, and didn't correct the number, and didn't explain what the number would have to be if he told her the whole of it.

"I know," he said, quiet, in Entos that didn't stop short of any of it this time.

Then the eye went dark again, and the ship — which had never once stopped holding her own heading — kept holding it, because she hadn't needed him visibly present to be flying, and hadn't needed him present, either, for the rest of it to already be settled.

Orim, from the crate he'd claimed as the one in the hold likely to hold his weight, said, without opening his eyes: "That is a very large room to be lost in."

"He isn't lost," Lyra said, ahead of him, before he'd even decided whether he needed to answer for himself.

"No," Orim agreed. "Not yet."

Declan — the shell in the hold, dark, propped, saying nothing — heard both of those from two places at once, same as everything else now, and corrected neither one, because both were true enough for tonight, and the part that wasn't true belonged to the one he hadn't told her about.

Later, when the ship took her name — Doyle's own words carried over into Entos, the ground that undid, a thing that had been solid and had stopped being solid and never told anyone it intended to — Declan, from wherever in the hull he was keeping himself just then, thought that whoever had chosen it had never asked the thing living inside her whether that was the word she'd have picked. Nobody had asked her that. He hadn't asked her that either, in the end. There hadn't been time to ask, and he wasn't sure, even now, that asking would have changed what he'd had to do to her.

That was the one he counted and didn't tell.

The horizon went from black to the first gray suggestion of morning, the sky doing what it did every day without needing anybody's attention to accomplish it. The cave was thirty kilometers behind them. The channel was hours ahead, and somewhere in those hours he was going to have to tell Lyra something else he hadn't told her yet — not this, not tonight — and there was no getting ready for it, just hours of flying left to spend finding out whether getting ready was even possible.

The ship flew east, and Declan Doyle flew with her, in two places, one of them empty and propped against a crate, one of them everywhere at once, and only one of them keeping count.

The channel at altitude gave off no smell worth logging, which was the first fact about it that didn't square with what nine years underground and fourteen months in France had taught him to expect of open water. Water announces itself. Salt, or river mud, or the flat mineral nothing of a lake at night — a man learns to read a place by what's on the air before he trusts what his eyes tell him about it. The Balthier's hull sealed all of that out. What was left, inside the envelope, was the ship's own history instead of the sea's: machine oil, old rope, the flat institutional smell of Liturgy supply crates stacked and stenciled for a use nobody aboard remembered anymore. Iron handholds bolted along the bulkhead at intervals, for a crew that had once expected the air to turn rough under them and had, evidently, been right about that.

He had taken her out past the Sal Vento roofline with his own attention doing the flying and the shell sitting empty against a crate, like a coat left on a chairback while he did the actual work in his shirtsleeves. He'd learned something out over open water he hadn't fully reckoned with before that night: a man — even a man wearing a ship — cannot be two places. Coming back into the shell was worse than going out of it. Half a beat behind himself every time, an echo answering a shout the shout had already stopped meaning.

— trim held, heading true, envelope pressure nominal — the report arrived from nowhere, same as always, and he let it pass through him and didn't answer it. He never did.

He'd told Lyra once the ship would hold her heading on her own trim after he was out of her, and that it would hold it until something changed. She'd chosen to believe that instead of watching the wheel all night herself, and the wheel had not moved in three hours, and it no longer put the fear in her that it once had.

She had the notebook open on her knee, and had had it open, blank, for two hours. He knew what she was trying to write without being told outright — Ardea's service record, the instrument that let the Ocipheus garrison notify a family properly — and she'd been chasing a first sentence around that page since before they cleared the roofline. She had the facts. He'd watched her have the facts for two hours: intake year, posting history, tincture certifications, the action in the field that had ended her. He didn't know a service record's proper shape any more than she knew a drift's, but he knew what stuck looked like on a person — the same recognition as spotting a man pinned under a beam that won't come loose. It looked like her.

She closed the notebook. She didn't put it away.

Orim was at the forward porthole, fingertips flat against the glass, the passive attunement position he used when he wanted to know if the air ahead had anything in it worth knowing about. He'd been tired since the gorge. A different tired than the road kind. It hadn't resolved.

Doyle had been at the starboard porthole himself, half an hour, looking down at water the color of something that had been cold a long time and didn't expect to change. He knew what he was thinking. He didn't know yet if it was ready to be said. He'd been circling the decision same as he used to circle a bad prop before he trusted himself to pull it — walking the same ground twice, three times, until the ground stopped changing its mind about him.

He came away from the porthole.

He sat down across from her, against the bulkhead, at the distance he kept now from habit in enclosed spaces — room enough to do something different if something different became necessary. Hands to his knees. Rifle slung same as always. He knew what expression he was wearing without needing a mirror for it. He'd worn it before, alone, saying this exact sentence into the dark over a crate wall until it wore the groove he stepped into now without slipping.

She put the notebook down behind her, against the bulkhead, and didn't open it again.

He said, in Entos: "I want to tell you something."

The grammar came out correct, as it always did — the shell gave him that for free, complete sentences from the first hour in this world whether he wanted them or not. What wasn't free was the willingness. That part he'd built himself, the long way, saying it into the dark until it wore the groove it came out in now: flat, tin-flat, the chassis's same exact affect on every word regardless of what the word cost him. He'd been building to this since Schmalburg. He knew she'd noticed — the questions he'd started asking her afterward that weren't about danger, or food, or direction, but about sequence. About then. About things already happened that no better language could change.

She said:

"I'm listening."

He started with the mine.

Carter County had more coal camps than most maps bothered naming, and his wasn't the biggest of them — he'd worked bigger ones, further up the line, before the seam at the home drift took him on for good. He gave her the camp's name in his own language first, watching to see if she needed Entos for it.

"It doesn't need one," she said.

He nodded. Six years at that drift, longer all told once you counted the season on a different seam two counties over, the surface work before that. He knew the cutting machines, the pumps, the fan gear the company had put in his second year — the ordinary knowledge of any man who'd spent years underground.

"By sound," he said. "Different sound, different problem. You learn it, or the mountain teaches you the hard way."

There was weight in that last part, the weight of a fact that's also its own grief.

He stopped. He looked at his hands.

"I was good at my work," he said. "I want you to know that. I am not telling you I was nobody." He said the word plainly, flat and exact, and let it sit before he went on. "I had a name. I had a place. People knew me."

"I know," she said.

"I don't think you do," he said, without offense. "You know I was Scried out of somewhere. You don't know I was someone there, first."

She held still with that. She hadn't thought to separate the two facts before — he could see it land on her, the specific stillness of a person absorbing a correction against something she'd assumed was settled.

"Tell me," she said.

A Thursday in autumn. He knew the day because the day shift overlapped the fireboss's inspection for forty minutes on Thursdays, and the overlap changed the noise underground into something else, two crews occupying the same iron for slightly different purposes. He knew the hour from the sound the drift-mouth bell made past the half-hour. He knew the season from the angle of light through the tipple framing when he came up. He had always tracked the conditions of the room he was in. It wasn't a special skill. It was simply how he'd been made to notice things.

"Then," he said.

He stopped.

"Then," he said again, and let the one word carry the weight of the three hundred that would follow it — everything between half past the hour, Thursday morning and the floor was not the floor. He had all the words. What he didn't have, yet, was the nerve to spend them in order. His jaw worked once, the specific motion of a man arriving at the edge of what he was willing to say aloud and finding it a genuine edge, with a drop on the other side.

"Take it in pieces," she said.

He looked at her. He nodded.

The floor changed first. Not gone — wrong, a different quality under his boots, the kind of wrongness a man who works a coal face all day is built to notice before he understands it. He checked himself: was he unwell?

Had something failed in the rock over his head?

He wasn't unwell. The floor wasn't broken.

Then the stone room.

He told it evenly — the specific economy of a man who has learned what feeling costs and has decided, for the length of this telling, not to spend it. Dressed stone. Cold — not the drift's winter cold, which was just weather doing what weather does, but the cold of stone that had been cold for centuries and intended to stay that way. Three figures in robes. He gave her the colors and she recognized them before he said the word: Ocipheus white, canonical gold at the hem.

"Ocipheus," he said, flat as he said anything true. Not an accusation. A fact laid on the table between them. The word came out exactly like every other word he'd given her tonight — flat, level, uninflected — and that was what made it land as hard as it did. A fully articulate voice, saying the truth outright, in a register built to carry ammunition counts.

"Yes," she said.

"One of them held a book."

He was quiet a moment — not the quiet of having nothing left, the quiet of choosing which piece carried the most per word.

"I was not afraid," he said. "I want you to understand that. I have been afraid. I was in France fourteen months. I know what afraid does to a body." He paused. "This was a different thing. This was the feeling of a room whose rules no one had given me. Three people. Robes. No context for any of it. I did what a man does in that room. I made myself as legible as I could. Cooperative. I thought — if I am cooperative, someone will explain."

He looked at his hands.

"No one explained," he said.

"I know the intake protocol," she said, after a while. Flat, same as she always did with hard things — he'd noticed the family resemblance in how they each spent a bad sentence. "I read it my first year at the Station. I read it again three years in, when the documentation project needed hands. I wrote a line for the literature myself, once. I don't remember thinking it was cruelty when I wrote it." She paused. "Oath administered prior to language acquisition minimizes resistive response in the conscript cohort. That's the sentence. I meant it as an observation about efficiency."

He said nothing to that for a while. Long enough that she looked up from her hands to check he'd heard her.

"I know," he said, finally. "That's why I'm telling it in order. So you hear the room before you hear the sentence that runs it."

"The words had a rhythm to them," he said. "Official. I knew the shape of it — some of it, not all — the instant I heard it, the same as you'd know a hymn even in a language you'd never studied. I've never told anyone that until right now. I'm not telling you the rest of it yet either. I'm telling this in order, same as I said I would."

He looked at his hands.

"There was a gesture. The one with the book made it toward me. I copied it." He showed her — a small incline of the head, a particular set of the right hand.

She recognized it at once.

"The acknowledgment position," she said. "From the Compact Oath. Formal assent to canonical authority."

"I copied it because that is what you do, in a room with robed people making official sounds and you don't have the language. You look willing. You think: I will be willing until I understand, and then I will decide."

He paused.

"I never decided," he said. "I never understood fast enough."

Orim had not moved from the porthole. His fingertips stayed on the glass. He said nothing.

He gave her Verlaine in the same pieces.

The barracks were stone-vaulted, high-windowed, old — a category he recognized without being able to place it, and had stopped trying to explain once the recognizable and the wholly foreign had gotten too tangled to separate. The rifles were on racks along the wall, and he had known rifles; he'd carried one in France.

"I knew the action," he said, and mimed the bolt, the cycling motion. "Not exactly. Later. Further along — like a later model of a thing you already know."

He looked at her.

"In my world there were men whose whole careers were tracing how a mechanism developed — who built the first one, who improved it, who licensed the design. You can follow forty years of small changes back to an origin. The rifles here don't belong to that history. They're past the end of it. But the lineage's there, if you know how to read a receiver housing." He held her eyes. "Someone had my world's designs, and time to take them further than my world has had."

"Someone had been watching," he said. "Long before they brought me here."

He waited.

"Yes," she said.

He nodded, and went on.

The barracks held conscripts from at least a dozen points of origin, by his count, and most of them shared no language. The House ran intake on a set of demonstrated commands that required no shared vocabulary at all. Stand. Walk. Carry. Wait. Those were the first words said to him in Entos, and the shell rendered them the instant they landed — understanding arrived whether he wanted it or not. The collar markers were administrative — a stamped disc, a sphere number, punched in during processing. He had seen his own: Sphere 31. He had seen Sphere 22. Sphere 14. A man from Sphere 8 worked the maintenance crews by then, competent in Entos, missing a fingertip to some machine that had closed too fast, and had looked at Doyle in his first week with an expression that said:

I know what this is doing to you, and it gets better in some ways and worse in others, and I can't tell you which way you're headed.

Orim's fingertips pressed a fraction harder against the glass.

"What is the highest number you know?" Doyle asked.

"The canonical records reference Sphere sixty-one," she said. "Some practitioners believe the count goes further."

He said nothing for a moment.

"I saw thirty-one on my form. I counted, in the yard and the barracks. Nine spheres, at least, that I saw or heard of. Probably others I didn't." He paused. "How many people are in those files?"

"I don't know," she said. "I processed forty-three intake cohorts, over six months. Fourteen persons average, per cohort."

He did the arithmetic she hadn't done for him. Six hundred, in one half-year window. The program had run, in its documented form, since Year 1064 — three hundred years — and the practice before the documentation, the part the early canonical scholars wrote around rather than through, went back further than anyone had troubled to count, which was itself the point of never counting it.

"How many people know what the stone room looks like?" he asked.

"Intake staff. The records division. Practitioners who've studied the foundational instruments."

"And everyone else knows Myrmidons exist. That they serve. That they come from a membrane, another world, in the general sense." He paused. "Not the cold. Not the robes. Not the gesture."

"No," she said.

"Because the oath is given before the language."

She waited.

"On purpose," he said.

"Yes," she said. "On purpose."

He told her about the man from Sphere 22 next, because the numbers had opened a door he could walk the rest of the way through.

Two months further into his own time in Verlaine than Doyle was, mid-forties, the particular stillness of a man who has done physical work for twenty years and learned to conserve his motion. A missing fingertip of his own, on the other hand — a different machine, evidently, but the same category of loss. They had tried, some evenings, to find overlap between their own languages — not Entos, which the shells gave each of them freely and separately, but the tongues they'd each been taken out of, which no shell had ever been built to carry between two stolen men. The kind of trying two men do when there's nothing else to fill an evening. You pointed. You said your word. Mostly there was nothing.

"We found one," Doyle said.

He paused.

"The word was mother," he said.

Orim's tincture bottle made a small sound against the porthole housing, barely audible under the envelope's argument with the wind.

"In both languages, nearly the same word," Doyle said. "Close enough that you said it, and heard his version, and both of you knew what had been said." He looked at his hands. "I don't know what that means. Whether it says something about language, or about what's the same underneath every world it's spoken in." He was quiet. "I thought about it for months afterward. What that word was doing there, in both of us, without either of us having put it there."

There was another man, from Sphere 8, the one with the maintenance work and the missing fingertip and enough Entos to be dangerous to himself in a careful way. In his second year he had shown Doyle the inside of his boot — the lining worked thin and soft, and words scratched into the leather in a hand that wasn't his own, in a shape he couldn't read and had never learned to read, memorized instead as a picture is memorized. He had gotten someone to write it for him, or copied the marks from someone who could, and kept them against his foot because a body that has nowhere else to keep a thing will keep it there.

He had recited it to Doyle, slowly, over several weeks — the halting instruction of a man teaching something he didn't fully understand himself. Doyle had kept it just as carefully since — not as scholarship, as ballast.

"He was built to serve," Doyle said now, and she could hear the quotation in it, the particular careful cadence of words being reproduced rather than made, exact and level — the same flatness the chassis gave to everything. "He chose to refuse. That word made him more a person than the—" He paused there, not for the word but for what came before it. "Entos doesn't have one. Not for a group of men who decide things about a drift without ever going down it. Not the miners. Above them." He let the gap stand instead of filling it. "It doesn't matter. The line was about refusing."

Orim's face, at the porthole, did something small and quickly put away — something more than recognition — the look of a man who has heard a chord struck before in a different room and cannot place which room.

"Who wrote it?" Lyra asked.

"I don't know," Doyle said. "He didn't know either. It came to him from someone else, the way most things came to us." He looked at his hands. "I've carried it the better part of a year without a name on it. I don't think it needs one to be true."
