Orim came to sit beside her at the cargo hatch in the third hour, having spent the crossing on the forward deck doing the thing he did when he was thinking — looking at nothing in particular with forty years of practice at finding something there.

"You're counting the flags," he said.

"Fourteen since Pontis."

"There's a cluster at the Archival Gate. That's the border town — historically significant, three posts, they all flag independently." He looked at the passing bank. "Named for Arnault d'Archival, who crossed this river in Year 545 in pursuit of a Calyx raiding party, planted his House mark on the far bank, and declared the river the border. The Calyx disagreed. The river disagreed the following spring by flooding and moving the bank fifteen meters. D'Archival's mark is now on the wrong side of the water it was meant to define. Verlaine still charges crossing tolls off his original notation of where the mark stood. The mark is underwater. The notation remains."

She had known the Accord. She had not known d'Archival. "You've been on this river before."

"Four times. Three verification contracts and once in my own interest." He glanced at her. "This is a country that takes its record-keeping seriously. The record matters here more than the fact. Bear that in mind."

"What are they watching for?" she asked, "if not us specifically?"

"Whether we are who the documents say we are. The documents say we are a Compact pursuit under Ocipheus authority. The documents are correct." He said it in the tone of a man willing to guess a thing before anyone had confirmed it for him, the way he guessed most things. "What isn't in the documents, if I had to wager, is that the hand that filed this still holds the pen. An instrument this clean, arriving this fast — someone wanted your pursuit stopped without ever having to say so to your face. I'd sooner assume the ground under it has already shifted, and be wrong, than assume it hasn't and be right too late to use it." He nodded, once, and went back to looking at nothing.

She remained at the hatch and watched Verlaine document her passage through its territory without her permission, which she had entered without Verlaine's permission, which seemed, on the whole, fair.

Bressant arrived in the early afternoon — a dense city, accumulated around a function, here the grain warehouse district handling Verlaine's upriver agricultural output. Buildings pressed together against the hillside behind it, leaving the landing frontage wide and practical. The Veil ran sixty meters across here, swift and dark with autumn rain-depth.

The Bressant landing's flag was red.

Two border soldiers waited at the landing approach — young, formal, doing this correctly because they knew it would be examined later. She showed the sealed authority. They logged her in with the precision of people who intended to do it right if it took all day.

"You have approximately forty minutes," the senior of the two said, "before interior command can coordinate a formal review response." He said it with the particular care of a man giving her everything he was authorized to give and nothing more.

"Thank you," she said.

The courier came off the barge and went to active protocol. She had forty minutes.

The route into the warehouse district ran her past the cathedral, and the route past the cathedral ran her past the intake station.

It occupied what had once been a canonical administrative annex — stone-walled, high-windowed, the vaulted ceiling the Liturgy favored for functional space set beside ecclesiastical authority, clerestory light falling onto a work floor that whoever repurposed it for Verlaine's conscription operations had not bothered to redesign. They had simply put trestle tables under the arches and begun filing.

She rode past slowly enough to see through the open door.

A Verlaine intake officer sat at the central table with a ledger and an ink register, working a stack of documents with the unhurried efficiency of someone three weeks into the same task. Beside the ledger, a stamp for the designation block — the M-prefix and intake serial, applied to every conscript document the instant the notation was complete. Beside the stamp, three completed files in a wooden box, corners aligned, waiting for a clerk to carry them to the garrison archive.

Three people had been through that table this morning.

Against the left wall, a rack: five bolt-action rifles, clean and maintained. A sixth space, empty — the sixth rifle presumably on the officer's back, or in the anteroom. Same manufacture as the checkpoint guards' equipment. She kept riding.

She could not read the files in the box from the road. She did not need to. She had handled enough Compact liaison paper to know the stock and the fold — Verlaine military intake, standard format — and she had known, administratively, what that format meant since she was twenty-two: the year she first met the phrase M-intake authorization, Sphere-origin conscript, Year-stamp in a coordination brief and understood it, correctly, as terminology. The form designation was what she had encountered for seventeen years. The three files in the wooden box were what the form designation meant. She did not examine the distance between those two facts. Forty minutes had no room for it. Neither had seventeen years.

The cathedral's north face rose to her left, Verlaine's canonical structure built for throughput where Ocipheus's was built for vigil — records entered and exited, people processed, the high windows sized for reading documents correctly rather than for sitting with them for seventeen years.

She found the road that ran along the grain district's south face and took it.

The southern approach was a narrow passage between two storage buildings, stone-floored, sheltered from the wind. She walked it slowly.

Three sets of boot-prints in the settled grit along the wall, dated by layer depth — the deepest three or four days old, overlaid by two days of weather. All three had been here three days back. The most recent layer showed two sets. The third was gone.

The third print was lighter than the other two: narrower heel, longer toe-box. Not Entos-standard equipment.

Two had continued north without pausing. The third had stayed behind — for hours at least, by the layering. She checked the direction of the remaining pair. North. The river barges running north out of Bressant served the Atrament rail junction at the border. She already knew where that led.

One of the three who had taken the Relic had spent hours here that the other two had not. She set it aside and kept moving, because the more useful question now was whether the third had gone on after them, or had stayed.

The lighter prints in the passage oriented toward the entrance — not a departure posture, weight forward, toward the opening, the angle of someone watching for arrivals rather than preparing to leave. Someone had waited here for hours. The most recent trace showed they had not yet walked away.

She checked her time. Twenty minutes.

The main warehouse access ran along the district's north side — loading bays, freight doors, the formal commercial entrance. She didn't use it. She went around to the service door on the east face, the one the loading crews used and the supervisors didn't watch in the middle of the day, because the middle of the day was when the loading crews were outside working the barge transfers.

Inside: the smell of grain, warm and dusty, the particular smell of a great deal of dry material in an enclosed space — and under it, faint enough that she nearly dismissed it, a thread of something mineral that had no business being in a grain warehouse at all. The floor ran in sections, sealed bins in long rows under the main span, a smaller room at the back for the premium contract lots. She moved through without hurrying, reading the bins as she passed. Standard rope seals, the kind the Bressant archive system required. All intact.

She reached the fourth row.

On the third bin from the left wall, the rope seal was broken — not cut. Worked loose from the peg, carefully, the kind of careful that took time and left the rope itself intact enough to be pushed back into approximate position. It would have read as sealed to anyone who wasn't examining every seal in the room. She had been.

She stood in front of the bin. She had had forty minutes when she entered the district. She had fifteen now.

She put her hand on the latch.

The copy desk faced north — a smaller room than the one she'd worked for most of the last three years, and she had been moved into it the same week the transit suspension crossed her desk, without anyone troubling to call it a demotion or asking whether she'd noticed that it was one. She had asked, in her first week here, whether the window's direction was a choice someone had made or merely a thing that had been allowed to happen to the room — and gotten, in answer, the particular silence a person gives when the question has an answer nobody enjoys supplying. In winter this meant the desk faced a column of pale light off the courtyard stones, light that did nothing useful except confirm the hour. She had spent three years at various desks in Liturgy copy offices, and every one of them faced somewhere inconvenient; the canonical administration had been built for permanence and ceremony, not for the people who worked inside it — the kind of thing she thought of, privately, as *architecture, or possibly theology.* This room was a high-ceilinged box that held the cold like old stone, two windows on the north face, one door, a row of shelves built for an old filing order someone had abandoned before her posting and replaced with one she was still learning the grammar of. Six weeks since the Tuesday the suspension had crossed her desk — six weeks in which, she would only piece together much later, her sister had already crossed two Houses and lost people doing it, none of it in any instrument Vega was yet permitted to read. She had spent the first three learning the lamp angle and the second three doing it automatically, the way a person learns to walk with a bad leg: efficiently, without grace, without complaint.

Her right shoulder ached by the second hour every day. The middle knuckle on her right hand stiffened by mid-morning and had to be pressed back sharply against the joint — one click, release, done — before she could reload the nib and continue. These were not complaints. They were conditions, and she had learned the difference because a Scribe learns any distinction worth keeping: eventually someone needed her to certify it.

The instruments arrived at the third bell, as they always did. The runner — a junior canon, fourteen years old, still wearing the expression of someone who had not yet learned what the documents he carried actually said — set the stack on the corner of her desk with the particular care of a boy who'd been told the documents were important without being told what that meant. In the first weeks here he had asked, out of some trained sociable reflex, whether she required anything else.

He had stopped asking in the third week, once he understood, without being told, that the answer would always be no. She had not asked him why he'd stopped. She was fairly confident she already knew.

Six weeks was enough time to learn what a stack of instruments held just by looking at it: the weight, the binding method, and — this was the part she loved best, if *loved* was a permissible word for it — whether the lead sheet carried the Canon's own hand or a secretary's, and above that, in smaller formal letters, the fixed opening rubric every canonical instrument wore regardless of what it contained: two or three words in the Received Tongue, rendered rather than read, the way she had been taught.

She could copy the shapes exactly, stroke for stroke, without knowing what tense they stood in; she loved the sound of them, old and patterned and cold — and only a half-beat later did she catch what the rubric was actually *for:* it meant this instrument is valid, it meant do not ask further, it meant the same thing every time no matter what sat underneath it. She had never been taught to read the tongue whole. She had been taught to render it faithfully and revere the rest.

The lead sheet this morning was in the Canon's hand. She had learned, by accumulation rather than by being told, what that meant — not that some office had processed the instruments below, but that they had been reviewed, personally, at the highest level, before they ever reached her desk. The stack was heavier than yesterday's. In the first weeks of the posting she had read every instrument before she began copying; now she read them in order, one at a time, finishing each before she touched the next. Accumulation was the danger. Read everything at once and she would understand the shape of it before she had language for the shape, and the act of copying would start to feel like something other than what it was supposed to be. She set the notation sheet aside and started with the second instrument.

The Carnyx document had a different texture, and she knew it before she'd read three lines. The Loera delegate had chosen deterioration where another might have written encroachment — the difference between a process and an actor, between something that could be managed and something that had to be confronted — and the Liturgy had refused him anyway, the careful trimming not having trimmed enough. Where the Loera document had the softness of a constructed argument, the Carnyx document had the density of a report.

The border commander was not asking for anything except to have what he had observed placed in the record. He had been to the eastern sector himself. He had brought a methodology section and a set of survey maps folded into the back cover, and she had to clear the auxiliary shelf to spread them properly — the paper was good quality and resisted the crease, the kind ordered by someone who understood this document needed to still be readable in thirty years, when someone wanted to prove they had received the report and done nothing with it. She weighted the corners with the inkwell, the lamp, and the stone she kept for the purpose, and the maps covered the desk and part of the shelf besides.

The field notation was unfamiliar, a dialect of marks she had to learn on the page. She read the legend twice, then matched the annotation types against the survey points — three of them, along the observed boundary, each carrying its own measurement method and margin of error. She added the margins against the measurements, twice, out of habit rather than doubt. The margins did not account for the difference. Fifteen years of documented observation, not drift, not measurement error: three separate points confirming each other — the loveliest kind of evidence there was, the kind that didn't need her to trust anyone, only to add correctly. The Wall had moved. She measured with her thumb against the boundary line at the earlier survey date and then against the current one. On a map at this scale the distance was a thumbnail's width. She had a precise thumbnail, trained to the canon's standard line width, and what it told her was not the same thing as a small distance.

She had located, in the standards register, the authority the counter-brief would cite:

*Assessment Protocol for Membrane Boundary Variation, Revision Four, Article Twelve, Year 1332 revision: A boundary variation falling within one standard deviation of the fifty-year mean, as calculated by the Liturgy's approved archive methodology, constitutes acceptable variation. Observation is required. Response is at the Canon's discretion.*

Above the vernacular title, in the smaller hand reserved for it, sat the same fixed Received Tongue formula she'd been rendering all morning — she knew its shape now the way she knew her own signature — and she recognized, with a dry flicker of pleasure, that it was the identical opening rubric that had sat atop the Loera instrument an hour before. Two documents, two petitioners, one recurring garment. She set the observation aside, unsure yet what to make of it.

The commander had measured fifteen years. The Protocol required a fifty-year mean. Its standard deviation, by the Liturgy's own methodology, absorbed fifteen years of change without approaching the threshold. This was not an error in the Protocol. It was what the Protocol had been built to do.

At the end of the data block the commander had added a rate projection: *high-uncertainty, extrapolated from 15-year sample.* If the observed rate held, the boundary would reach the first civilian settlement outside the exclusion zone in approximately forty years. He had put it there knowing it would be read by a Scribe before it reached anyone with the standing to act. He had done what he could, which was to get it into the record, because the record was where things went to matter or be buried.

She was twenty-four. In forty years she would be sixty-four, if she lived, which she probably would, and the settlement outside the eastern exclusion zone would be inside it. She looked at the number for a long time before she began copying.

She copied it accurately and folded the maps carefully — along the existing creases, not new ones — and held them a moment before she put them in the review sleeve. The survey points. The margin of error at each. The specific weight of *high-uncertainty* written by a man who understood exactly how certain he was. She sealed the sleeve and set it on the transfer stack.

The counter-brief arrived while she was finishing. The runner set it on the corner of the desk and was gone before she could look up; she heard the door click behind him. She had not heard him come in. She finished the last line of the Carnyx copy, set it to dry, and picked up the counter-brief.

Three paragraphs. The Canon's characteristic cadence — institutional and polished, nothing citable against him in a subsequent review, every sentence defensible alone. The Loera sector conditions fell within acceptable variation; sector commanders were reminded that local observational data should be interpreted against the long-term baseline record, which was the Liturgy's to maintain. The eastern sector's survey methodology was noted as non-standard, and its findings would require reconciliation with the Liturgy's established baseline before any action threshold could be assessed. The Canon did not say what the action thresholds were. She had not seen them specified in any instrument she had copied in six weeks.

The final line sat by itself, in the disposition field, under its own small closing rubric: the same fixed shape she had begun to know the sound of without being able to say what it meant, the one that always sat over a refusal the way a wax seal sits over a letter — not the message, just the thing that makes the message official. Beneath it, in the vernacular hand every Scribe was drilled to render without hesitation:

*No action indicated at this time.*

She had been writing this line for three years. She had written it for sector correspondence and maintenance requests and inter-House petitions and resource-allocation appeals and land-dispute referrals and medical-supply authorizations from the Wall rotation posts. She had written it for garrison-strength reviews and water-quality reports and census tabulations from the outer zones. She had loved the phrase once, a little — four words, the same rubric standing guard over them every time, tidy as a closed gate. It had taken her three years and one morning with a commander's survey maps to notice that the gate was always closed, that the rubric never varied with what stood behind it, that *no action indicated* was not a judgment reached but a shape reused — the same garment on every refusal, cut once, worn a thousand times. She did not know what the words underneath had originally meant. She was no longer sure that mattered as much as what they had been made to do.

She applied the notation to both the Loera and Carnyx instruments. She folded the counter-brief and added it to the Loera file, and set the sealed sleeve on the transfer stack. It would go to the archive at the end of the day, catalogued under *Review Deferred: Sector Correspondence,* filed between a supply reassessment and a quarterly water-usage report from the eastern garrison. Nobody would look at it again until someone needed to prove they had read it. That was what it would be for.

The stack was higher than yesterday's. Tomorrow it would be higher than today's.

## The WC-Eirene Units

An asset write-off crossed her desk an hour before the WC-Eirene units came through the courtyard — routine registration, the ink still fresh, the kind of instrument she processed by the dozen without once looking past the rubric to what it retired. NORTHERN ROUTE RECONNAISSANCE — HULL DESIGNATION BALTHIER, OCIPHEUS STATION COMMISSION. STATUS: ADMINISTRATIVE LOSS, FLIGHT RECORD TERMINATED. No board of inquiry cited. No recovered wreckage logged, no crew accounted for, no successor hull requisitioned to replace her on the roster she'd been struck from. A ship simply stopped, on a Tuesday six years past, and nobody since had asked why loudly enough for the asking to reach a page.

She had learned, six weeks into watching one suspended transit authority hide behind eleven pages of unrelated adjustments, what an instrument that answered no questions was usually built to prevent. She copied the write-off anyway — that was the job, not the judgment — and set it in the outgoing stack, and did not write down the thought that followed it: that a vessel logged this cleanly missing had not necessarily gone down anywhere at all.

The WC-Eirene units came through the courtyard in the middle of the afternoon.

She had moved to the window to stretch her hand — the middle knuckle had stiffened again, earlier than usual — when she heard them before she saw them: iron in deliberate motion on stone, a low consistent percussion, lower than the Heloths on the city roads and slower and in a different register altogether. The gait of something heavier. Something not built for speed.

The first unit came through the gate, and she counted as the rest followed. Twelve. Taller than a tall man, iron housings built wide and low at the shoulder for impact absorption rather than deflection, the tracking assembly that served as a head set lower than a man's head and canted slightly forward, rotating through the slow deliberate arc she recognized from the evaluation summaries: *active acquisition, registering the space around it* — she had rendered that phrase in a dozen instruments and only now, watching the arc happen in the actual stones, did she hear what a strange, bloodless way it was to describe a machine deciding what in a room might need to die. The handlers walked alongside rather than ahead — she had filed enough summaries to know why. A handler in an active unit's forward registration field created a compliance conflict the unit resolved by following rather than being followed. Walking alongside was correct procedure. Maintenance speed — not operational pace, not inert — was correct procedure. Twelve units crossing a courtyard in file, led by handlers doing everything by the book, was not, on its own, alarming. She took it in with the same reflex she brought to instrument volume and lead-sheet weight and the Canon's cadence. She missed nothing. That was the office.

The volume had tripled in six weeks. She had filed the first evaluation summary under a provisional designation, origin notation *sphere-42*; by the third summary the provisional flag had been dropped, quietly, the way a word stops being *allegedly* and starts just being the word. She had filed seven since. She had not been tracking the increase against anything, because tracking accumulations against each other was not within her assignment.

The units turned at the loading-dock approach and moved toward the south utility wing, handlers holding their sidewalk positions through the turn. She watched until the last unit cleared the corner and the courtyard stood empty again except for the food-service cart and, at the far end, a Heloth courier idling in the shade with the stillness of a machine waiting rather than switched off.

She knew the south utility wing. She had been thirteen years old when the lock authorization for its staging hall came through the copy desk where she was doing her junior apprentice hours. A senior Scribe had handed it to her because it was a straightforward maintenance lock — an instrument that required documentation but not judgment, the appropriate kind for an apprentice still learning the judgment part. She had copied it in the hand she was still correcting then, the one that pressed too hard on the downstrokes because she had not yet learned to let the weight do the work, and had filed it and not thought about it again. The authorization specified no end date, which was unusual. She had not known then what unusual looked like. That had been eleven years ago.

The staging hall had not appeared in any instrument in six weeks.

It was not locked now.

She returned to her desk and made no annotation. The courtyard was not an instrument category she had been given to work from. She finished the maintenance authorization for the south utility wing — expanded storage calibration, lower west section, the fourth of the week, the fifth if she counted last Thursday's, which she did, because she counted everything — and added it to the stack.

She went to the registry room in the late afternoon, when the light in the main office had gone gray enough that she would need to angle the lamp again and she was tired of angling the lamp.

She had a legitimate purpose, or told herself so going in. Her sister's name had appeared in thirty-one instruments she had processed in six weeks. Each was individually within the scope of her assignment; together they mapped to an operational structure she had been copying without being given the shape of it. Understanding the structure was not intervention. Knowing what she was recording was what let her record it accurately. She was a Scribe. Accuracy was the virtue she had been certified to practice, and if that argument was doing more work than she'd asked of it, she chose, for the moment, not to notice the strain. She signed the access log with her name, the time, and *cross-reference, canonical processing* in the purpose field, and went to find the Ocipheus muster.

The Templar deployment registry was a bound volume, thick-spined, the pages dense with the specific notation of active service records — house of origin, posting date, current station, active assignment, any suspended authorities. Not House soldiers, not conscripts: the Liturgy's own field corps, the ones who had chosen the institutional mission over every other claim on them. Each entry carried a name and a rank. The Liturgy did not reduce its Templars to a number, whatever it did to its machines; it kept that distinction, formally, whatever else it failed to keep. She had filed volumes like this in her apprentice years without reading them, and the filing had taught her the structure well enough to move through it now. The room smelled of old ink and the cold that comes off stone kept deliberately cold. She found the Ocipheus section and turned the pages carefully, using the flat of her finger rather than the tip; the paper had the dryness of decades in an unheated room.

She had known the name the instant she saw it, six weeks ago, before the ink under her hand had finished drying. What she had not had — what she had come to this room to find — was the shape the name fit inside: the weight of thirty-one instruments in the same authorization chain, the structure with Ocipheus at one end and the Canon at the other and, in between, a suspended transit authority that none of the instruments she had copied troubled itself to explain. She had been carrying the name for six weeks the way a Scribe carries the shape of an instrument before she has finished reading it — present, felt, refusing to resolve into language — and she had allowed herself to keep processing accurately rather than follow the shape to wherever it led. That had been a choice. She was looking now at what the choice had produced.

She found the entry.

*Dame Lyra, Ocipheus. Templar. Current status: deployment, active. Transit authority suspended, Canon's instrument —* and the reference number she had copied and filed and cross-referenced and cited in three subsequent instruments. She had handled that number thirty-one times.

Posting date, three years prior — the same cycle in which she herself had been certified and taken her first desk. They had been in different cities since. They had written letters. Her sister had told her, every time she visited Ocipheus Station, that the station bread was not worth eating, and Vega had made not listening a habit in return.

She had been at this desk eating a roll of that same bread the morning the transit suspension arrived, six weeks ago. The runner had brought three instruments. She had read her sister's name before her hand had finished the second line of the copy, and she had put the roll down for a reason she had not let herself name at the time. The suspension was the second instrument. She processed it anyway, in under an hour, sealed the canonical original, filed it with her working copy, and moved to the third instrument, because that was the discipline.

She had known. She had copied it anyway.

She stood in the registry room a long time, long enough to notice how cold it was and how still she had gone in it, both hands gripping the spine of the volume, her right middle knuckle pressed against the binding without her having decided to press it. She released it. She did not find having known, and having copied it anyway, any more consoling than not-knowing would have been. She replaced the volume. She had made no annotations. Her name was in the access log. She returned to the office.

The instruments she had copied that day were dry. She aligned them and moved them to the transfer stack; the runner would carry them, in the morning, to the sealed archive, where they would become canonical and unalterable, the official record of what had been decided. She would not see most of them again.

She kept working copies. Every Scribe did — not canonical, not official, nothing the Liturgy needed to acknowledge, just her own hand, her own reference, in the box in the lower left drawer. It was heavier than it had been at the start of the posting.

The transit suspension from six weeks ago sat near the bottom. She found it by the texture of the page — she had pressed harder than usual that morning, the nib had been cold, the lines ran slightly heavier than her standard hand. She had not noticed at the time. She noticed now.

She set it on the desk and picked up her pen. She did not know why, exactly, except that her hands had been doing something all day — copying, measuring, folding, unsealing, resealing — and hands accustomed to doing something reach for what's nearest when the day runs out. She wrote her sister's name in the margin, in the larger hand she had used before the canonical script and the certification, the one she still used in letters: a little more room in the vowels, the first letter held a beat longer.

She wrote the name.

Then she drew a line through it.

This did not remove it. The name stayed under the line, the ink only slightly darker where the stroke crossed the letters, the letters still in the shape she had known since she was old enough to know her sister's name — because a line drawn through ink does not take away what is underneath. It only says that someone drew a line through it. She could see it. She would always be able to see it. It was, she thought, the most honest disposition notation she had entered in six weeks — the only one with no rubric standing over it.

She put the copy back in the box and closed the drawer.

Outside the window the courtyard was empty. The Heloth was gone. Whatever waited in the south utility wing's staging hall was in it now, unlocked for the first time in eleven years, delivered by handlers following correct procedure. In the morning the runner would come, and she would know something about the day's business by the weight of the stack before she read the lead sheet, because six weeks had trained the reflex, and the volume had gone on increasing at a rate she had not been tracking against anything.

The Carnyx maps were in the review sleeve, bound for a shelf between a supply reassessment and a water-usage report, filed until someone needed to prove the Liturgy had read them. In her own head the survey points stayed where she had put them: three positions along the eastern boundary, the margin of error at each, the line at both dates, the rate projection in the commander's careful field hand. *High-uncertainty, extrapolated from 15-year sample.* Forty years.

She was the record.

She had understood this in the abstract at the start of the posting, when a senior Scribe explained what canonical notarization meant: the instrument said what the instrument said, you said it again in the canonical hand, and it became true in the saying of it. That was the arrangement. That was the whole of the office.

She was understanding it differently now. There were things she had said in the canonical hand that she was carrying in her own head alongside the things she was authorized to carry, and neither set was separable from her body, and her body would go on existing after the transfer stack had been sealed into the archive and made official and unreachable. The Carnyx commander had put his projection in the record because the record was where things went to matter or be buried. She had done what she was authorized to do: copy it accurately and send it to be buried. The measurements lived in her head now, beside her sister's name under a line that had not erased it. Neither had a canonical form. The archive kept no instrument class for them, no disposition field, no rubric she'd been taught to render, no space to enter the four words she had been writing for three years.

The institution had built the arrangement with that in mind, she thought — a Scribe who would be furniture, who would render the sound of a thing without asking what it meant. It did not seem to have considered what happened when the furniture began keeping track of itself. Or it had considered this, and the arrangement was working exactly as designed — the not-knowing had always been the feature, not the flaw. A small, cold, patterned beauty, the kind she had loved the sound of for three years before she caught, this once, what it was for.

She did not know which was worse.

She angled the lamp for the last time and covered the ink.

Bressant was three things stacked on top of each other: the Veil River's low north bank, the road down from the eastern passes, and three hundred years of grain dust worked into the mud between them.

Timber and stone, raised to hold weight and shed rain and no further — the discipline of a working district, not the discipline of pride.

Cargo tags hung pole to pole between the rows, half gone soft and unreadable in the damp, and nobody had replaced them, because the carters already knew their own loads and a tag was a courtesy Bressant paid only when a patrol made it pay, and patrols came through on a schedule the district had long since memorized.

Thirty years of Verlaine mobilization had trained this ground out of asking who moved through it before dawn, and trained it well — she counted four buildings on the approach with doors that opened inward only, the mark of people who had learned that an outward-swinging door announces itself to anyone watching the street.

She held ground while Orim found his wall. North-facing, always, when he was scrying for something that had come south to north — he had stopped needing a reason for the orientation forty years before she'd met him, and she had stopped asking for one.

He took the tincture from his breast pocket, counted two fingers to three, and went still. Not more than three counts — she'd seen him pay for a fourth once, years back, a week of nausea logged against a single mistake he had never once repeated. She had stood this same watch behind him more times than she'd bothered to log, and the discipline of it — hold position, watch the street, say nothing until he surfaced — was one of the few things about him she had never needed teaching twice.

He opened his eyes with his report already assembled, which was the correct way to do it.

"The Relic passed through. Four days ago. The trace ends at the second dock — they took a commercial barge north."

He looked past her, at the tree line where the road ran out and the district's outer fields began.

"There's something else in that district. Old residue. Not the standing-army kind — those go quiet inside a year, because a mind trained to stop remembering leaves nothing behind to find. This one hasn't stopped."

She read the cluster the way she read any block she meant to enter: for the exits, for the sight-lines, for what a man hiding there would need.

"A person?"

"A mind."

He put the vial away.

"Whatever's wearing it forgot to let him forget."

She was already moving.

The tree line ran along the district's outer field, scrub oak and something like birch gone silver in the grey morning, and Orim had pointed her at it rather than at the warehouses. *Whatever's wearing it forgot to let him forget.* She read the ground with the same close attention she gave any approach she meant to make alone: the trunks wide enough to matter, the sight-lines a man with a long gun would want and the ones he wouldn't have thought to deny himself.

He had a sight-line on her from the first line of trees. She knew this the way she knew weather — not from anything she could point to, but from the specific stillness a wood holds when it isn't empty. She kept walking. Fast movement announces intention as clearly as a shout; a woman crossing open ground at a working pace announces nothing.

The shot did not come.

She reached the first trunk wide enough to matter and put it between them, and in the half-second that cost him a clean line, she read what the delay meant: not a man deciding whether he could hit her. A man who'd had the shot and had not taken it, and was now working out, too late, what that decision had cost him.

She closed the second trunk before he'd finished working it out.

He found her again through the scope at eleven yards, which was close enough that the scope was already the wrong tool and too far for him to know it yet. The shot went where the barrel was pointed a half-second before she was — she'd given him the angle on purpose, coming off the second trunk at a line no rifle could correct for fast enough, and the round went through the space her shoulder had occupied a stride back and did nothing but announce, uselessly, that the fight had started.

The bolt-action bought her the rest of the distance. A man works the bolt, chambers, resets his cheek weld, finds the sight picture again — four actions, each with its own small cost in time, and she had spent seventeen years being the reason those four actions never finished in time. She took the second half of his rebuilt sight picture on her shield, the round skating off the boss with a sound like a struck bell, and by the time the bolt cycled again the rifle was a club-length weapon in a fight that had already closed past clubbing range.

She put him on the ground with the shield's edge, not the sword — a Templar's first choice, when the first choice is available, because a shield can end a fight a blade can only decide the terms of. He went down against a root the size of a forearm, the rifle skittering free of both his hands, and she had her knee on the stock before he'd finished falling and her blade at the black jointed housing where a man's throat would be before he'd finished deciding whether falling was the end of it.

He did not reach for the rifle again. He went still the way something goes still when it has run out of options it is willing to spend, and the oval receptor where a face should have been held on her, unlit, giving nothing back to read, and under her knee and blade both, so did he.

She had killed things that fought less honestly than this and felt less before doing it. She held the blade where it was and gave him the three seconds a person gets before a Templar's mercy runs out on a contested field, because Orim's word had been *mind*, not *weapon*, and she had learned to leave room for the difference even when the room cost her something.

He used the three seconds to speak.

It came up out of the chassis's throat flat and metal-toned, without inflection, in no cadence she'd have called speech if she hadn't already caught the shape of it a hundred times in a hundred canonical documents — the Received Tongue, the fixed dead formula the Liturgy dressed its most sacred instruments in, the one she had learned to render without understanding a word of it:

"Ave Maria, gratia plena, Dominus tecum—"

Her blade did not move. Her attention did.

He was not reciting an instrument. No Scribe's hand had ever set this shape in an archive she'd copied — the meter was wrong for law, the repetitions wrong for doctrine, and under the flat delivery, for the first time since she'd found him, something that was not procedure at all: a man's voice, badly out of practice at being afraid out loud, doing the one thing a body does with no other options left to spend.

He got through it once. Then, quieter, the syllables changing shape, something shorter, something that landed with the particular weight of a door being pulled shut from the inside:

"In manus tuas, Domine, commendo spiritum meum."

*Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.*

She did not have the words. She had the shape of them, close enough to the Received Tongue's own dead grammar that her hand — three years of copying that grammar into a canonical archive without once being told what it meant — understood the sentence a half-beat before the rest of her did: a man lying down for the night not knowing if he would rise, saying so, to whatever was listening, because it was the one sentence built to be said with a blade already at the throat.

He was not chanting a formula. He was praying. And the language he was praying in was not his own tongue rendered strange by a translation faculty — it was the Liturgy's own dead grammar, the one thing in this entire encounter that had no business belonging to a stolen mind off a Sphere none of them had ever named.

She held the blade a moment longer, because seventeen years of drill did not release its grip in the space of a single prayer. Then she took her knee off the rifle stock, and stepped back a half-pace, and did not sheath the sword — but she lowered it, and that was the whole of the mercy she had to give, and she gave it.

"Where," she said, "did you learn that."

He answered her in the same flat, metal-toned voice, in the plain vowels of a man from somewhere none of them had set foot, laying the words down deliberate, like he had all the time there was and none of it to waste proving so.

"My mother taught it to me. Before any of this." A pause, the receptor holding on her, unlit, giving nothing back to read. "I did not expect to need it again so soon."

She did not have an answer for that. She stood, and stepped back a further pace, and did not sheathe the sword, but she let the point drop toward the ground, which was as much of an answer as she had to give a man she had just put on his back under a tree with a blade at his throat.

The rifle lay where it had skittered, a stride off, in the roots. He looked at it. He looked at her. He did not move toward it.

"Take it," she said.

He read the whole of that the way a man reads an unfamiliar mechanism before he puts a hand to it — the same wary attention he'd given the hand and the sheathed blade a moment before combat made both of those things irrelevant, weighing what it cost her to say and what it would cost him to refuse. He rose, retrieved the rifle, and slung it over his shoulder rather than raising it, and she felt the old pull toward her own belt a half-beat before she'd chosen to feel it, seventeen years of drill outrunning her judgment — and he saw that, and stopped, hand on the sling, and held there: *the rifle comes. Your call.*

She breathed once. She nodded.

He moved when she moved, holding a body-width of distance between them — not submission, the working spacing of a man who wanted room to act if action became necessary, though something in the angle of him had changed since the trees, and she thought it was not trust, not yet, but a decision, the shape a decision takes once it is made and cannot be unmade. On the tree line's edge, where the warehouse district began, she raised one finger, pointed at the buildings ahead, raised it again. *One person, ahead.* His hand found the sling and stayed there. Ready. Not anticipating.

Orim stood in the passage, back to the entrance, watching the loading yard. He didn't turn.

"Eleven minutes before the manifest closes."

"Trace runs north from the second dock."

She glanced at the automaton beside her, watching him read Orim's stance with the same close attention he'd given hers a few minutes and one prayer ago — the turn coming at the sound of their footsteps and not the sound of a weapon.

"Whatever's in there. It's what you said."

Orim turned and gave him the attention he gave everything small: complete, unhurried, a scryer's habit of the specific over the general. He took in the rifle. The riveted plate. The worn patch at the left knuckle-joint where a hand had gripped it too many times in the dark. Stamped along the collar housing, in the flattened block lettering Verlaine used for anything it didn't intend to explain: **M-1018883.**

"M-101," Orim said, reading it aloud, for the record.

Something moved through the automaton's stillness that her hand, her blade, and the open lid had not put there. He straightened, minutely — the way a man straightens at his own name in a stranger's mouth — and answered in a voice that came up out of the chassis's throat, flat, metal-toned, without inflection.

"M-101."

It was the first sound he'd made in front of anyone but her. Drilled, unhesitating, correct — offered the way a captured soldier gives rank and serial number and stops there, because it's the one truth he can't be made to regret.

Ardea came round the north corner — come the legal way, days longer, on a soldier's book nobody had thought to suspend — took in the rifle, took in Lyra.

"You're bringing it," she said.

Not a question — a professional logging new intelligence and rebuilding her plan around it in real time.

"Him," Lyra said. "Yes."

Ardea took it in without visible reaction and moved on.

"The courier carries four poorly."

"He walks."

"He walks well," Orim said, ahead of the obvious follow-up. "A Myrmidon shell doesn't tire. It dents, or it doesn't. It never sits down."

Ardea looked at him a beat longer than required.

"That's not a comfort."

"No," Orim agreed.

She had read the intake literature the way she read all literature assigned to her: a problem, categorized, set aside, held at professional distance. An M-prefix serial branded a Myrmidon — a mind Scried out of a living man on some other Sphere, hauled up through the warm gold between worlds, installed without ceremony in a shell built to be replaced, not repaired. She had read the specification sheet on the shells themselves once, in an intake briefing years back: no life-support architecture, no provision for feeding or rest, because a Myrmidon required neither and Verlaine had not paid for capacities it would never draw on. Not a captured man. A stolen one, wearing the only body Verlaine judged worth spending on him. She had read the phrase *complete linguistic disjunction upon initial Sphere crossing* in a footnote and set it aside as a curiosity — nothing more. She was standing in a passage in Bressant with the footnote's subject a meter off, having just had him hand her, unasked, the one word he owned outright, and she found she had no ready frame for what that actually was.

"Eight minutes," Ardea said.

"We'll call him that," Lyra said. "M-101. Until he tells us different."

Orim glanced at her — not disagreement, closer to recognizing she'd taken the harder, more honest option when a softer one had been sitting there for the taking. She could have handed him a name of her own choosing, the way a quartermaster tags an unclaimed effect, and it would have cost her nothing and given him nothing either. She'd used the one true thing stamped on him instead, which was uglier, and, she judged, more his.

He'd followed all of it — the naming, the reasoning under it, Ardea's clock-counting, the whole exchange three strangers had conducted a stride from him as though he were freight that happened to have opinions. He'd followed the warehouse before that. He'd followed the latch, Orim's read of the collar, every word since. What he did with any of it he kept to himself. He kept it a moment longer.

Then he didn't.

"It'll do."

The voice came out of the chassis's throat again — flat, metal-toned, the same instrument that had returned his number to Orim a minute before. But this was not the one drilled syllable, offered and nothing else, that rank and serial number had been. It was a full sentence, unhurried, in the plain vowels of a man from somewhere none of them had set foot, each word laid down deliberate, like he had all the time there was and none of it to waste proving so.

Ardea went still in a different register than before.

Lyra recognized, under the sentence, the exact shape of what Ardea had just set aside — *complete linguistic disjunction* — and watched it land on her: that whoever wrote the phrase had never stood in a room with the thing it claimed to describe. There was no disjunction. There never had been. Lyra had known that since the trees. He'd understood the warehouse. He'd understood Orim reading the stamp off his own collar. He'd understood Ardea calling him "it" twice in one breath and let both land without comment, the way he let everything else pass, and had simply not, until this exact moment, chosen to answer in front of anyone but her.

"You speak?" Ardea asked.

Not a question. An objection lodged a beat too late to do any good.

"I do."

The receptor was already on her before he finished saying it.

"Gave the number first. Seemed the truer thing to lead with."

Nobody spoke for a stretch that ran a half-second past comfortable. The flatness of the delivery did double work: the voice of a man choosing his words with care, and, to ears that hadn't learned better yet, indistinguishable from the voice of a slow mind reciting something taught to it. Ardea caught the difference before she trusted herself to speak again.

"Seven minutes," Ardea said, recovering the one piece of the moment still hers to hold, and was already moving.

## The Houndstooth

Getting him aboard the Heloth courier took three steps: show him what it was, show him where to hold, confirm he understood the second step meant something and wasn't obedience for its own sake. He approached the machine's shoulder housing with the care of a man who already knew what machines could do and was working out this one's category — not fear, assessment. He studied the joint construction a long moment before he set his hand where hers had been, and didn't look at it again after. He watched the terrain instead, the whole run out of the district, both hands on the bar, weight distributed correctly — the posture of a man who'd done this before, or something close enough to it.

He didn't tire on the run to the dock. Six miles by her count, mostly downhill grade, and his stride never lengthened or shortened to compensate for it the way a tired man's does without his noticing. She was watching him closely now — had been watching everything about him, whether she meant to or not.

The *Houndstooth* was loading grain at the second dock, bound north on the ordinary commercial run to the Atrament processing centers — unremarkable, seventeen barges a week this season, the manifest stamp worn shallow from four years under the same clerk's hand. She bought passage for four on a Calyx guild seal she'd carried since a posting six years back, paid in credit vouchers, and the dockworkers gave M-101 the look they gave anyone unfamiliar — brief, categorical — and went back to loading grain.

Below, the hold smelled of river mud and old rope. Hammocks along one bulkhead, a bench along the other, a small iron stove bolted forward behind a mesh screen — the one open flame a grain barge tolerated below decks, and tolerated barely, one hand's width of clearance to the nearest sack of dry grain on either side. She took the bench. Ardea took the hammock farthest from the hatch. Orim found a crate by the porthole, the position that let him watch the river and think at the same time, which he seemed to manage without particular effort at either.

M-101 stood at the foot of the companionway a moment, reading the space the way she'd learned to watch him read every space: the hammocks, the hatch, the three strangers already distributed through the hold, the corner that gave the longest sight-line on the only exit. He found it — against the casks, farthest from the hatch — sat, set the rifle across his knees, and let the receptor dim. Not dark. Not lit. Something between.

The barge got underway. She felt it in her inner ear, the small unhinging from the shore, and opened her notebook to a clean page and did not yet know what she meant to put on it.

The stove burned low and orange behind its mesh. For the first hour of true dark the only sound in the hold was the river against the hull, Ardea's slow breathing in the hammock, Orim turning a page of nothing in particular, and M-101 sitting motionless against the casks, the receptor holding its half-dim, not gone out.

She watched him longer than she'd meant to.

He didn't sleep. She worked this out slowly, the way a fact gets reported by the body an hour before the mind agrees to accept it: a person drifts, startles, shifts weight and resettles, eventually wants water or the rail or simply to move. He did none of it. She had stood two-hour watches beside men who fought sleep the whole length of them, and knew every tell of it — the slow blink lengthening, the chin dropping and catching. He gave her none of those tells to read, because there was nothing in him built to produce them. The receptor held its ember-glow as long as she watched and gave no further sign, and somewhere in that unbroken stillness she stopped counting it as rest and started counting it as something closer to standing watch on himself.

What the shell wouldn't report to her, the fire reported to him.

Not sleep. She wouldn't have a word for what she was seeing until someone put the language to it much later, and the language would only confirm what her body had already decided that first night, unassisted: a shell built like his didn't rest, because rest is a thing a body sets itself down into, and Verlaine had built nothing into him able to set anything down. What happened instead — on the first night since the taking, quiet enough, still enough, safe enough that the idling routines finally dropped toward whatever the shell called low power — wasn't gentler than sleep. It was worse. Nothing to wake him from, because nothing in him had gone anywhere to be woken from. The mind in the housing was left, for the first time since the taking, with nothing left to attend to but itself. And itself was a groove worn deep by months of running, one idling didn't smooth over. It found the groove at once, the way a drill finds a bore it's already cut, and began again from the start, because starting again was the only shape left to make.

He sat in the orange half-dark of a stove he couldn't feel the heat of, motionless to any eye watching, and behind the receptor a man who existed nowhere the receptor could show her was living it again, in full sentences, in a register nobody in the hold would hear:

*Not pain, first. Displacement. A hook set through the mouth of something that never knew it was suspended in warm gold water until the water was gone, and him with it, going up.*

*Then no body, no up, no edge to the dark — the wreckage of a life turning past him out of reach, debris and not pictures — then weight, wrong weight, a line of them, black and identical, and a voice reading a number off a sheet the way a clerk reads a manifest, and him stepping forward because the number, ugly as it was, was the only thing in the yard that belonged to him and to no one else.*

*Then — always then, the groove narrowing at the same place it always did — a gunship, a ring in its flank stencilled with a number that wasn't his number. Turret #34. Below it, a settlement, roofs and a road and smoke still climbing off half the chimneys — the kind of ordinary that meant people had eaten breakfast there that morning. And the mechanism Verlaine had wired into the housing beside whatever he still was, offering him a solution. Range. Bearing. A tone that meant one thing.* Loose.

*He does not argue with it. There is no argument to have with a thing that does not listen, and no half-beat left to have it in. He goes instead — out of the ring and into the small dark of his own shell, three rings down, empty and cold and entirely his. It takes the length of a held breath. The turret's aperture goes dark mid-tone, still offering its solution to nobody.*

*Then — the one honest report the shell ever gave him, the only thing that ever reached him whole, no half-beat lag, no flatness, none of the sense of being briefed on his own body by a stranger — the smell. Burnt ozone. Cooked wire, scorched housing. Some circuit in the empty ring seizing on itself, waiting on an order nobody was left to carry out. The single true report of that entire day.*

*Nobody comes to the turret ring after. A robed figure down the ship makes a note on a board, brief — and then the recalibration: not destruction, adjustment, the volume on the thing that moved him turned down rather than silenced. Returned to the line inside the week. Obeying again, the half-beat where he used to have a say in it shorter every time, until he could no longer find the seam where it used to be.*

*The tone offers the solution again, somewhere else, some other day. It always offers the solution again. No floor to this room, no door out of it, because the loop doesn't know it's already ended — ending was never built into it.*

Across the hold, in the part of the night that belonged to the living, she saw none of it and all of it. What reached her was smaller, and came without translation: the receptor's ember-glow, steady an hour, then guttering. Not going dark. Flickering, fast, three small drops in the low red glow, evenly spaced, gone before she could swear she'd seen them. Somewhere in the shoulder joint a servo ticked once, faint — a lock testing itself against a door it already knows is barred. And under the river-sound and Ardea's breathing, thin enough she nearly dismissed it as imagined, a thread of the same mineral smell she'd caught in the grain bin that morning. Ozone. Faint. Present. Gone before it earned the name of a smell at all.

She didn't know what any of it meant. She knew only, watching it, the particular cold of standing outside a room where something was happening that she had no vocabulary for yet, and that whatever it was, it wasn't rest, and it wasn't nothing, and it repeated — three flickers, stillness, and a long while later, three more, evenly spaced as the first, the way a held position repeats when it hasn't been given leave to stand down.

The fire ticked in its screen. The river went on being a river. None of the words reached her, none of the pictures, no part of the number screaming under the number he'd given Orim for his own. What reached her was the guttering, the small dead servo-tick, the ozone-thread under the woodsmoke — not much, and enough to keep her watching him long after watching him stopped being required of her.

She closed the notebook without a line written in it, and looked at him across the hold — the ember of the receptor, the rifle across his knees, the stillness that wasn't rest — and understood, the plain unornamented way she understood most things that mattered: she'd gone into a grain warehouse expecting to pull out a person hiding from a war, and had instead pulled out something the war had already finished with and thrown away, and it hadn't stopped thinking the whole time it had been thrown away, and this — not the theft, not the Calyx squad's ten-day lead on them, not the barge or the border or the smoke waiting on the Atrament horizon by morning — was the thing she was going to have to find room for.

Seventeen years in the Order had given her a doctrine for almost everything she was likely to meet on a recovery run. It had given her nothing for this. He had a voice. He'd chosen, twice now, exactly when to spend it. That was not a small fact to have learned about a machine on the first day of knowing him.

Orim, without opening his eyes, said from his crate by the porthole:

"He's not sleeping."

"No."

"Good," he said. "Someone should keep the first watch who isn't tired."

She held her eyes on M-101 a while longer. Then she picked the notebook back up, because there was work to be done, and it seemed to her, watching him watch nothing in the almost-dark, like the only honest thing left between them.

The roof was the first thing Declan checked — a boy raised under Unaka rock checks a roof before he checks anything else — vaulting starting thirty feet up, ribs cut into the stone to carry a weight some long-dead mason had judged sound enough to leave standing. He was three thousand miles and one body away from Carter County and he still did it, still ran his eye along the seams the way his father used to before he'd let a man set a pick to coal. Rows of narrow bunks ran wall to wall, straw under dark wool, the floor given over to housing a great many bodies with minimum expense of space or comfort. On the far wall, a rack of bolt-action rifles stood where he supposed pole-arms once had.

He smelled the place before he understood anything about it — metal-oil, wet wool, the sourness of men who had not been warm enough for long enough. He was shown a bunk. He lay on it and thought, in his own language, in full sentences, that he did not know where he was, and that not knowing was going to be the condition of things now — weather to be managed, not solved.

The first word that mattered was *kal.* Stop. He understood it the instant it was said — the shell had given him the whole of the language before he'd taken ten steps in the new body, complete and instant — but understanding a word and commanding a body somebody else had built to obey it in the same half-second were not yet the same skill. He learned the gap between the two from the gap between moving and impact: from walking on when the column had already stopped, from the hand that closed on his collar and hauled him into a wall hard enough that the impact reached him not as pain but as a jolt through the frame, a half-beat delay between the shove and his body registering it. The men nearby made a sound. Not laughter. Recognition.

*That one will learn.*

He set it aside as possibly encouraging.

After *kal* came the equipment — the lock, the sling, the cleaning kit, sounds his mouth had never needed before, though the shell made them without being asked. He understood every word the moment he heard it. What took the week was matching a body he'd had for eleven days to objects it had never held, fast and clean enough that nobody's attention came looking for the man holding them wrong.

By the end of the first week he could load, clean, and stand to inspection without being corrected twice for the same fault.

There was a particular quality to the confusion in some of the others — not the ordinary confusion of a man wondering why he'd been ordered to do something pointless, but confusion with no category to settle into. He recognized it because he had it himself, and because once, crossing the washroom, he had caught the same look passing over the blank dark oval where his own face should have been, in the tin sheet someone had hung for a mirror and never bothered to polish. He saw it and moved on, because moving on was the only motion available to him that cost nothing.

Some of the others had buried the look deep enough that it only surfaced at night. Sphere 22 — the only name Doyle had for him, the number stamped where a unit designation went — had been in Verlaine two years. His Entos came out even and unhesitating. He took his ration without looking at it, filled the gaps when Doyle fell silent mid-order, and was extremely good at being somewhere else when things went wrong. There was no face to read, but the motion gave everything away, if you watched long enough: Sphere 22 moved like a man who had stopped being surprised.

There was also Sphere 14 and Sphere 8, glimpsed more than known — a nod across the mess line, a shared five minutes on latrine detail. He would not have called any of them friends. He would have said, if willing to say much of anything yet, that they were people the same thing had happened to, which was not friendship but was not nothing.

On the third day they moved him to the range.

He drew a rifle from the day issue and his hand went to the bolt before the trainer had finished demonstrating on the man beside him. Lift, draw back, seat the round, drive forward, lock down. He did not decide to do this. The motion arrived the way *kal* had arrived — ahead of thought, the shell's half-beat lag catching up to an intention that had already, somewhere behind it, been executed a thousand times in a body that no longer existed.

He knew this mechanism.

*Bolt-action. Box magazine, five-round. Machined stock, not stamped.*

The words arrived unbidden, some part of the shell running an inventory nobody had asked it to run, flat and immediate — exactly as *kal* had arrived on the first day. Not this model — the lock housing was wrong for what he knew, the magazine cleaner than anything on the diagram in the ironmonger's window on Cress Street — but the family of it, the idea. His world had drawn the blueprint. This world had cut the finished part. He had Entos for all of that — *blueprint*, *prototype*, *descent* — and said none of it. There was no one present he trusted with a sentence that size, and admitting he recognized a weapon's ancestry was the kind of fact, once spoken, he would never get to take back.

The trainer looked at a man standing at ready with a loaded rifle he had not been taught to load, asked something that in any language would have meant *when did this happen?*, and went to fetch a second trainer.

They turned the rifle over between them, handling it like something they had not expected. Later he found, stamped into the receiver, an angular notation it took him four months to read whole: SPHERE-SOURCE PATTERN — DESCENT CORPS AUTHORITY — NOT FOR CIVILIAN REGISTRY. The institution had known exactly where the weapon's ancestry lay, stamped that knowledge into the metal, and issued the rifle anyway — worried, in writing, about distribution rather than origin. He kept it to himself. In a body that answered to somebody else, it was safer held than said.

They put him in the front row for the rest of range day. The word the trainer used for him afterward had an approving shape. He said nothing about it and moved on.

The man from the close world came in the second month, off a transfer batch from the eastern intake station. There was no reading a trade off a chassis built identical to every other chassis in the hall, but motion was not identical. This one's hands went to a tool with the ease of a man who'd spent a working life at a bench — an economy in the wrist, no wasted travel, the discipline surviving the change of hand the way *kal* had survived the change of everything else. Whatever age he'd been, in whatever body he used to have, the tempo said *not new to this.*

Doyle's own hands knew coal, not a bench. Six years at the home drift had given them their own economy — the cutting machines, the pumps, the fan gear, the particular readiness of a man who works by sound because sound gets to him before sight does — but none of that travels to a vise or a lathe, and he watched the other one work with the plain, uncomplicated envy of a man recognizing a skill adjacent to his own and not his own at all. He'd sat the Forest Service exam near the end of his six years, meant to trade the seam for fire towers and section lines and land he'd walk for a wage — three months out from the posting when the draft notice came, the mine still the only trade his hands had ever actually been given time to learn. His hands only knew a rifle as a man knows a thing taught fast, out of necessity, laid down over six years of an entirely different discipline — not as this one knew a bench.

In the dark after lights, Doyle said something in his own language, not expecting anything, only to hear himself say it — and the shell carried it out flat and finished. The other one turned toward the sound and answered, and the two flat voices understood each other completely, on the first exchange, because the gift underneath the chassis did not care whose original tongue it had been built from.

It was not the understanding that took a week — understanding was free. What took the week was everything the understanding made possible, and neither of them was in a hurry to use it. They spent the evenings trading how much of home the other was willing to say out loud — the coal camp, for Doyle; the bench and the machine floor, for him — each admission held out and taken and not repaid immediately, because repaying too fast would have meant it hadn't cost anything.

The first time Doyle laughed since he'd woken into any of this was over nothing worth the name — some small, stupid overlap, each having assumed for a week that the other was a different kind of prisoner than he was. It should not have been funny. It was.

The man had been at a machine floor when it happened to him too — had not chosen to come, did not understand what he'd been brought here for. This was not a surprise. It was confirmation, which was a different animal: it did not change anything, only put weight underneath what he already believed.

He asked once, in the dark, where the man had been taken from — not out of ceremony, only to have one fact about him that wasn't Verlaine's to hand out first. The answer came back short, in the flat finished voice the shell gave everyone: "Somewhere with a river." Nothing more, and Doyle understood, the way you understand a door somebody has shut on purpose, not to press for the rest of it. A man got to keep back whatever the shell hadn't already taken from him. He'd have wanted the same courtesy extended to the one name he was still keeping for himself. Nobody had asked him for it yet. Nobody would, until somebody finally mattered enough to be told.

By the third month he could follow orders instantly, without the half-beat of resistance that used to cost him a shove into a wall — not because he understood them any better than he had the first week, but because he had stopped making it wait on his consent before it carried the compliance out. Conflating the two — understanding and consent — was the mistake the trainers made about him for months, and it worked in his favor. The name of his own rifle was still the only word in the whole language he said with anything like ease.

He had Entos for *loyalty.* For *betrayal,* for *injustice,* for *conscription* — the shell had given him the whole architecture of it the day it took his voice, complete and instant, nothing withheld. What he did not have was standing to use any of it. A man could own the word *betrayal* outright and still have no right to it, in a war he had been dropped into without a side. He had asked Sphere 22, once, carefully, where a particular man from the barracks had gone, and been given a word back — *solen* — and understood exactly what it meant before the shell finished saying it, though nobody explained it and nobody needed to.

Word came down like it always did: a board, a note, a passing voice that didn't slow to make sure he'd heard it.

*Sector four. Non-recoverable.*

He knew before he asked whose designation went with it — the specific, sick certainty of a man who's found his own name on a casualty list before his eyes have actually landed on it — some part of him had already put it together and did not want the answer confirmed. He asked anyway, because not asking would have been its own kind of answer, and got back four digits Verlaine had stamped a bench-worker's stolen mind with, the same flat administrative way his own had been read off a board the first cold morning.

*M-774.*

He had never once heard the man use it. In seven months of borrowed evenings they had traded coal seam for machine floor, whittled matchsticks for whatever a man Somewhere-With-A-River did with his hands when there was nothing left to build, laughter over nothing worth the name — and never once, not once, had either of them reached for the numbers stamped on their intake forms, because the numbers were what Verlaine called them and the evenings were the one place that didn't have to be true.

*Non-recoverable* did not mean dead, technically. It meant a shell too damaged to be worth the extraction detail's time, mind and all, and Verlaine did not spend a line item distinguishing the two outcomes, because for Verlaine's purposes there had never been a difference.

He sat with the board's flat little sentence for a while — a stone he'd just found out he'd been carrying. Somewhere with a river. He had never learned which one. He understood, turning that particular gap over, that this was the last of it — the last thing this place had left to take from him that he had not already, in some fashion, given up in advance. There was nobody left here whose good evening cost him anything to lose. There was nothing left here that he owed anything to, except the number stenciled on his own shell, and a number does not need a man loyal to it.

He did not decide anything that night. He simply noticed, the way a man notices a door left open in a house gone cold, that there was no longer a reason he could name to keep walking back through it every morning.

The order to advance came on a road that was not a good road, in weather that had committed to being bad. Low cloud. The smell of rain that hadn't started yet but had made up its mind. Mud spreading in from the margins now that it had decided to.

He reached the ridge with the rest of the column and looked down into the valley. Two forces, converging from different angles toward the same low ground his own column was descending into. He did not need the tactical picture to read the geometry — a boy who had grown up watching coal cars run fixed track out of the Unaka seams understood paths that don't bend for anything, and what happens when two of them try to take the same rail at the same time. He did not know whose flag either force carried, if either carried one, or what either side was fighting for. He did not know, past the plain fact of an order, what he himself was fighting for. He had nothing on either side that was his — no officer whose authority he'd chosen, no allegiance made with his eyes open, only an oath taken on a day he barely remembered as his own, in a voice that hadn't been fully his either.

The engagement started below with a sound he knew before he'd finished hearing it. Some scanning function supplied the classification anyway, flat and unasked-for — *repeating, bolt-action, standard infantry pattern* — cataloguing the report the same way it catalogued everything else, whether he wanted the information or not. A bolt mechanism makes the same sound regardless of which country machined it; Entos had not changed that just because he was no longer anywhere near home.

He turned around.

He walked back up the road while the column went forward and down, the noise of it first close and then receding, and nobody stopped him, because everyone forward of him had somewhere more urgent to be. He walked until the sound was behind him, and then distant, and then gone, and kept walking anyway, north, because north was away, and away was, for the first time in seven months, a decision that was entirely his.

Bressant was large enough to disappear into — anonymity, he was learning, was mostly a function of volume. He found the grain district by smell before he found it by sight — dry warmth, faintly sweet, close enough in principle to the mule barn behind the tipple back home, the feed they kept for the animals that hauled coal out of the dark, that some very old part of him relaxed at it without being asked to.

He slept three nights in the first warehouse he found, then moved when the section showed signs of regular inspection, and moved again the week after, learning the district the only way it could be learned: which yards kept irregular schedules, which foremen watched the perimeter and which didn't. He had looked plausible his whole working life, compact and unremarkable, and overlooked was now the entire strategy.

He did not need to eat, not in the sense the word insisted on — whatever kept the chassis running would never announce itself as hunger. And yet some old, stubborn part of him went looking for food anyway out of habit, the way a man reaches for a door handle in a house he no longer lives in — took what passed for it when a warehouse offered spillage, drank from the runoff between the yards, because his body had spent thirty-odd years being fed on a schedule and had not yet been told, in any language it trusted, that the arrangement was over.

He kept the rifle. This was not practical — it was heavy, needed keeping dry, and was not the kind of thing a district laborer carried, which meant concealing it added difficulty to every entrance and exit he made. He kept it anyway, because it was the one thing here he had never once been uncertain about. Everything else — the language, the oath, the intake forms, the things he'd learned to leave unexamined — had come to him in conditions of partial understanding. The rifle was comprehension without conditions. He was not going to set it down now.

He had said almost nothing of Entos unprompted in seven months — not ordered out of him, not repeated back to a trainer, not issued at all. The shell had given him the whole language complete on the first day, every word at once, nothing rationed and nothing withheld; what was scarce was never the vocabulary. It was the willingness. What follows were not words he happened to have picked up. They were words he had chosen, on his own account, to spend.

*Faeb.* Factory.
