He'd worn it before, alone, saying this exact sentence into the dark over a crate wall until it wore the groove he stepped into now without slipping.

She put the notebook down behind her, against the bulkhead, and didn't open it again.

He said, in Entos: "I want to tell you something."

The grammar came out correct, as it always did — the shell gave him that for free, complete sentences from the first hour in this world whether he wanted them or not. What wasn't free was the willingness. That part he'd built himself, the long way, saying it into the dark until it wore the groove it came out in now: flat, tin-flat, the chassis's same exact affect on every word regardless of what the word cost him. He'd been building to this since Schmalburg. He knew she'd noticed — the questions he'd started asking her afterward that weren't about danger, or food, or direction, but about sequence. About then. About things already happened that no better language could change.

She said:
"I'm listening."

He started with the mine.

Carter County had more coal camps than most maps bothered naming, and his wasn't the biggest of them — he'd worked bigger ones, further up the line, before the seam at the home drift took him on for good. He gave her the camp's name in his own language first, watching to see if she needed Entos for it.

"It doesn't need one," she said.

He nodded. Six years at that drift, longer all told once you counted the season on a different seam two counties over, the surface work before that. He knew the cutting machines, the pumps, the fan gear the company had put in his second year — the ordinary knowledge of any man who'd spent years underground.

"By sound," he said. "Different sound, different problem. You learn it, or the mountain teaches you the hard way."

There was weight in that last part, the weight of a fact that's also its own grief.

He stopped. He looked at his hands.

"I was good at my work," he said. "I want you to know that. I am not telling you I was nobody." He said the word plainly, flat and exact, and let it sit before he went on. "I had a name. I had a place. People knew me."

"I know," she said.

"I don't think you do," he said, without offense. "You know I was Scried out of somewhere. You don't know I was someone there, first."

She held still with that. She hadn't thought to separate the two facts before — he could see it land on her, the specific stillness of a person absorbing a correction against something she'd assumed was settled.

"Tell me," she said.

A Thursday in autumn. He knew the day because the day shift overlapped the fireboss's inspection for forty minutes on Thursdays, and the overlap changed the noise underground into something else, two crews occupying the same iron for slightly different purposes. He knew the hour from the sound the drift-mouth bell made past the half-hour. He knew the season from the angle of light through the tipple framing when he came up. He had always tracked the conditions of the room he was in. It wasn't a special skill. It was simply how he'd been made to notice things.

"Then," he said.

He stopped.

"Then," he said again, and let the one word carry the weight of the three hundred that would follow it — everything between half past the hour, Thursday morning and the floor was not the floor. He had all the words. What he didn't have, yet, was the nerve to spend them in order. His jaw worked once, the specific motion of a man arriving at the edge of what he was willing to say aloud and finding it a genuine edge, with a drop on the other side.

"Take it in pieces," she said.

He looked at her. He nodded.

The floor changed first. Not gone — wrong, a different quality under his boots, the kind of wrongness a man who works a coal face all day is built to notice before he understands it. He checked himself: was he unwell?

Had something failed in the rock over his head?

He wasn't unwell. The floor wasn't broken.

Then the stone room.

He told it evenly — the specific economy of a man who has learned what feeling costs and has decided, for the length of this telling, not to spend it. Dressed stone. Cold — not the drift's winter cold, which was just weather doing what weather does, but the cold of stone that had been cold for centuries and intended to stay that way. Three figures in robes. He gave her the colors and she recognized them before he said the word: Ocipheus white, canonical gold at the hem.

"Ocipheus," he said, flat as he said anything true. Not an accusation. A fact laid on the table between them. The word came out exactly like every other word he'd given her tonight — flat, level, uninflected — and that was what made it land as hard as it did. A fully articulate voice, saying the truth outright, in a register built to carry ammunition counts.

"Yes," she said.

"One of them held a book."

He was quiet a moment — not the quiet of having nothing left, the quiet of choosing which piece carried the most per word.

"I was not afraid," he said. "I want you to understand that. I have been afraid. I was in France fourteen months. I know what afraid does to a body." He paused. "This was a different thing. This was the feeling of a room whose rules no one had given me. Three people. Robes. No context for any of it. I did what a man does in that room. I made myself as legible as I could. Cooperative. I thought — if I am cooperative, someone will explain."

He looked at his hands.

"No one explained," he said.

"I know the intake protocol," she said, after a while. Flat, same as she always did with hard things — he'd noticed the family resemblance in how they each spent a bad sentence. "I read it my first year at the Station. I read it again three years in, when the documentation project needed hands. I wrote a line for the literature myself, once. I don't remember thinking it was cruelty when I wrote it." She paused. "Oath administered prior to language acquisition minimizes resistive response in the conscript cohort. That's the sentence. I meant it as an observation about efficiency."

He said nothing to that for a while. Long enough that she looked up from her hands to check he'd heard her.

"I know," he said, finally. "That's why I'm telling it in order. So you hear the room before you hear the sentence that runs it."

"The words had a rhythm to them," he said. "Official. I knew the shape of it — some of it, not all — the instant I heard it, the same as you'd know a hymn even in a language you'd never studied. I've never told anyone that until right now. I'm not telling you the rest of it yet either. I'm telling this in order, same as I said I would."

He looked at his hands.

"There was a gesture. The one with the book made it toward me. I copied it." He showed her — a small incline of the head, a particular set of the right hand.

She recognized it at once.

"The acknowledgment position," she said. "From the Compact Oath. Formal assent to canonical authority."

"I copied it because that is what you do, in a room with robed people making official sounds and you don't have the language. You look willing. You think: I will be willing until I understand, and then I will decide."

He paused.

"I never decided," he said. "I never understood fast enough."

Orim had not moved from the porthole. His fingertips stayed on the glass. He said nothing.

He gave her Verlaine in the same pieces.

The barracks were stone-vaulted, high-windowed, old — a category he recognized without being able to place it, and had stopped trying to explain once the recognizable and the wholly foreign had gotten too tangled to separate. The rifles were on racks along the wall, and he had known rifles; he'd carried one in France.

"I knew the action," he said, and mimed the bolt, the cycling motion. "Not exactly. Later. Further along — like a later model of a thing you already know."

He looked at her.

"In my world there were men whose whole careers were tracing how a mechanism developed — who built the first one, who improved it, who licensed the design. You can follow forty years of small changes back to an origin. The rifles here don't belong to that history. They're past the end of it. But the lineage's there, if you know how to read a receiver housing." He held her eyes. "Someone had my world's designs, and time to take them further than my world has had."

"Someone had been watching," he said. "Long before they brought me here."

He waited.

"Yes," she said.

He nodded, and went on.

The barracks held conscripts from at least a dozen points of origin, by his count, and most of them shared no language. The House ran intake on a set of demonstrated commands that required no shared vocabulary at all. Stand. Walk. Carry. Wait. Those were the first words said to him in Entos, and the shell rendered them the instant they landed — understanding arrived whether he wanted it or not. The collar markers were administrative — a stamped disc, a sphere number, punched in during processing. He had seen his own: Sphere 31. He had seen Sphere 22. Sphere 14. A man from Sphere 8 worked the maintenance crews by then, competent in Entos, missing a fingertip to some machine that had closed too fast, and had looked at Doyle in his first week with an expression that said:

I know what this is doing to you, and it gets better in some ways and worse in others, and I can't tell you which way you're headed.

Orim's fingertips pressed a fraction harder against the glass.

"What is the highest number you know?" Doyle asked.

"The canonical records reference Sphere sixty-one," she said. "Some practitioners believe the count goes further."

He said nothing for a moment.

"I saw thirty-one on my form. I counted, in the yard and the barracks. Nine spheres, at least, that I saw or heard of. Probably others I didn't." He paused. "How many people are in those files?"

"I don't know," she said. "I processed forty-three intake cohorts, over six months. Fourteen persons average, per cohort."

He did the arithmetic she hadn't done for him. Six hundred, in one half-year window. The program had run, in its documented form, since Year 1064 — three hundred years — and the practice before the documentation, the part the early canonical scholars wrote around rather than through, went back further than anyone had troubled to count, which was itself the point of never counting it.

"How many people know what the stone room looks like?" he asked.

"Intake staff. The records division. Practitioners who've studied the foundational instruments."

"And everyone else knows Myrmidons exist. That they serve. That they come from a membrane, another world, in the general sense." He paused. "Not the cold. Not the robes. Not the gesture."

"No," she said.

"Because the oath is given before the language."

She waited.

"On purpose," he said.

"Yes," she said. "On purpose."

He told her about the man from Sphere 22 next, because the numbers had opened a door he could walk the rest of the way through.

Two months further into his own time in Verlaine than Doyle was, mid-forties, the particular stillness of a man who has done physical work for twenty years and learned to conserve his motion. A missing fingertip of his own, on the other hand — a different machine, evidently, but the same category of loss. They had tried, some evenings, to find overlap between their own languages — not Entos, which the shells gave each of them freely and separately, but the tongues they'd each been taken out of, which no shell had ever been built to carry between two stolen men. The kind of trying two men do when there's nothing else to fill an evening. You pointed. You said your word. Mostly there was nothing.

"We found one," Doyle said.

He paused.

"The word was mother," he said.

Orim's tincture bottle made a small sound against the porthole housing, barely audible under the envelope's argument with the wind.

"In both languages, nearly the same word," Doyle said. "Close enough that you said it, and heard his version, and both of you knew what had been said." He looked at his hands. "I don't know what that means. Whether it says something about language, or about what's the same underneath every world it's spoken in." He was quiet. "I thought about it for months afterward. What that word was doing there, in both of us, without either of us having put it there."

There was another man, from Sphere 8, the one with the maintenance work and the missing fingertip and enough Entos to be dangerous to himself in a careful way. In his second year he had shown Doyle the inside of his boot — the lining worked thin and soft, and words scratched into the leather in a hand that wasn't his own, in a shape he couldn't read and had never learned to read, memorized instead as a picture is memorized. He had gotten someone to write it for him, or copied the marks from someone who could, and kept them against his foot because a body that has nowhere else to keep a thing will keep it there.

He had recited it to Doyle, slowly, over several weeks — the halting instruction of a man teaching something he didn't fully understand himself. Doyle had kept it just as carefully since — not as scholarship, as ballast.

"He was built to serve," Doyle said now, and she could hear the quotation in it, the particular careful cadence of words being reproduced rather than made, exact and level — the same flatness the chassis gave to everything. "He chose to refuse. That word made him more a person than the-" He paused there, not for the word but for what came before it. "Entos doesn't have one. Not for a group of men who decide things about a drift without ever going down it. Not the miners. Above them." He let the gap stand instead of filling it. "It doesn't matter. The line was about refusing."

Orim's face, at the porthole, did something small and quickly put away — something more than recognition - the look of a man who has heard a chord struck before in a different room and cannot place which room.

"Who wrote it?" Lyra asked.

"I don't know," Doyle said. "He didn't know either. It came to him from someone else, the way most things came to us." He looked at his hands. "I've carried it the better part of a year without a name on it. I don't think it needs one to be true."

Later, once he trusted himself to ask, he had put the stone room's actual question to a Verlaine intake administrator: what had the words meant. The man had told him it was the oath of service, binding him to canon law for the term of his conscription.

"I asked him if it was valid," Doyle said, "if I hadn't understood it?"

She was already waiting for the answer.

"He said that was a theological question, and he didn't have the training to address it."

"The notation," Doyle said. "On the rifle."

"Yes," she said.

"I've seen the pattern before. In my world. Men who studied where designs came from could see the gaps — pieces that weren't native to a lineage, things adapted in from somewhere else, a long time back. We had theories about it. A lost civilization. Older than us. We thought: they built the first things, and disappeared, and we found what they'd left and carried it forward." He paused. "We were proud of that. The search for the origin. The respect for the debt."

He looked at his hands.

"We were right that the knowledge wasn't originally ours," he said. "We were wrong about the civilization being lost. You didn't disappear. You just kept taking."

She held very still.

"I'm not angry," he said, in the even way he said accurate things — not flattened by distance, simply stated without adding weight to a thing that was already heavy enough to carry on its own. "I don't have the strength for it today. I'm telling you because you have the most of the language, and because your institution wrote the forms I put my mark on, and processed the files that had me in them before I had a name for Entos. I think you should know that one of the people in those files is telling you this himself."

"I know," she said.

"I have known, and not known, longer than I'd like to admit."

He looked at her, and didn't recognize what came back at him — the first time in four months her face hadn't been legible to him inside the two seconds he usually needed for it.

He sat with that a while before he told her there was one more thing, and that he'd put it last on purpose.

"There's one part of it I've been sitting on since before I had a name for anything else in this world," he said. "I want to say it now, while I've got the rest of it said."

She waited.

"You have a name for the Canons' rite-tongue," he said. "The one no scribe gets taught whole. The one that comes down over a rite, or a writ, or the dead, and nobody but a Canon reads the whole of it."

"The Received Tongue," she said.

"That's the name for it, then." He turned that over once, set it down. "I didn't have a name for it, the first time I heard it. I didn't have anything else yet either. Not Entos. Not you, or Orim, or a shell that answered when I told it to move. It came at me raw that first time, unlaundered — the one thing in that whole stone room that didn't arrive already translated for me. And I knew it anyway."

Her stillness had a different quality to it now than it had all night. He'd learned four months of her stillnesses without meaning to, the way a man tracks a room's noise without meaning to, and this one didn't match any he already knew.

"Say it," she said. "If you're going to."

He said it.

Level, unhurried, the same flat tin delivery the shell gave every sentence he'd spoken tonight, sacred and profane alike — the shell had never once made a distinction between the two.

"Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine."

Nothing in the hold answered it. The envelope kept its argument with the wind. Orim's fingertips didn't move on the glass, though something in his shoulders did.

"It says: grant them rest, forever, Lord," Doyle said. "That's the whole of it. One of those words is a name for God I don't think you use for anything else, and none of it is stranger than a stone somebody paid a mason to cut." He looked at his hands. "That's the same shape of word that's cut over the door of the church back home, and into fieldstone in the yard behind it, on markers going back further than anybody living remembers to visit. A schoolteacher in a one-room house with a stove that never drew right made every boy in the county say it until we could say it without thinking, whether or not the meaning ever stuck — the same as we said our times tables. That's where I know it from. Not from anything holy. From a stove-warmed room and a graveyard full of my neighbors."

He looked up.

"It's not a mystery," he said. "It's not the voice of anything. It's a language nobody living where I'm from speaks outside that stove-warmed room or a Sunday service, and it hasn't been spoken like that in about ninety years. It's old. It's dead. And it is not yours."

She didn't say anything for a long moment. He let her have the moment. He'd learned, from her, that a testimony wasn't done being given just because the mouth had stopped moving.

"The first word," he said, when she still hadn't spoken, "the very first sound made over me in that stone room, before the tally, before the numbers, before I had a shell or a name for a shell — was that same word. Requiem." He said it again, plain, the schoolboy shape of it instead of the holy one. "It means rest. That's all it ever meant. They took my name and my hands and nine years underground and the whole of what happened to me in France, and the first word they did it with was the word for rest." He paused, and the pause carried what the sentence before it hadn't. "I have carried that since the stone room without telling a living soul, because there wasn't one soul in this whole gold-lit place who I thought would believe the man with no country that your God's own voice was a dead schoolboy tongue off a Tennessee hillside. I'm telling you because you asked me to say it, and because you've heard it said over your own dead more times than I've heard it said over anything. I thought you should know what you've been hearing."

She sat with the notebook shut in her lap and didn't reach for it. Her hand found the strap of it instead — the specific white-knuckle grip he'd seen on new recruits handling a rifle for the first time, not from lack of respect, from too much of it arriving all at once.

It was Orim who broke first, not her.

He turned from the porthole. It was a small movement — he turned, and stood with his back against the hull, looking at neither of them in particular. His face had the quality Doyle had seen once on a foreman reading a tally that had come up short two shifts running: the look of a man confronting something he'd spent years managing not to look at straight on, and could no longer keep at the distance of the abstract.

"I have said that word," Orim said. "Over field-dead. Over departures. Over you, Doyle, at your own commissioning oath, though you'll have no memory of it being said a second time by a different mouth. I have said it more times than I have fingers and toes to count on, in the tone we are taught denotes reverence, and I did not know, until a minute ago, that I was saying rest the way a stonecutter says it."

His voice was even — not flat, even, the way an instrument reads even when it is accurate on both sides of a scale. "I have read intake reports for forty years. Verlaine commissioning requests. No names. Sphere designation, skill classification, intake number." He looked at the hold floor. "I knew what I was reading. I knew what M-cohort, Sphere thirty-one, intake ninety-seven meant, the way a surgeon knows what a wound classification means without needing to see the patient." He paused. "I told myself I was being accurate. That someone else would do the work if I didn't. That knowing the cost made the cost somehow -" He stopped. "I don't have the word either. Not in Entos. Probably not in any language."

Doyle looked at him.

"I can no longer say I did not hear it," Orim said. "I'm telling you that so you know that I know."

He didn't say more. He turned back to the porthole, fingertips returning to the glass, the passive attunement settling over him like a posture he had held for fifty years because it was the shape that went with hearing things accurately, and accuracy was the only thing he had left to offer anyone.

Doyle looked at the back of Orim's head a moment. Then at Lyra.

She didn't reach for the notebook. She didn't reach for anything. He'd learned, by now, that this was what her particular kind of nothing-to-say looked like from the outside — not empty, just working through something too large to hand back in words yet.

"I'm not asking you to fix it," he said, after a while.

"I know," she said.

"I'm asking you to know it. There's a difference."

"Yes," she said. "There is."

The silence that came after it was a different silence than the one before — not comfortable, not meant to be, but the silence of a thing said and no longer capable of being unsaid, which sat instead of pressing forward. He watched her sit with it. The notebook stayed shut behind her the whole time, through the whole of what he'd given her — the first testimony he'd have bet she'd ever taken down in nothing but memory, nothing a vigil rotation would ever get to close out as no action indicated.

"What do you call this?" Orim asked, from the porthole, without turning. "Not the ship. This — what just happened. In your own tongue."

The question dropped into the quiet like a stone into still water. Nobody answered at once. The envelope kept its argument with the wind. The gray at the portholes had gone from night-gray to the paler gray that meant the sea had decided to be seen.

Doyle said a short phrase in his own language. She caught the shape of it more than the whole of it, and offered the nearest Entos she had.

"The ground undone."

He looked at her. The vowel was wrong; he adjusted it.

"The ground that undid," he said. The construction wasn't quite the shape his own language would have given it, but it was the shape Entos grammar allowed, and it carried the weight regardless — a thing that had been solid, and had stopped being solid, and never told anyone it intended to.

Orim didn't answer that, still facing the water, in the manner of a man who'd asked a small question and gotten back something too large to hand back a reply to.

Lyra found the notebook and opened it. Not in the shape of a research entry — something she didn't yet have an institutional box for. She wrote *the ground that undid*, Doyle's words, and beneath it: *Doyle. Sphere 31. Thursday.*

She closed it.

The Calyx uplands came up on the eastern horizon three hours later — first a darkening in the gray that was more solid than sky, the specific dark of a thing that had stood in the same place a long time and did not intend to move for the wind's convenience. Then the particular black of high karst country, the gray limestone she'd told him weeks back she'd only ever studied on cartographic plates, and was now, abruptly, simply seeing.

The wheel by the aft bulkhead began, without a hand on it, to answer to a hand somewhere else — Balthier gathering herself for the descent to come, a held breath about to let go. He'd have to go back into her soon, down into the river gorge by feel, same as he'd lifted her clear of Sal Vento; the small shell that carried the rest of him would go still again on the floor, and somebody would need to stand near it, because a shell with nothing in it was a shell anyone could claim. He'd stopped finding that strange around month three. It was just a fact of travel now, like weather.

Lyra looked at the coast.

She'd told him once, some evening weeks back when neither of them could sleep, about a Relic she'd recovered years before this one — a tangled Verlaine provenance dispute, the better part of a season's work. She'd been thirty-two, entirely certain of herself, wrong about two of three key facts and right about the outcome anyway, and had set the whole business aside as a lesson in professional humility before moving to the next assignment.

She didn't have that certainty in her now. He recognized the look anyway — the bearing of somebody handed a fact that restructures everything standing behind it, walking forward into ground she hadn't had time to survey. He didn't know if she'd trained for uncertainty or just gotten used to other people's. Tonight looked like the first time it had been entirely her own.

Doyle came to stand beside her at the forward porthole.

He didn't speak at first. He looked at the coast. She looked at the coast.

After a while he said, in Entos: "What will you do with it? When you have it?"

He meant the Relic, and she knew it without him needing to spell out which them. Not a weapon, whatever Sanctorin actually wanted from it — not by her own account, given to him weeks back over a different fire. The founding canon called it the Eye That Remembers and never explained further, and she'd told him once, half-laughing at herself, that she'd served the Vigil seventeen years without ever once asking why a thing built only to remember needed three locks, a vigil rotation, and a Canon's countersignature standing between it and anyone who might want to look.

"I don't know yet," she said.

"But not what they want you to do with it."

She looked at him.

"You would have given it to them, before Bressant," he said. "I don't know who them is. But you would have. You were the kind of person who gave things to the right authority."

"And now?" she asked.

"Now you know I am in the authority's files."

She looked at Calyx, closer now, more specific — the scarps resolving into individual faces of old-bone rock in the coming light, the moor somewhere above them she couldn't yet see but knew was there.

"Yes," she said.

He nodded. He turned from the porthole and went to find a place to settle before the ship began her descent — a place near enough to his shell that when it went still, someone guarding it would only have to look, not search. He felt her watch him go.

Caer Glas was ahead, close enough now that the moor above the scarps had come clear in the gray, green going black going green again as cloud crossed it. He stood a while longer near the place he'd chosen, not because there was anything more to see there than a minute before, but because a man who has just spent the whole of what he was carrying needs somewhere to stand while his hands remember what to do with themselves.

He'd told it in order, the way he'd promised himself he would — the mine, the France of it, the stone room, the number that ate his name, and the last thing, carried longest, said last on purpose. It didn't feel like relief. It felt like a weight handed off to somebody with two working hands to carry it, instead of one man alone in a gold-lit hold with nobody who'd believe him.

Behind him, he heard the notebook open, and then, after a while, close again without the pen ever having moved on it.

Somewhere below decks a lamp had gone out and been relit with a different fuel — yggdra kindling, the ship's own dry stock of it, and the smoke of it came up through the grate at his feet before the wind took it. He went still over it for exactly as long as the earlier stillness had taken him, out at the trees, before the Rod had failed. Not the same stillness. A softer one, the kind a man doesn't fight.

Lyra didn't ask.

She'd learned enough of his stillnesses tonight to know this one wasn't hers to have — not because he'd said so, he hadn't said a word about it, but because a man who spends an entire night handing over everything a stone room and a war took from him does not owe the one thing he chose, on his own, to keep. She had a name for what he was doing, from her own life, though she'd never once needed the exact fit of it before tonight: some doors you don't knock on twice, because the first knock already told you there was somebody standing on the other side of it, holding still, hoping you'd walk on.

She let him have it. He never told her the smoke reminded him of anything, and she never asked what it was he wasn't saying. It was, she thought, the only part of the whole testimony that hadn't cost him something to give her — because he hadn't given it to her at all, and they had both, without a word passing between them on the subject, agreed that was exactly as it should stay.

Caer Glas was ahead. He left Lyra with what he'd given her, because that was hers to carry now, the same as the rest of it.

## Caer Glas Moor

Lyra found the moor the way Wren had said she would — by the smell first, wet stone and old iron, and then by the particular quality of quiet a piece of ground keeps when a great many people have died on it and nobody since has found a use for it worth the trespass.

"They'll have made camp on the east lip," Wren said. "High ground, sightlines both ways down the gorge. It's what I'd have told Esvane to do, if she'd asked, and she never once needed telling."

"You know her that well."

"I know the ground. She trained me on ground like it for two years before she ever trusted me on this one." He did not look away from the ridge while he said it. "Trusting the ground and trusting the man standing on it were two different lessons. I only ever finished the first one."

Doyle's scan found the fire twenty minutes later — a thin grey thread rising where the wind should have scattered it and hadn't, which meant somebody was tending it carefully enough to keep it low and warm rather than bright and visible. Professional discipline. Esvane's discipline, specifically, the kind that didn't change just because the job had gone wrong.

Orim watched Wren watch the smoke a moment longer than the smoke required.

"Last chance," Orim said, not unkindly. "Nobody would follow you up there and call it a betrayal of anything, if you'd rather not be the one standing in front of her when this happens."

"She'd know I sent someone else." Wren shouldered the strap of nothing he was carrying — old habit, an empty hand still bracing for a weight that wasn't there. "I'd rather she see the whole of it. She taught me that much, at least — a debt gets paid in person, or it doesn't count as paid."

The fire went out from under Esvane and Petra both at once — Esvane's doing, a heartbeat before anyone understood anything else, because putting out your own fire before you can be sure who's found it was the second lesson she had ever taught anyone and the only one that had actually kept people alive.

She saw Wren before she said anything. He watched her see him — watched the half-second where whatever she'd have said if it had been strangers on that ridge simply didn't arrive, and something else took its place instead, flat and final and entirely without surprise in it.

"Of course," she said. Not to him. To the general unfairness of a universe that worked this way. "Of course it's you standing there."

"Esvane -"

"Don't," she said, and drew.

He never afterward could put the order of it back together right, only the pieces of the bill as it came due. Esvane turning — too late, the only warning any of them got. Doyle's shape inside her guard before she'd finished the turn, the rifle stock into her forearm to spoil the draw, two rounds close enough that the report and the impact arrived as one event instead of two. She went down against the cairn stone with the particular finality of a body that had simply stopped taking instructions, and whatever she was owed for twenty-three years of hard knowledge went out of her eyes with no more ceremony than a lamp starved of oil.

"Wren." Not fear in it. Command, right to the end of her. "Go."

That was her whole payment to him, spent in a single word on the boy who had already gone, and he had no way to make change on it either way.

Petra was already moving, and he understood a half-second too late what she'd seen that he hadn't — not flight, angle, fifteen years of finding soft gates translating on the instant into finding the one place a body could stand between an archer's line and a boy who had never fully belonged to any of them.

His whole body had already started the motion that would have carried him clear — the automatic first half-inch of a fold before conscious thought caught up to it — and it went nowhere, because there was no fold in the world that put him between an arrow already loosed and the woman who had decided, before he'd finished flinching, that this was hers to take instead of his.

The bolt that should have opened his back found her instead, low, under the ribs, and she went down without a sound that carried past the wind working the gorge, one hand still closed around the coil of wire she'd been needling him about a minute before. The wind kept working the gorge exactly as it had all morning, indifferent to the difference between one heartbeat and the next, and for that one heartbeat his legs would not carry him the two steps to where she had fallen.

He went to his knees beside her because there was a debt in that, too, and it took exactly as long as it took to understand there was nothing left to pay it with. His hands found the wound before his mind agreed to look at it — too much give under the cloth where there should have been none — and some old habit in him went on assessing anyway: too low, too deep, no fold in the world that reached from where he knelt to wherever the bolt had already taken her.

Her mouth moved. No sound came out with it. Her hand was still closed around the coil of wire she'd been needling him about a minute before, and he left it closed, because her hand had chosen, at the end, to be holding something instead of nothing, and that seemed like the one thing left he had no right to undo.

He would carry that unfinished sentence the rest of his life, the elegy that never got past its first breath, and there would be no ledger anywhere that let him close the entry.

They found the case where Esvane had set it down, careful even in her last unhurried minutes, on a flat shelf of rock a man could find again in the dark. Doyle lifted it like something worth more than everything else in the conversation — carefully, and without opening it.

Nobody had opened it. Wren had told them that much three nights back, on the road, in the flat recitation of a man reporting facts he'd rather not have owned in the first place — that the box had come out of Ocipheus already locked, that none of the three of them had so much as tried the latch, because a professional in this trade learned early which boxes you carried and which boxes you asked questions about, and this had been, from the first hour, very much the second kind. He'd seen inside it exactly once, in the archive, in the half-second between Esvane lifting it and the alarm starting — warm light, wet at the edges, a shape he still didn't have honest words for — and had spent every night since being grateful he'd never had to decide whether to look again.

"Wet at the edges how," Lyra had said.

"Weeping. Like something that hadn't finished healing." He'd looked at the case like a debt he'd already decided wasn't his to pay. "I wouldn't touch it. For what that's worth."

It was worth exactly as much as she made of it, which turned out to be very little. She took the case from Doyle now without ceremony — the same flat claiming she gave most things that were, from this morning on, unambiguously hers to carry.

Behind her, Orim had gone very quiet, the particular quiet that came before he said something he'd been saving.

"Not yet," she told him, before he could. "Whatever it is, it can wait until we're somewhere the dead don't have to listen to us discuss it."

They buried what there was to bury, which was not much, and left the moor the way they'd found it — quiet, unclaimed, waiting on an account forty-one years overdue that today had settled without actually closing.

Wren did not look back at it, walking out. He had, by then, nothing left behind him worth the look.

The fog at Caer Glas Moor did not fall like rain elsewhere falls. It simply arrived at ground level and declined to leave, a grey that sat in the folds of the karst like water that had forgotten how to run downhill, and through it the moor-hounds could be heard before they could be seen — a low working conversation from the kennels below the hall, dogs bred for generations to track a scent across broken limestone and never once asked to track this one. Wren had grown up under this particular grey. He walked into it now the way a man walks into a house he still owes rent on and has stopped pretending he doesn't.

The hall at Caer Glas Moor was older than the battle it commemorated, which made it older than most things that called themselves old. Its outer wall still carried, at shoulder height, the pale scar-line where the original stone had been cut back and reset after the Nine Days fighting had gone through it — a repair visible the same as Calyx stonework was visible everywhere, not concealed, not apologized for, simply there, doing its work. He had rehearsed telling Lyra about it a hundred times on the road here and said none of it, because at the vault door she stopped on her own — a habit she'd picked up with doors since — and read the line cut into the lintel long enough ago that the letters had worn as soft as the ones at Twr Brennid.

*Nine days the field held. On the eighth, it broke.*

"Everyone agrees on the nine," Wren said, at her shoulder, in the flat voice of a man reciting something he had been given before he was old enough to argue with it. The words came up in his chest before he'd thought to shape them, the way a hymn comes up in a body that learned it before it learned to want anything else — and some part of him that was still eleven years old, kneeling on the cold floor of this exact hall, straightened without asking him the moment he started.

"The battle ran nine days. That much the records match on both sides — Liturgy and Calyx, the Ocipheus canon and the family rolls. It is the eighth day nobody agrees on. Seven witnesses gave seven accounts of what happened when my ancestor's man went down under the Liturgy banner — his Champion, if you want the wall's word for it, though nobody in this house has used it plainly in forty-one years — and the case left Calyx hands, and none of the seven match, and there was never an eighth witness to settle it. My family has been counting that day for forty-one years. It is said Pallor's Long Seat keeps a gap of the same shape. We got there first, on our own ground — we did not need Pallor to teach us how to count what we do not have."

He looked at the lintel a moment longer than he needed to. The letters didn't need reading anymore — he'd had them by heart since before he could read anything else — but looking at them was a discipline, the same one that had put him on his knees on this floor as a boy until the recitation came out clean and unhurried, no matter what was actually happening in his chest while he said it.

"I told you I grew up with it. This is the it."

Einmar was waiting past the vault door, in a room that held the family's accounting much as the Long Seat was said to hold Entos's - corrected genealogies on every wall, the newest entries the cleanest because they had not yet been proven wrong. One volume on the table between the chairs had never been corrected, not in the forty-one years since, because there was nothing to correct it with: a slim iron-bound ledger, its spine stamped in the family's own hand, The Calyx Family's Eighth-Day Account of the Battle of the Nine Days. Seven testimonies inside it. No eighth. There had never been an eighth to add. He looked older than he had looked on the moor the day before, which should not have been possible in one night, and Wren knew, better than Lyra could, that yesterday's collapse had not finished; it had simply stopped being visible from a distance. The Log had carried the shape of it ahead of them, the way it carried everything now - no names, no particulars, only a garrisoned-post relay confirming a Calyx contractor down and a recovery party inbound, enough for a man who'd been waiting forty-one years for bad news to know which kind had finally come. There was a chair near the hearth with a folded grey cloak across its arm that nobody had moved. Wren did not call it mourning, even in his own head. It was Esvane's coat, empty.

Wren let himself look at it exactly once - a door he already knew better than to open - and made himself finish the room instead - the genealogies, the ledger, the two chairs - before his eyes could go back to it. He remembered the collar of it gone thin and pale from years of the same hand turning it up against harbor wind, and put the memory down carefully, the way he'd learned to put down anything he couldn't afford to hold.

"You came for the rest of it," Einmar said. Not a question.

"Esvane would have made you wait for tea first. I do not have her patience for the forms."

He said her name and did not stop or falter, which Wren recognized as an injury, the wound already past the stage where it announced itself. Wren said nothing to that either. He had spent half his childhood learning exactly how much of his uncle's grief he was permitted to acknowledge, and the old rule held even now, with Esvane's coat six feet from both of them and neither man looking at it.

Lyra told him what she had seen at the Forge Hearth, because he asked, in the same plain forensic terms Wren had heard her rehearsing under her breath for a hundred kilometers of road, not knowing then who she meant to finally say them to: the membrane at Hearth-Seven slack and overpigmented, healing at maximum load and still losing ground; Orim's Rod meeting nothing at Hearth-Eleven, not resistance, not membrane, an absence where a door should have been. Einmar listened as Esvane must have taught him to, without interrupting, and when she finished he did not offer comfort or contradiction. He offered the family's seven.

"Seven days of the nine are agreed history," he said.

"The eighth is where the accounts stop matching and the family has never closed the file, because closing it would mean choosing which witness lied, and every Calyx Knight in the forty-one years since has looked at the seven and found himself unable to make the eighth match any of them cleanly. We do not call it recognition, the way Pallor's Long Seat is said to. We call it the day nobody can agree on. It comes to the same shape. Whatever you have assembled on the road here, the eighth of it is not going to be handed to you by me or by anyone at this hearth. It is in the ground at Sinter, the same as it was on the eighth day of the battle — not withheld, just not yet witnessed by anyone who could tell it straight afterward."

"That is not comforting," Lyra said.

"No," Einmar agreed.

"It is just old. My family found out a long time ago that some things only resolve when you are standing where they happened, with everything you already know in your hands, and that no account given afterward, however honest, carries the same weight as the standing did. Esvane used to say the law works the same way. You can write the finding. You cannot write the moment the finding became true."

Wren kept his eyes on the fire because it was easier than keeping them on the cloak, and because hearing her name said plainly, in this room, in Einmar's flat recounting voice, did something to his throat he had no intention of explaining to either of them. He had heard her say that line herself, more than once, to some magistrate too pleased with a verdict to notice how little it had settled. It was strange, hearing it come out of a mouth that had never once heard her say it — stranger still that Einmar had gotten the cadence right anyway.

He looked at the folded cloak on the chair and did not touch it.

"Wren will tell you the same, if you make him. It is the one part of this house he never had reason to doubt."

Wren did not correct him and did not confirm it, and found, searching himself for the argument he should have had ready, that there wasn't one.

Einmar looked at Wren for a long moment, the particular look of a man weighing something he had weighed before and did not enjoy repeating.

"You could stay," he said. "Officially. I could write the account so the fifth cousin acquitted himself well and lost good people doing it honorably, and the House would believe what I wrote, because I am the one who writes it." He did not make it sound like an offer, exactly. "You would be received. Fed. Given a room with your name already carved somewhere on this wall, because it always was. And in a year, perhaps two, somebody with a better claim and worse patience would start asking why the boy who lost Esvane and Petra came home instead of finishing the job they'd been sent to do — and I would not always be the one left answering for you."

"I know how the house talks," Wren said.

"I know you know. I am telling you anyway, because your cousin never did, and I have had thirty years to notice what that cost you." Einmar looked at the cloak on the chair once more, and still did not touch it. "There is no clean account here, Wren. Only the one you can live inside. A hero's welcome and a target on your back, or a long walk with strangers into ground that kills Champions. I am not going to pretend those are equally bad choices. I am only telling you that neither one is safe, so you at least get to choose which unsafe you'd rather carry."

Wren did not answer him that night.

He answered three days later, on the road east, when Lyra asked him — not why he was still walking with them, but how far he meant to go.

"Further than Calyx would ever let me stop," he said. "I've spent my whole life being somewhere I was sent. I would like to find out, once, what it's like to be somewhere I chose." He adjusted the case's strap on his shoulder, the way he always did when he wanted his hands to have something correct to do. "And I would like to know if what Petra and Esvane spent themselves on was worth it. Calyx will never tell me that. Calyx doesn't ask the question."

Wren did not disagree. He was seven the first time someone let the shape of the debt slip in front of him without meaning to - a groom in the yard, talking past him as adults do past children they've forgotten are listening, saying only that the family had been owed something for forty-one years and would likely go on being owed it. He had not understood the words. He had understood, instantly and completely, the tone - the particular flatness reserved for debts nobody actually expected to see paid.

He carried it the same way now, one day added to the count: Esvane and Petra, the ledger not even opened yet. Two accounts, forty-one years apart, neither one closing.

He did not look at his uncle when he said it. His hands, at his sides, had gone still with the specific effort of hands that needed to not shake. Einmar did not look away.

Three days before any of that — before the road east, before the answer he'd give her there — Lyra had asked Einmar for a moment alone before they left.

Wren did not ask why. He had learned young which doors in this house closed on him and which didn't, and this, apparently, was still one of them. Einmar only nodded and led him out, and the vault door shut behind them with the particular weight Calyx doors were built to have, meant to be heard closing. They stood in the corridor without speaking, the cold coming up off the flagstones the way it always had in this part of the house, no matter the season.

Wren had waited outside this door before, as a boy, small enough that the corridor had seemed to run the length of the house, counting the joints between the flagstones because counting was a thing a body could do with its hands full of nothing. He had been told he would understand once he was older. He understood now that he had grown up and the door had not, and that the only thing that had changed since was how much he now had waiting on the other side of it to lose.

Einmar did not fill the silence, and Wren did not ask him to. It was, of the two of them, the closest thing to comfortable either had managed all day.

When Lyra came out she had the case at her hip and a stillness on her that had not been there going in — the particular quiet of someone who has just been shown something they cannot immediately afford to react to, her eyes somewhere past the corridor wall, still half in whatever the vault had shown her.

She did not make him ask. She told him, plainly: the Relic had shown her the theft itself, the archive at Caer Glas Moor on the night it happened, seen through the hands of the one who took it, and those hands had moved with the specific deliberateness of someone who meant to return what he was removing. She had already known who. The Relic had only confirmed what kind of taking it had been.

Wren said nothing to that. There was no debt in it he could pay from where he stood, and he had learned not to reach for one that wasn't his to settle. He kept his hands loose at his sides instead, the old discipline of a man who had spent a childhood in this house learning exactly how much of another person's grief was actually his to carry, and found, as he so often did lately, that the answer was less than he wanted and more than he could put down.

Outside, the fog had begun to lift off the lower slopes, and their gear was already loaded and lashed in the yard, Doyle moving down the line of it with the flat patience the shell brought to every mechanical task, Orim watching the moor the way a man watches ground he has been told is haunted and has decided, professionally, to believe. The cold had teeth in it this early, and Wren felt it settle into the shoulder that always took weather first these days, an old ache that had nothing to do with folding and everything to do with sleeping badly in this house even as a boy.

Wren crossed the yard with the eighth theory still an open shape in him, no closer to filled than it had been at the vault door, and understood that his own house had given Lyra exactly what Pallor's would have given her — not an answer, a map, drawn by a different hand on the same ground — and both maps pointed the same direction: south and east, toward the last friendly port before the Gate. He was leaving Caer Glas Moor with the family's account no more settled than when he'd ridden in, and two new names on a different ledger that would never balance against it either. He did not say that. He shouldered his kit and went to help Doyle finish.

He did not look back at the hall before the road bent and took the choice away from him. He never did. It was one of the few habits he'd kept from that first year on the road with Esvane and Petra, and he had never worked out whether it was discipline or just a way of not having to know what he would feel if he looked.

They went on toward Port Gadriket, and whatever her sister had sent ahead in her place.

## The Road East

The road east from Caer Glas Moor gave them time the moor itself never had, and it was somewhere on that stretch — the third day, the fourth, Orim stopped marking exactly which — that he first watched Lyra settle into a habit he recognized without needing to be told where she'd learned it.

She carried the Oculus Lacrimans Vigilantiae now, sealed in its travel case — no heavier in the hand than a good lantern, for something that remembered seven hundred years — packed at the center of her kit with a weight distribution she was still working out by trial, the hard road teaching her faster than he could have. He had given her the cloth without explaining why the case sweated, and she had not asked him to account for it since, which he took, correctly, as a kind of trust she had not yet had full cause to extend. Every second evening, sometimes sooner if the day had been wet, she unsealed the lid and found the lining faintly damp, faintly warm, as though the thing inside ran a low fever of its own that never broke. She wiped it down with the soft cloth he had given her for the purpose, and the cloth came away beaded gold at the folds, a thin bright residue she rinsed clean in the nearest water without once pressing him for an accounting. Then she re-laid the lining and re-sealed the case and packed it back into the kit the way you'd settle a sleeping animal that had only just quieted. Not yet a question she had put words to. Only a habit her hands were still learning to perform for something that could not perform it for itself.

He did not say any of this to her. He kept walking beside her instead, at the pace the case's weight had taught her to set, and let that be the whole of what he offered.

They lost the light two hours before they meant to. The road narrowed, the tree cover came in over it, and her shoulders were already up around her ears by the time she noticed.

The whistle came first — deliberately human, pitched to carry over hooves — and it was answered from the far side of the track before she had finished turning her head. Five of them, maybe six, coming out of the treeline in the particular ragged discipline of men who had once had uniforms and had since had time to think about what the uniforms had cost them.

"Deserters," Doyle said, already turning his shoulder toward the nearest one. "Verlaine cut, by the boots. Hungry, not stupid."

Hungry was the dangerous kind. Hungry did not want the argument. Hungry wanted the case at her hip and an estimate of what taking it would cost. She stepped between them and the wagon and gave them the estimate — sword out, weight back, nothing said.

The one in front — broad, missing two fingers on his sword hand and compensating for it with an economy of motion that said he'd had a year to practice — had already worked out that the small dark shape leaning slack against the wagon wheel was worth nothing and the case at her own hip was worth everything, and he came at Doyle's undefended flank the half-second Doyle's attention went somewhere it couldn't come back from in time.

It should have worked. Lyra was still three strides out and knew it.

Wren was not.

He did not run the distance. He was simply between the deserter and Doyle's shell, with no ground crossed to get there. The downswing met air. It kept going, because a man's weight goes where he sent it whether the target is still standing there or not, and it carried him a half-step past his own guard — which was all Wren needed to put the knife in under his ribs from behind.

The deserter went down without understanding why. The others understood a great deal faster, and reconsidered the whole encounter in the time it took two of them to look at each other.

"That's not possible," one of them said, backing up.

"It's not," Wren agreed, and did it again — not far, four feet, enough to put himself behind the man's shoulder instead of in front of it — and after that there wasn't much of an argument left to have.

The rest ran. Lyra let them.

She found Wren afterward wiping the blade on a fistful of dead leaves, methodical, not looking at what he'd done to earn the wipe.

"You could have told us that's what it looks like," she said.

"You'd have wanted a demonstration," he said. "This was cheaper."

"How far can you go? At once, I mean. Not blinking — the other one, through things."

"Far enough that it's never once been the reason I lost a fight." He straightened, folded the knife away. "Far enough that it costs something every time, which is the only part worth remembering."

He didn't say what it cost. She didn't ask, not yet. But he had gone grey around the mouth in the last four feet of that fight, and he had not gone grey once in the fight before it.

The common room at Greilsburg held about as many bodies as the Number Four washhouse on a Saturday, and smelled about the same — wet wool, coal smoke, spilled beer gone sour in the floorboards. Nobody had looked at their table twice in an hour. That suited him.

Orim was two mugs into something the innkeeper called wine and the company store back home would have sold as vinegar, and had got to the part of an evening where whatever he said came out shorter and further from the point. Lyra had her back to the wall on principle, watching the room with the same restless attention she gave everything, half a conversation behind because she'd never learned how to just sit in a place.

"There's no more," the innkeeper had said, an hour back, setting down what turned out to be the house's last bottle of anything worth drinking. "Cellar's dry till the cart comes Thursday."

Wren hadn't said anything. Wren had just looked, briefly, at the floor.

Doyle caught it. Verlaine had spent a year teaching him to watch where hands went, and had never once asked whether he wanted the skill.

Ten minutes later Wren reached down to retie a bootlace that didn't need retying, one hand dropping under the table for perfectly boring reasons, and for about as long as it takes to say the word "gone" it simply wasn't there anymore — not under the table, not attached to anything, gone into whatever Wren went into when he went — and then it was back, holding a bottle with a cellar's worth of dust still on the shoulder of it, and nobody in the packed common room had looked over even once.

"Innkeeper said there wasn't any more," Doyle said, flat, not quite a question.

"There wasn't any more upstairs," Wren said, and worked the cork with his belt knife like a man who'd done it a hundred times in rooms exactly this loud. "Man never counted what's still down in the cold end of the cellar behind the good cask. I looked."

"You looked from here."

"I looked from here."

Orim, three mugs deep by then, turned the bottle once in his hands, read the dust on the shoulder and the hand-cut wax under it, and settled on: "Well. That's one use for it nobody's account of the Nine Days ever mentioned."

"Family gift," Wren said, pouring. "Nobody ever taught me it was for anything grander than this. I found the grand uses myself, mostly this year, mostly because I had to."

He didn't say it like a complaint. Doyle let that sit. He'd heard a lot of men explain what they were good at. That was the first one he'd believed.

"To the cellar," Orim said, raising his mug, "and every locked thing that ever stood between a man and what he actually needed."

They drank to it. Lyra, Doyle noticed, was smiling into her own mug in a way she probably thought nobody at the table could see.

## The Senior Scribe

The dispatch note arrived at the sixth hour, on paper thin enough that Vega could see the Second Chancery's watermark through it before she'd broken the seal — a nice touch, that, the kind of institutional vanity she had always found more endearing than a serious notary probably should. She read the clause twice before she let herself have a feeling about it, because that was the rule she had made for herself in this job: the instrument first, the person second. The instrument was short. The feeling, when she finally let it in, was not.

She had been at her desk since the fourth hour, which was not unusual. She arrived at the fourth and departed at the fourteenth and had been doing so for three years, and the Liturgy's administrative schedule had arranged itself around this without comment, same as it arranged itself around good furniture: with a gratitude that never rose to acknowledgment. She had her desk. The desk faced two windows. The windows faced the courtyard. The courtyard was empty most days. This was the shape of her work, and she had always rather liked the shape of it — there was a pleasure, wasn't there, in a life you could describe in one sentence and have the sentence be true?

The dispatch was from the Office of the Senior Scribe. Not Subcanon Malvar's office, not the Canon's administrative staff, not anyone in the vertical line she filed things upward to. The Office of the Senior Scribe was a horizontal function — advisory, archival, the Liturgy's institutional memory rather than its executive arm, which was a distinction Vega had found, the first time someone explained it to her, unreasonably satisfying. It had been housed in the same three rooms since Year 1105 and was staffed, currently, by one woman who had been in those rooms for forty-one years and had made herself, in that time, as indispensable as the furniture and considerably harder to move.

Senior Scribe Brentha Osel. Vega had met her twice. Once at the orientation for new Registry appointments, where Osel had delivered a three-minute address on the canonical responsibility of the witness function that Vega had found, at the time, professionally sound and personally uninspiring — she had even, God forgive her, taken notes on the phrasing rather than the substance, because the phrasing was better than the substance deserved. Once in the corridor outside the map archive, where Osel had stopped her and asked, without preamble, whether she had found it interesting.

Vega had asked: found what interesting?

Osel had said: the work. And walked on, leaving Vega to turn the question over for the better part of a week — a clause that read simply and wasn't.

The dispatch note itself was brief, brief in the particular way that meant somebody had drafted six longer versions first.

V. Athen-Moor — You are requested to present yourself at the Office of the Senior Scribe at the eighth hour. Bring your notary seal. — B. Osel

No travel instruments. She noticed that — she noticed everything — and then noticed herself noticing it, and set both aside, unwilling to have an opinion about either one yet. She read the note twice more and folded it into her working-copy folder, which was not where it belonged — it belonged in correspondence — but the working-copy folder was what she had been carrying with her everywhere for eight months, and the dispatch was now part of the same pattern as everything else inside it, and the pattern was where it belonged, whatever the filing schema said.

She had two hours. She spent them at her desk, working through the routine instrument queue with the methodical focus that had always been her professional strength and had become, lately, something she leaned on more heavily than she used to. Methodical focus was the one thing she still had full access to. She could look at an instrument and see its form, assess its completeness, certify its disposition, even when — especially when — the instrument was one small tile in a mosaic she was also, separately, trying to see the whole of. The two processes ran in parallel. She had learned to let them.

At the eighth hour she went to reach for her travel bag out of some old instinct she caught herself in the act of — packed, she realized with a certain wry alarm, from a week ago, for no destination she had let herself name — and then did not pick it up. Bring your notary seal, the note had said. Not the bag. She left the bag exactly where it was, put the seal in her coat instead, and went to the Office of the Senior Scribe with the specific, slightly chastened feeling of a woman catching her own hope before it could embarrass her.

Brentha Osel was seventy-three and looked it plainly: accurately, without distress, the years worn as information rather than apology. Her desk was smaller than Vega's and covered in materials that were not canonical instruments — reference compendiums, historical registers, the bound record of a review session from Year 1337 that Vega recognized by its binding stamp before she recognized anything written on it, and set it aside. Osel looked at her exactly as she had in the corridor: deciding how much of what she knew she was going to say.

"You've been keeping a working copy," Osel said.

It was not a question.

"Yes."

"For how long?"

"Eight months."

Osel was quiet a moment, turning the Year 1337 record over without opening it.

"The current Canon Immaculate has been in his position for eleven years," she said. "Before him, Subcanon Treye Falconer held it for twenty-three years and retired to farm his family's land in Calyx. Before Falconer, Canon Immaculate Amaris Dort held it for thirty-one years and died at her desk." She set the record down. "During the current tenure, the Vigil line's garrison rotation was extended from eight months to twelve, and six months ago the Liturgy's permanent contingency reserve was unsealed under a standing-order renewal certified by a Registry notary." She looked at Vega directly. "You certified it."

"Yes." She heard her own voice do the small flat thing it did when it wanted to sound more composed than she was.

"Did you read the form?"

"It was correct."

"The form is always correct," Osel said. "The Canon Immaculate's office is very good at correct forms — I have never once caught them in a comma out of place, which ought to be a comfort and somehow never is." Her chair creaked as she turned in it, an old sound from an old chair. "The deployment roster for the war construct evaluation cohort. Did it come through your queue?"

"No. The evaluation certifications came through. The roster itself was convened under Article Eighteen."

"Membrane-breach classification." Osel nodded once, as though confirming an answer she had already written down somewhere. "The breach they were authorized against has not been publicly announced." A pause, not for effect — for accuracy, the kind Vega herself would have insisted on. "It's the Sinter Zone."

Vega said nothing for a moment, which for her was a confession — she was a woman who filled silences the way other people filled forms, promptly and by habit, and the fact that she didn't now told Osel everything the silence was designed to withhold. The working copy was in her bag. She had reached that conclusion three weeks earlier and had spent the three weeks since hoping it was wrong, the specific hope of a woman waiting for a citation to turn out misprinted, right up until she checked the original and it wasn't.

"I can't stop it," Osel said. She said this plainly, with the flatness of a thing that is true and unpleasant and has been lived with long enough to stop requiring feeling. "I have been a notary for forty-one years and a Senior Scribe for twelve of those, and the thing I was given the authority to do is witness and record. I do not authorize. I do not command. I do not stop." She folded her hands on the desk. "What I do is write it down. And what the canonical instrument set will require, when it is convened at the Zone, is a notary present at the record's edge before the record closes over it."

"The instruments haven't been convened yet," Vega said.

"No. They haven't." Osel held her eyes. "When they are convened and sealed, they cannot be unsealed. What a notary observes beforehand, in the conduct of her professional preparation function, is a different category of record entirely — a lovely piece of drafting, that distinction, I've always admired whoever first thought to write it in. It's the only door in the whole architecture that opens the wrong way." She turned the Year 1337 record over once more, not opening it — the unnecessary handling of a woman who already knew what was in it. "The Liturgy does not keep a vault to keep things safe, Athen-Moor. It keeps a vault to keep things unusable. I have watched it do that with smaller truths than this one for forty-one years." She let that sit. "I need a record at the Sinter Zone before Sanctorin convenes the instrument set. A record of what has been moving north. One whose seal is already on the account of what happened at the crater aperture before that account has been authorized for redaction."

"You're sending me to be a witness."

"I'm sending you to be the record," Osel said. "These are not the same thing."

She let this settle too, patient as sediment.

"I can't send your body," Osel said, and here, for the first time, something almost gentle came into it. "You know the arithmetic as well as I do. Ocipheus keeps every road ending at a quay — that's half of what being from here means, the knowledge in the bone that you cannot simply walk away from this place. The fastest hull on the water is eight weeks to the Gate on a fair wind, and Sanctorin does not need eight weeks to convene an instrument set. By the time you made landfall the thing you were sent to witness would already be sealed, and you'd have crossed an ocean to arrive precisely too late — which is, I promise you, the single worst outcome available, worse even than not going." She almost smiled. "Ink is faster than you are, Athen-Moor. It has always been the only thing in this world faster than a person. That's the entire reason the Liturgy bothered inventing notaries."

"Then your sister is there, or will be. Dame Lyra." Osel said the name without particular affect. "Not because I arranged it. Because the recovery instrument pointed that direction, and so did your sister's competence, and so did the fact that she cannot, under any circumstances, leave alone a thing she has been told to leave alone." Something in Osel's face came as close to warmth as it appeared able to come. "I thought you should know, before I tell you what I actually need from you."

Vega took a breath and let it go, and made herself ask the question in the shape it deserved rather than the shape she wanted.

"What do you need me to do?" she asked.

"Write it," Osel said. "Seal it. Send it ahead of her."

She said this in the tone of someone who had given the instruction before, or who had held it long enough that the giving of it had become necessary rather than merely practiced. Vega understood the difference. She had spent three years learning to hear it.

The Templar order kept archives the way the Registry kept queues — small, unglamorous, load-bearing. A waystation was three rooms and a courier roster and, in every one Vega had ever certified paperwork for, an archivist whose entire professional life was making sure that whatever arrived sealed stayed sealed until the person it was addressed to arrived to break it. Every waystation kept a second road as well as the archive — a sealed shape at the yard's edge, wired for Morse, that could put a message on some other Station's terminal glass before a ship had even cleared the harbor mouth. But a Log arrived readable by whichever Infused Templar was standing at the terminal when it came in; it did not arrive sealed for one pair of eyes only, and what Vega meant to write was not, in the end, Log traffic. The waystations sat along the roads a Templar travelled because a Templar had to be able to find one, which meant that once Osel's people confirmed the line Lyra's party was cutting east — the same recovery instrument, the same stubborn unwillingness to leave a thing alone — the road told you where the archives were before anyone told you anything else.

Vega did not sail to Sinter. She could not — the days would not add up, and a body that set out now would make landfall a season too late to be anything but a mourner at a grave already sealed. So she would send the record by ship, as Osel had told her to, and let ink do the travelling a person couldn't. What Osel had not needed to be told was the other half of it: that a notary who set the words Sinter Zone under her own seal, who wrote P-7-R out in her own hand, could not afterward go back to a desk facing an empty courtyard and wait to be thanked. The instruments would leave Averlyne. So, and soon, would she — though not east to the Gate, and not toward her sister. That road belonged to some later chapter of her life than this one.

What she did first was write.

The first instrument went out on a Loera packet inside nine days — the same low fast two-master line that carried the Registry's ordinary mail, the purser writing Registry, north-bound, Port Gadriket in the manifest hand she used for everything, no different from a hundred other sealed cases she had carried without asking what was in them.

It was the smallest of the three documents Vega would eventually write, and the most careful: a notarized account of Article Eighteen's true classification, the war construct evaluation cohort's actual convening cause, the words Sinter Zone set down in her own hand under her own seal where no later redaction could pretend the words had never existed.

She dated it. She did not sign it as Vega. She signed it as the Registry required a witness instrument to be signed, which was, she thought, the honest way — the record didn't need her name. It needed her seal.

The second went nine days after that, once the requisition paperwork for the reserve's movement crossed her own queue and she recognized, before she had finished reading the routing code, the property mark she had certified the unsealing of six months before: P-7-R.

She had not seen the ships. She did not need to. She had seen the instrument that told the ships where to go, twice now — once when she certified its unsealing without reading what it truly was, and once now, watching the same reserve's transit paperwork arrive for her signature as though nothing about it had changed since.

The contingency reserve has been unsealed three times in recorded canonical history, she wrote. The Year 1312 catastrophe. The Atrament border action of Year 1354. And now, in material transit, toward the Sinter Zone, under a standing-order renewal I certified myself.

She looked at that sentence for a while, the way she had learned to. Then she wrote, beneath it: I am not the person who authorized its release. I am the person who certified the authorization. She did not underline it. She did not need to.

The second document went to the waystation at Port Gadriket, filed under the Templar archivist's own seal on top of hers, to wait in a room with a window on the harbor for a party of five that had not yet arrived and would not know, walking in off the muster, that the record had beaten them there.

The third she wrote last, and it took her longer than the other two combined, because it was the one that mattered and she had never in her professional life had to draft something that mattered in quite this particular direction. A canonical witness instrument was composed, by law and by three hundred years of unbroken practice, in the received tongue — the sacred official language every Registry notary learned to render before she was old enough to ask why, the beautiful stamped shapes Vega had always loved for the pure pleasure of the forms themselves — a music she loved without ever translating a word of it. She had rendered thousands of lines of it. She had never fully read it — her own language got that kind of reading; this had never needed to.

She minded now. She wrote the entire body of the instrument in it anyway — the full account, everything Osel had laid out across that small crowded desk, everything the paperwork had confirmed since, set down in the tongue that made it canonical, that made it a thing Sanctorin's own instrument set would one day have to reckon with rather than simply deny. That much, procedure required, and Vega had spent three years being a woman procedure could rely on.

Eleven years lay between her and Lyra, and a whole vocation stacked on top of them. Vega had come late — the child nobody had been young enough to plan for, born to parents already tired of the work of it — and by the time she was old enough to follow her sister down a corridor, Lyra was half-grown and half-gone. Seven, Vega had been, the winter Lyra took the oath and went to the Vigil. She had spent the years since doing precisely what she was doing now: setting careful words in front of a sister who was always a step ahead and half-turned away, and hoping one of them would land. She had even followed her into the Liturgy. She told herself it was the work — and it was the work — and it was also the shortest road to an hour in the same room as Lyra, once a season. A person could hold both of those true at once. Notaries did it for a living.

But procedure did not require what came after it, and she wrote that part anyway, in her own hand, in her own tongue, breaking the form for the first time in eight months of keeping one — not a notary's line but a sister's, set below the seal where the instrument's formal record ended and something else began:

Sister, I pray these words reach you in time. Loyalty to an unreciprocating thing isn't virtue. It's just fear disguised as principle. If this costs me my desk — and it will — look for me at Pallor before you look for me anywhere else. House Pallor keeps its own accounts and asks the Liturgy for nothing, and eight months of reading the Liturgy's filings has taught me to trust a door there more than any door I have left at Ocipheus.

She sealed it. She sent it ahead of her sister, into the last waystation on the road before the Gate, to sit in an archivist's careful keeping and wait — patient as only ink can be — for Dame Lyra to walk in off a road she did not yet know had already been written about, and find, before anything else at Sinter could tell her a different story first, her own sister's account of it, sealed, dated, and true.

Vega left Averlyne three days later, before dawn, on a Loera corsair that asked no questions — Loera hulls never did; it was half of what the House was for.
