A low black two-master built for the work Loera kept quietest about, its master paid in Registry coin and a sealed letter he would never be able to read. She did not sail east to the Gate. She went the other way — east and north, toward Pallor and its long cold coast, where a woman with a good hand and no name worth wanting might vanish into the clerical bones of some fjord garrison and outlast whatever the Zone was about to become.

She stood at the rail and watched the island go grey behind her and did not know whether she would ever stand in a room with her sister again. The ink would reach Lyra. She might not. That was the shape of what she had chosen, chosen it by the same rule she chose everything by — the instrument first, the person second, and the person, this once, was herself.

They would not meet on this road. Some later one — another shore, another year — perhaps. She sealed that hope same as she sealed everything, and did not break it to look.

## The Gate

Lyra put the strait at seven hundred meters, narrowest point, grey water, and didn't need the sergeant to tell her the smell under the naphtha was the thing the naphtha was burning for.

She had expected a wall. Entos called it a Gate - soldiers' habit of sizing any border down to a word small enough to carry. What she found was a shoreline: fortified towers on both banks, boats holding position against the current, bows angled into it, and between the water and the first course of stone, a burn crew of six working a black stain with two flamethrower rigs and the discipline of men who had run this same watch longer than they cared to count.

The stain moved. Black, light-eating, coming up out of the tideline in slow fingers that found the mortar joints and settled there.

"Ichor," Orim said. Unnecessary. She had read the word in six after-action reports and the color still hadn't prepared her.

The burn crew worked it by the book: short bursts, held low, one man on the line while a second covered the water at his back in case the stain reconsidered the fire as an argument. It went up clean - no smoke worth remarking on, a bright collapsing crackle, the stink of scorched rot under the naphtha - and where it burned the stone came up pale after, cauterized rather than healed. She watched a finger of it reach a coil of dock cable, watched the fire take the cable before it closed, watched the crewman's face register nothing at all. She took that in too.

"Fire's the only thing that takes it clean," the garrison sergeant told her, when asked.

"Cut it, it grows back doubled. Burn it, it stays burned."

He reported it with the flat unsurprise of a man reporting weather.

The officer had a name for the shape seated against the log-house's north wall, folded down out of the wind to a height that still cleared the eaves, watching them with the specific patience of someone who has been asked to wait before and expects to be asked again. "Ser Vaen," he said, when Lyra asked. "Pallor. He escorts the assessment teams in, when there's an assessment team foolish enough to want one."

Vaen unfolded off the wall at his own name, unhurried, the way a derrick comes upright in stages rather than all at once. Older than Lyra by a decade at least, built along the same lines the Gifted Ceremony built everyone along, though his had clearly been given far longer to work — a chest broader than a doorway, a scar closing one eyebrow at an angle that made him look permanently skeptical of whatever he was looking at, which today, from some distance above her, was her.

"Templar Ocipheus," he said. Not a question. Word traveled ahead of a Templar with her particular week behind her.

"I need an escort past the checkpoint," she said. "Not an assessment. Further in than an assessment goes."

He looked at her the way a man looks at a bill he already knows he can't pay and intends to pay anyway. "How far in."

"As far as it takes."

He was quiet a moment, weighing something that wasn't her authority — she had none left worth the name — and wasn't the pay, because there wasn't any offered. "I've buried six of my own on this ground," he said. "None of them past the first quarter mile."

"I know."

"You don't," he said, without heat. "Nobody who hasn't done it knows." He looked past her, at Doyle, at Orim, at Wren, cataloguing them the unhurried way a professional catalogues anything he's about to be responsible for. "But I've watched enough good people go in with a bad reason and come out fine, and enough with a good reason not come out at all, and stopped believing the reason has anything to do with it." He shrugged, the specific economy of a man who has made this decision before and knows exactly what it costs to make it again. "I'll take you as far as the ground lets me."

"Thank you."

"Don't," he said. "Thank the ones who come back."

Vaen was posted at the second tower, and she had taken the whole measure of him before she'd finished crossing the yard — the way you read weather closing in, except the weather in this case was standing on two legs and was easily twice the height of the tower door he'd have to duck through to use it.

Thirteen feet, near enough that counting the last inches felt like an argument not worth finishing. He'd braided his hair — russet-red, going copper where the light caught it — into a single rope thick as a mooring line, tied off at the small of his back so it wouldn't catch on anything that would never reach high enough to matter. His clothes were sewn from bed linen: dozens of sheets, by the look of the seams, stitched into something that could pass at a distance for a soldier's coat, because no loom in Entos wove a bolt wide enough to dress a man his size, and somebody — a quartermaster, a wife, a sister, Lyra never learned who — had solved that the only way it could be solved.

He was sitting when they arrived. Sitting, because standing put his head above the tower crenellations, and the garrison had asked him, politely, not to give the far bank a silhouette to shoot at. Sitting, he was still taller than Doyle standing.

"Little Sister," he said, and got up anyway to say it properly, unfolding in stages like a derrick going vertical. Not condescension. Recognition — one soldier naming rank to another — and under it something that would have been pity, if pity were a thing this man still had storage for.

"You're posted here?"

"My turn in the rotation." He said it without weight, reporting his own conscription like weather. "Champions cycle the Gate, House by House. A Loera corsair runs eight weeks each way from wherever you're called from, so nobody crosses for less than a year's duty — the travel alone would waste the posting otherwise. I'm eight months into mine."

Wren, who did not startle easily, had gone very still and was working out how much wider the doorway at Sal Vento would have to be, if it ever came to that. Doyle ran his three-height scan out of pure procedure and got nothing back in any of the three bands that matched what his eyes were reporting — the Champion registered, on the shell's own ledger, as unclassified, mass exceeds calibration. Orim didn't scry him. He didn't need a rod to confirm it.

"Eighteen infusions," Vaen said, before Lyra could ask, because everyone always wanted to ask and it was faster to answer first. "Near the top of what the Liturgy's ever signed a writ for. One a year, near enough, from my fourteenth to my thirty-second, and then they told me that was all my frame could carry without the bones going soft at the joints instead of thick. I stopped growing taller four years ago. I have not stopped eating."

He said this last with the particular satisfaction of a large man who has never once in his life been asked to leave food on a plate.

Lyra carried three infusions, and had believed, until this exact minute, that she understood the size of that gap. She did not. She asked him — because someone had to, because the question sat in the space between them like a held breath — whether it changed anything else. The mind. What a person was, under that much rebuilt bone?

"No." He said it simply, without the weight she'd braced for. "Whatever the infusions grow, they don't touch that. I think the same as I thought at fourteen. Slower, some might say" — and here something moved at the corner of his mouth that in a smaller man would have been called a grin — "though I've had thirty years of people saying it behind a hand they thought I couldn't see over."

He asked about her sister, having heard — everyone at every post between Ocipheus and the strait had heard by now — that the Athen-Moor girl carried a letter she hadn't opened. He asked without prying, the way a big man learns to ask everything, because a big man who pries gets treated like a threat and a big man who doesn't gets treated like company.

He told her, unprompted, that he meant to walk them across himself. Not the boat — the boat was for cargo and for men who needed the water between them and Sinter to feel like a margin. He meant to go in on foot, at the head of the column, because a man his size standing between a Sinterspawn breed and four exhausted travelers was worth more than any letter of passage the garrison could stamp. He'd walked escorts in before. None past the second waystation. He thought, this time, with eight months of the ground already under him, he might make the third.

Lyra let herself, for the length of that sentence, believe him. It felt like setting down a pack she hadn't noticed she was still carrying.

It happened forty minutes later. Too fast to take in, in the moment; too slow after, in memory, every second stretched to carry what it held.

The water went concave first — not a wave, the absence of one, a bowl of surface drawing down around a point forty meters off the near tower, like water pulling toward a drain before the drain's been found. What came up wasn't the long dark coiling mass the burn crew had trained their whole watch to expect. It came up jointed, plated at the head and thorax like something that should have fit in a net, if the net had been woven for a creature the size of a river barge — and behind the plated mass, uncoiling out of the water in lengths that kept arriving after the eye had already decided it was done arriving, a tail built of nothing so simple as bone. Rib on rib on rib, hooked and hinged, clutching at the air. The burn crew, already moving, already screaming for the flame lines, had no word ready for it. Someone shouted shrimp — the first small true thing a mind can hold when the large true thing won't fit — and it stuck, because soldiers name what they can bear to name and leave what they can't for later.

The fire found it and it screamed — the first sound any of them had heard a Sinterspawn make that wasn't pressure felt in the sternum, an actual voice, wet and enormous, and for one clean second Lyra let herself believe the fire alone would be the ending.

Then the tail came around, and it wasn't aiming for the tower. It was aiming for the one thing on the quay that stood a chance of stopping it before it reached the boats, and Vaen was already moving to make sure that guess was correct.

He went in with nothing but his hands and the flat of a blade too small for him, drawn more from muscle memory than any hope it would matter, and he was right that it wouldn't — the tail took him around the chest before the blade found anything to open, and the ribbed length of it closed like a fist, slow and total, no hurry in it at all, the unhurried certainty of something that had never once needed to hurry.

Lyra heard bone. Not his — hers, in the private register behind her sternum where his ribs and her ribs had briefly become the same fact.

He did not go down easy. Both hands found the seam where the plated thorax met the base of that terrible tail — the one soft place a creature that size hadn't thought to armor, because nothing before this had ever had the leverage to reach it — and he drove both thumbs in and pulled, forcing open something that was never meant to be opened by hand.

Lyra heard the spine go. A sound like a green branch breaking inside a drum, once, and then the whole jointed length of the creature's tail lost its grip in the same half-second it lost its argument with gravity, uncoiling off him in a boneless fall that took the last of its scream down into the water with it, and did not come back up to finish arguing.

It let go because the wound was more than even something that size could stand on. It let go too late for the man it had been killing, and took the rest of itself, wounded and still moving, back down into the dark the fire hadn't reached — which was not the same as beaten, and everyone standing on that quay understood the difference immediately.

Vaen didn't fall so much as arrive at sitting, the way he had been sitting when they'd found him, except now nothing in him unfolded back up. Lyra reached him in four strides that felt like forty. Up close, in the last of the light, he looked less like a monument than he had all afternoon — looked, for the first time since they'd met him, like a man, tired, glad of somewhere to sit.

What he said to her then, she has never once repeated, to Orim or to anyone standing on that quay who would have given a year's wages to have heard it. She knelt with him until there was no more use in kneeling, and then she stood, and she did not cry where the burn crew could see it, and she did not tell any of them what a Champion's last accounting sounds like when there's nobody left to report it to but the person he's decided to spend it on.

Something else moved beneath the settling grey while she knelt there — vast, unhurried, gone before the eye could be sure it had been there at all, a displacement felt in the boat hulls before it was seen anywhere. Nobody named it. There would be time to name it later, on the far bank, when naming it wouldn't feel like an invitation.

Nobody moved for three seconds that felt considerably longer. Then the far tower's lieutenant was screaming the burn crew back to the line, the boats were coming about, and the water — what was left of it disturbed — settled back to grey and gave nothing more away.

Orim didn't speak for a long stretch.

"Six," he said, finally, very low. "He told you he'd buried six."

"Seven now," Lyra said.

Then: "That's what it costs to make one of them bleed. And we still have to cross."

Wren had gone pale and still, staring at the place on the quay where a very large, very gentle man had been sitting a minute before.

Doyle ran his three-height scan again, low, middle, high, and logged nothing in any of the three bands that told him what he'd just watched.

Lyra's hand had found the seal of her sister's waystation letter before she seemed to know it had moved, and then didn't break it, because there was no line in her sister's notary hand that could have held what the quay had just taken from her.

They crossed at dusk, in a boat the garrison sergeant wouldn't meet her eyes to hand over, past the scorched black stain the burn crew was already back to working, because the Ichor didn't pause for what had happened here, and past a length of quay stone still faintly warm where a man twice anyone's height had sat down for the last time.

The far bank came up out of the grey water, dark, waiting, entirely unconcerned that it had just been introduced.

The water took the boat from underneath before anyone heard it coming.

Not a wave. A wave announced itself, gave you a swell to brace against. The boat simply stopped being where it had been, canted hard to port on something that had come up under the keel and closed. After that there was only noise — wood complaining, black water over the gunwale in a sheet, Wren already moving with no order given.

She saw the tail before she saw anything else of it — long, segmented, bone-pale where the crater-things had all run to black, whipping clear of the water and back under it again almost too fast to have been real at all, wrapped once around the keel and pulling.

"Out," Doyle said, not loud, which was somehow worse than loud. "Everyone out, now, this side."

Nobody argued with him. The boat went over a second later. The water took her breath out through her teeth and did not give it back for four strokes. In those four strokes there was no Vaen, no crossing, no case at her hip. Only up, and how far.

She came up swearing. Wren was already up, one hand locked in the back of Orim's coat, walking the old man backward toward the shallows. Doyle did not surface so much as arrive — the shell too dense to float, coming up out of the silt on its feet. She counted them. Four. She made herself say it aloud. "Four."

Whatever had taken the boat did not come back. It did not need to. It had already gotten what it wanted, which was apparently only ever the boat, and by the time all four of them had found footing in water shallow enough to stand in, there was nothing left on the surface to mark that anything had been there at all — no tail, no wake, nothing but four people standing waist-deep in the last of the light, breathing.

"Something in the water," Lyra said, when she had breath enough to say anything.

"Something with a tail," Wren said. "That's all I saw. A tail, and then not-a-boat."

Lyra put her hand to the case at her hip. Still there. She counted the four of them again anyway.

She didn't speak until the crossing was most of the way done, the grey water closing behind them and the garrison's lights already a smear on the bank they'd left.

Orim didn't ask her to. He had escorted enough of the newly dead-eyed and the newly widowed across enough black water to know that a woman holding a folded quiet like that would talk when the quiet stopped being hers alone to carry, and not one half-second before.

Not the words. Whatever passed between her and Vaen at the end, she gave no one the words, and Orim understood without being told that no one ever would get them. What she gave him instead was the shape of what they added up to. Vaen had meant to walk them in himself — on foot, at the head of the column, past the second waystation and, with eight months of the ground already under him, maybe the third. He'd said as much before the water went concave, in the flat, unhurried certainty big men reserve for anything already decided — not a plan still open for argument. He would have taken the worst of the crossing into a body built to take it, and the four of them would have gone into Sinter with an escort no House and no letter of passage could have bought them at any price the Compact recognized.

That was gone now, and it was, Orim understood — not as information but as loss, the limestone-deep kind that arrives in the body before the mind has caught up with it — very possibly the worse loss. Worse than Vaen himself, which was an obscene thing to let cross a mind and he let it cross anyway, because grief does not wait politely for a body to finish sorting out what it has actually lost.

They came up out of the shallows without the boat, the crossing behind them by more effort than eleven minutes should have cost and the last of the garrison's light behind that.

They moved up the bank by habit: Lyra forward, Doyle running his scan in three bands, the Calyx boy at the waterline watching the far shore with the expression of a man who had come to understand something about himself on the crossing and had not yet decided what to do with it. Orim did not move. He had come out of the water and stopped where the bank began.

The smell was wrong. Not as a survey report would describe wrong — anomalous atmospheric and biological conditions, the standardized language built to survive an auditor rather than the thing itself. Wrong in the way his body remembered from before the documentation had existed.

The rock below the tideline was old limestone, grey-blue, shaled in the pattern particular to this shore and no other shore he had stood on in fifty years of standing on shores. He had stood on it once before. He knew, without examining the knowledge, which part of himself remembered it and which part had read about it. The distinction was not ambiguous.

He had been a child. That had been Year Zero.

Lyra came back for him. She had the gift — one of several she had not been taught and would not acknowledge — of knowing which silences wanted breaking and which wanted acknowledging before they could be walked through. She stopped at arm's reach and waited.

"The Rod," she said.

"Quiet," he said. "Not the refusal at the Forge Hearth. That was a door closing." He did not look at her. "This is quiet the way a site goes quiet after it has been active long enough to stop needing to demonstrate what it is." He let that sit. "I am familiar with this shore."

She waited. She was very good at waiting.

"A powerful island nation of Sphere 31," he said, "not unlike Ocipheus in several martial respects, endured once a tragedy much like Sinter's. At the end of a long campaign of conquest, their enemy let the power of the stars fall upon them. Those who lived were haunted the rest of their days." The water made its small continuous sound against the limestone. "They had a word for such survivors."

He picked up the Rod's case from where he had set it down without noticing he had set it down.

"Hibakusha."

He said the word as a man finally sets down something he has carried the whole of a working life without occasion to use aloud. It was heavier outside the chest than inside. He had known it would be heavier. He had arranged, across the whole of a working life, not to find out.

The others were waiting at the treeline. He walked up to where they stood, looked at the zone ahead, and said nothing more about it — which was the most he had ever said to anyone on the subject, and which he had now finished saying.

Caer Dyn was Calyx's, not Sinter's - a forward post Calyx had held since before the Compact had a name for what it was holding against, close enough to the old border that the maps still argued about which side of the line it sat on, and far enough inside what used to be Sinter that nobody serious still made the argument out loud. Wren had known it would be there. He had not said how he knew, and Lyra had stopped asking him things he answered better by simply producing them.

The Balthier came down over the pass at Caer Dyn in five turns, not four - she counted them - she counted anything a ship did on final approach, because a ship that did the expected thing in the expected order was doing its job. She had watched Calyx groundcrew walk her out of a revetment cut into the hillside an hour before, the kind of dug-in shelter a garrison builds when it expects its aircraft to need hiding from something more than weather, and had not asked how long the ship had sat there waiting, or who had been paying to keep her fueled and answerable. Some debts of Wren's ran deeper than the ones he mentioned. The pilot flew by instrument report rather than judgment, trusting a hundred readings faster than a man could weigh them himself. At four hundred meters the ship stopped being flown. For the length of one breath it belonged to someone else entirely - the hum in the hull plating dropped a register, the yoke went still under no one's hands, and the small black shape strapped into the navigator's seat sat upright the way a soldier sits upright at reveille.

"M-101," Doyle said. To no one. Confirming himself - a man checking his own name after a concussion, to be sure the correct one had come back into the body.

He had been the ship for the descent. Now he was the shell again - the replacement, not the one Verlaine had built him. Acquired on the same terms a man acquires anything he did not choose: the alternative was staying gone. Wider in the shoulder joint than the old shell. The optical receptor sat off true by roughly half a degree, so that when he tracked a target the whole small frame overcorrected a fraction on the turn - a defect she had logged in the first hour on this shell and had not stopped logging since. He talked less than he had before the moor. She had not determined whether that was the shell's doing or his own, and she did not ask a man questions he had not chosen to answer.

Orim had the Rod's case out from under his coat before the ramp was fully down. He did not open it. He held it like a soldier holding a weapon he expects to need and has stopped trusting to fire.

The ship put down in a stone corridor between two peaks that had stood quarantine-adjacent six generations running, and had taken the quarantine's particular stillness onto itself - not the stillness of nothing moving. The stillness of things that had learned, across six generations, to move only when they judged themselves unwatched.

The gate stood a kilometer on.

They walked it.

The Vigil patrol kept a single stone building at the narrows, two rooms, a departure log bolted to a table in the format the Compact's commission had standardized in Year 1274. Five entries above hers in three days: an inspection team, a specimen collection detail, a maintenance authorization for the trail. The officer on the rotation was young. Verlaine-trained — she read that off him before he spoke, off the stance alone. He set his rifle down before he opened the log. Muzzle out, not muzzle in. Five seconds told her what she needed of a Vigil soldier, and those five seconds told her enough.

He looked at her transit authorization a long time.

"You want to cross," he said. Not a question. A man buying himself time to read a document a second time without admitting that was what he was doing.

"Yes."

"This designation code-"

"Year 630. Ocipheus Station. Vigil mandate." She waited while he found the clause. "The authorization predates the Compact's perimeter structure. It supersedes it. Fourth clause."

He read the fourth clause. He read it again.

"The last authorized descent on this access was Year 1342," he said. "Descent Corps salvage detail. Membrane specimen recovery. Four operators."

"Three returned," she said. "I've read the report."

He looked up at that — not at the number, which was in the log for anyone to find, but at the fact that she had reached for it before he'd finished offering it. He did not comment. He looked instead at her party: Orim with the Rod's case held against his ribs like something that might need to be put down in a hurry; Doyle with the rifle slung and the stillness of a man reading terrain rather than waiting on permission to; Wren at the back, watching the gate with the same habit he'd brought to everything since Caer Glas Moor — from the outside in, building the picture in pieces before he let himself look at the center of it. The officer's eyes stayed on Wren half a second longer than they stayed on the others. Perhaps because they were close in age. Perhaps because Wren was looking at the zone's threshold as if he expected to understand it from here, and was in the process of discovering that he would not.

He stamped the logbook. He stamped it a second time, which was not procedure.

"The commission will want a return report," he said.

"Yes."

"I mean the actual commission." He stopped there. He had started a sentence he decided partway through not to finish, and the second stamp was what he said instead of finishing it: that he did not believe the standard chain was where this descent belonged.

"I understand," she said.

He reached for the gate release, and then his hand stopped short of it — not a refusal, something worse, the arrested motion of a man who has just seen a reason he cannot yet name. He was looking past her, down the log, at a line she had not been shown.

"Year 1342," he said again, and this time the number came out wrong, careful — the tone of a man realizing, too late, that he should not have said it so freely the first time.

He turned the log so she could read it and pointed at the entry above the salvage detail — not below it, above it, dated the same week: a Vigil field annotation in a hand three commissions old. Perimeter designation revoked pending mandate review. Authorization holders to be detained at the narrows. He looked up at her, and the young steadiness had gone out of his face and left something closer to apology.

"Your clause supersedes the Compact's perimeter," he said. "It does not supersede this. This is Vigil-internal. Year 1342, Ocipheus authorizations were flagged for detention, and the flag was never lifted, because the office that could lift it stopped answering in 1351."

He set his hand flat on the log, not on the release. "I can stamp your transit. I cannot open this gate to a flagged holder without a countersign from a mandate authority that no longer exists. And the standing order for a flagged holder who insists-" he did not finish that either, but his eyes went, once, to the rifle he had set down muzzle-out, and came back. "I would have to call it in. And the moment I call it in, this stops being four people and a logbook."

The gate stayed shut. The zone lay on the other side of it, and the only road to the crater ran through a countersign a decade past the death of the man who could have given it.

Wren had been quiet through all of it — the particular quiet he went to when a problem had a shape he already recognized.

"You don't have to open it," he said.

The officer looked at him like a man wanting very badly to be able to agree with the sentence. "The gate doesn't open itself."

"It doesn't have to open at all." Wren nodded at the logbook, not unkindly. "You never touched the release. Nobody called it in. Four people were here, and then they weren't, and the gate never moved. Write it up as an equipment fault on your own patrol log if it eases anything — the Zone breaks things. Everyone already believes that about it."

The officer looked at him for a long moment — at the case at her hip, at Doyle's stillness, at whatever he'd decided about a boy who talked like that about a Vigil-sealed perimeter — and set his hand back on the logbook instead of the release.

"I never saw you," he said. "Understand that's not permission. That's just what I'm going to tell the truth about, if anyone asks, because it happens to be the truth."

"That's all we needed it to be," Lyra said.

She put a hand on Wren's shoulder. He was warmer than he should have been, and shaking very slightly, and he did not look up at her.

He folded them through, one at a time, the gate's iron and stone passing around each of them the way water parts and closes over a hand pulled back out of it, and took the longest over the last of them. On the other side, the young officer was already bent back over his logbook, writing nothing down.

## The Zone

The zone began on the other side of it, and no report in the Vigil archive had ever recorded what it actually felt like to cross it — and she had read most of what the archive held. Standard language: anomalous atmospheric and biological conditions consistent with sustained membrane-adjacent activity. Accurate. Built to survive contact with an auditor, not contact with the thing itself.

The Vigil veterans had a shorter line for it. The ground pays attention.

The air changed before she had gone ten meters past the gate. Not colder. Not warmer. Thicker — the pressure air carries before a storm commits to being a storm, a weight she'd stood picket in enough weather to recognize before anyone said the word out loud. Bluer than the light she'd walked in the last three weeks. Filtered, as glass filters a color out of what passes through it without removing the light itself. Every membrane tear was rimmed faintly gold where the skin had never fully closed. She had written papers on this. The papers had not told her what it cost to stand inside the sentence.

And then, at no distance she could mark, the ground began to pay attention.

Directional. Ahead and below. Steady, not pulsing — the signature of something that had been doing this a long time and would keep doing it whether or not anyone logged it as notable. It had found her instead. That was the order of things here, and she noted it as fact rather than argue with it.

"It started for me at the gate," Orim said, at her shoulder. He had not reached for the preparation in his breast pocket. She had expected him to.

"I've heard the veterans describe this my whole working life. I assumed they were building it up." He looked at the ground like something that was looking back without eyes to do it with. "They were not building it up."

"The Rod?"

"Still," he said. "Not the soft refusal I got at the Forge Hearth. That was a door closing. This is — still. Nothing pushing back because there is nothing to push against." He kept his hand in his pack, not drawing anything out of it. "In fifty years of contract work, that has not happened to me at a live site. Only at dead ones." He looked at the trees. "The creature in the gorge — Sphere-119, the notation on Doyle's catalog — the Rod had a designation for that. An address, however old. Here, there is no address. I am standing inside a live site and the Rod cannot find the surface." He paused. "I have not had a word for that until today."

She had expected something like it. The Forge Hearth had refused him outright, and the Forge Hearth held only a fraction of what lay ahead of them now. A Rod-reading assumed the membrane was a surface — something with a face you could turn toward the light and read. Whatever this was had stopped being a surface a long time ago.

He did not move again for the length of three breaths — the same held-still she'd seen young soldiers go when the first real memory of a fight came up from wherever discipline was supposed to keep it down, except she had never caught Orim rehearsing a discipline like that, not once in four hundred miles. His hand stayed empty in the pack. He was looking past the treeline at whatever the ground did out there that wasn't ground anymore, and for the first time since she'd known him, she watched him look his age.

"At the shore I gave you the word," he said. "I did not give you the rest of it, because I had arranged, across a working life, never to be asked for the rest of it, and a man does not undo an arrangement like that twice in one week for free." He let the trees hold his attention longer than the sentence needed. "I am telling you now because the Rod has just told me something the shore only implied."

She waited. She did not make him ask twice for the waiting.

"I was born under this sky before it was called a Zone, Lieutenant. Before there was a fence, or a Watch, or a Rod bred to stop reading at a border. I was a child the day the Bolide came down, and I was carried west through what is now the Pass by people who did not all make it as far as I did. No House raised me after that. I made my own way from Calyx onward, and let people believe whatever was easiest for them to believe about where a boy my age had come from — Calyx-born, most often, because a boy who says he is from Sinter gets a particular kind of look that he does not care to earn twice, and I have found it costs a man less, across a long enough life, to let a convenient lie stand than to keep correcting the true one." He said it the way he had confessed the Forge Hearth refusal to her — nothing held back now that the holding back had stopped doing any work. "I am one of the very few people left alive who remembers what was actually here, before the reports started standing in for it."

The Rod stayed in his pack. Watching him not reach for it again, she understood he had already told her the only thing it could have told her — and told it better.

She did not thank him for it. She kept it instead.

They picked up the column an hour past the gate, moving along a fire-break road the surveys marked as decommissioned — too straight to be anything the Zone had grown, too disciplined to be anything living out here on its own account. Twelve, she counted, in loose march order, rifles slung the Compact way, and at that range she couldn't have named a house from the cut of a coat alone.

She didn't need the coat. She had the standard, and the standard told her everything the coat would have: the twin spires of Ocipheus Station worked in grey thread on a field the exact blue of the Templar mantle she'd worn out of that same Station three weeks and four hundred miles ago. Not Vigil. Not Compact commission. Hers. A scout element, most likely, ahead of a larger deployment — the kind of thing the Station sent when it wanted a thing found quietly before it committed a name to finding it.

"Ours," Orim said quietly, reading her stillness rather than the column. Not a question.

"Mine," she said, and felt the correction leave her mouth before she could stop it, and let it stand, because it was more honest than his word had been.

She ran the numbers the Station had trained into her without asking whether she wanted them: twelve rifles, a scout element ahead of something larger, here for the same reason she was, or close enough to it that the difference wouldn't survive a conversation. A month ago she would have gone to them. Would have named her rank and her authority and trusted the Article Nine hearing that came after it to sort a suspended Templar from a traitor, because that was what the process was for, and the process had never once failed her before this year.

She did not move toward them.

That was the whole of the decision, in the end — not a vow, not a document, nothing she'd remember composing afterward. Just the absence of a step she would have taken a season ago, standing in for everything that step used to mean. If it came to a choice between that column's twelve rifles and the road to the crater, she already knew, with the same flat certainty she'd once reserved for arithmetic, which twelve she'd spend. And when this was done — if there was a when — she was not planning to hand Balthier back to the roster that had written her a widow's write-off six years early. The ship was hers now, the way the decision was hers now. She'd stopped waiting for anyone senior to make it for her.

The column passed a quarter mile north and never broke stride. Nobody on either side fired a shot. She counted that, too, and did not mistake it for mercy.

The trees were wrong, and it took a second look to place where. Longer gaps between the lower branches than growth should allow. Straighter in the grain than growth should run. The leaves gave back light a shade off the light that struck them — the Year 1337 survey had logged it as evidence of progressive adaptation to anomalous light conditions. She had read that line as documentation for seventeen years. She read it now as a description of what stood in front of her.

Doyle came up on her right, saying nothing, running the three-height horizontal scan she had watched him run in six environments: low, middle, high, repeat. The new shell ran the pattern a fraction of a second slower than the old one had, a hitch in the shoulder actuator on the turn from middle to high. He had not commented on it. She had not asked. He kept it to himself, even mostly voice-box and borrowed steel.

Wren moved behind them, breathing through his nose, watching the tree line with the same patient assembly he'd brought to every strange thing since Caer Glas Moor.

They had passed two more of the Zone's preserved dead on the way to this ridge, and she had stopped needing new words for either. The first, two kilometers back, had been small enough to miss — half a meter of crystalline growth fused into a tree root, a creature from some smaller Sphere caught mid-crossing and sealed rather than left to die by ordinary means, one limb still reaching toward a world that no longer existed on its side of the tear. The veterans had a name for that kind — the Still Faces, for the expression each one kept, mid-reach, mid-plea, toward whatever they'd been crossing away from — and Orim used it without being asked to, the way he used any name a person had earned by dying somewhere specific rather than just dying. Deeper in, in the shadowed stands, a pod of what the veterans called Glass Whales had lain in the postures they'd died in, eighty or a hundred years gone: six to nine meters, filter-feeders out of some high-methane Sphere no Entos biology had a name for, their long filtering organs visible through the crystal like something diagrammed rather than lived. The membrane had given them two to four hours of this world's air before it killed them, by the commission's estimate. It had kept the shape since. The Zone buried nothing. It sealed and displayed, the way an insect keeps its prey, and after the second sighting she understood she would spend the whole crossing doing this — cataloguing, moving on, cataloguing again — because stopping to properly grieve each one would mean never reaching the rim.

The Singing Spires came last, and were the only one of the three still doing anything. Not in the Year 1337 survey — first logged in the Year 1354 emergency assessment, crystalline growth in clusters two to three meters, source Sphere unidentified. They are still vibrating, the assessment had said, and for seventeen years she had read that as an academic curiosity worth a footnote.

She understood it now as a field report. The Spires carried a resonance from wherever they had come from — some frequency of an atmosphere or a ground condition that was not here — and had not lost it in fifty-nine years of standing in the wrong world. She felt it in the sternum before she saw the cluster: a vibration running outward from its center, parallel to the ground's attention and unaware of it, two frequencies sharing a chest cavity without troubling each other. Whatever was making new things deeper in — she didn't have a name for that yet, not until the ridge — hadn't started here. The Spires and the Whales and the Still Faces were only ever dead weight, singing or silent, in the wrong world. She filed the difference without knowing yet why it would matter.

Orim went around the outside of the cluster rather than through it. She did not remark on it. He had fifty years of knowing where not to place a boot.

The rest of them read his line before he had to explain it and fell in without a word passed between them — three weeks in the field had taught a company to trust a scout's feet over his mouth. Lyra logged the detour anyway: degree, distance, the shape of ground he'd chosen not to cross. A route chosen around a hazard was a fact in its own right, and she had stopped trusting memory to hold what the page could hold better. They left the Spires singing behind them and started up toward the pass.

The road came down off the pass in switchbacks — six of them, by her count, cut for cart traffic that hadn't moved on this grade in longer than the ruts suggested. At the bottom the ground opened into cultivated land: hedgerows, a drainage ditch, a gate hung on hinges gone stiff with weather.

She'd taken the sighting from the height of the last switchback, before the land closed in around them, and she held it now as she held every reading that mattered: logged, timed, not repeated aloud more than once. South across the valley, on the horizon, something moved that was too large to be a hill and too wrong in its slow wet shift to carry any name the maps gave it. At range it read as motion only — a mound the color of muscle left too long in weather, hauling itself forward by a process she couldn't name, taking in anything its leading edge crossed. A stand of trees went into it while she watched. No sound reached her from that distance. No struggle she could see.

Wren had gone still beside her.

"That's not going to reach the road," Wren said. "Not today."

Lyra hadn't asked about tomorrow. She'd fixed the thing's position against the sun, logged it privately — the same instinct that kept Doyle's own readouts to himself — and gone on down into Greymarch. Seventeen years of Vigil training gave her no procedure for a horror that size. The procedure that existed was: keep walking, and trust the walls to hold longer than she needed them to.

She'd walked a hundred farm districts in those seventeen years. She knew this one's shape before she knew its name. Orim found the name half a kilometer back, on a boundary stone, moss-grown, the lettering shallow: GREYMARCH COMMONS. Under it, smaller, a magistrate's name, dead by whatever calendar the stone kept.

"Farming district," Orim said. "Big enough for its own boundary stone. Not big enough for its own garrison. Forty families here. Maybe fifty."

"Would have been?"

"Yes."

The fields confirmed it before anything else did. Not fallow — fallow had a rotation behind it, a farmer's choice. These fields had stopped mid-season: grain gone to seed, lodged flat in a weather event nobody had lived to bind and stack after. A hay rick lay collapsed on one side, black with rot that took years, not one bad autumn. Whoever worked this ground last had died before Lyra was born. The roof beams of the nearest farmhouse still held their shape rather than their collapse — recent enough for that.

The quiet was the detail she logged hardest. Farmland was never quiet; even abandoned, it argued with itself — birds in the hedges, insects in the grass, small systems still running without hands to direct them. Greymarch had none of that. It carried the same stillness she'd been walking inside since the gate: not an absence of movement, but movement that had learned to happen only when it believed itself unwatched.

"Doyle."

"Nothing moving." The receptor swept low, middle, high — the hitch in the shoulder actuator catching on the turn from middle to high, same as it had for weeks now. "That's not the same as nothing here."

"No," she said. "It isn't."

They went in through the gate gap rather than over the hedge. Wren checked the hedge first and found it grown through with something pale, faintly luminous, that none of them wanted to put a boot near. Single file down the track — wide enough, once, for two carts abreast.

The first body was in the yard of the second farmhouse, thirty meters off. At that range she took it for a scarecrow — wrong posture, arms out at an angle no living shoulder held more than a few seconds, torso reading flat as canvas stretched on a frame. At twenty meters the shape resolved: a ribcage opened outward like a door built to swing on hinges it didn't have. She didn't revise the read again. Nothing left to revise it into.

The dead man — she made herself hold him as a man, not a specimen, the way Orim held the Still Faces by name rather than number — had been out in weather long enough that most of what marked him as a person was gone. Boots, mostly rotted. Belt buckle, corroded green. Hands folded in his lap, arranged there once, by someone, before whatever came after made the arranging meaningless.

His ribs had opened from the inside.

The sternum hadn't broken under force. It had forced outward, in two clean halves, hinged — though no human sternum is built to hinge, and this one had learned to anyway, some time after whatever put him in the ground was finished with the rest of him.

Inside the cavity, where a heart and lungs had done the ordinary work of keeping a farmer alive for however many decades he'd managed, there was a nest.

She wouldn't have named it that on her own. It took Orim's voice at her shoulder — flat, on purpose — to give it the word.

"Nest," he said.

She'd have reached for something else, given a moment longer to sit with it — a word with less to do with what birds built. But he said nest, and nest had edges she could hold without holding what it implied. She let it stand.

Black. Not shadow-black, which is an absence, but the black of something wet dried into itself in layers — glossy where thin, matte where built up thick — draped over the ribs' inner curve. Threaded through it in three or four places: shapes with the wrong proportion of a thing not finished growing. Not eggs. Not larvae, though the word wanted to apply and she let it stand, provisional, until a better one came — fetal in the sense of underdevelopment, limbs folded in configurations that hadn't decided their final use, joints doubled where a joint should run single, slick with the same ichor filling the cavity around them.

"They use the chest," Orim said. "Not the whole body. The chest."

"Why the chest."

"Don't know." He said it plainly — no reflex authority left in him after fifty years of being asked. "Warmth, maybe, while there was some to have. Room, maybe. I know the pattern. Never known the reason. Not starting to pretend I do, now."

Wren had gone to the doorway rather than the yard. His voice came back low, controlled — the voice of someone who'd decided a while back that surprise cost more than readiness.

"More inside."

Four more, in postures the household died in, not arranged into: a woman at the hearth, a smaller shape in a cot Lyra made herself look at once and didn't look at twice — not weakness, but because the part of her that catalogued horror needed room left for whatever came next. Each opened the same way. Each held the same black nest, at different stages — one nearly empty, ichor cracked like old paint; one recently disturbed, something hatched and gone, black smeared wet down the ribs in a trail she didn't follow past the doorway.

"How old," she said.

"The house? Twenty years since anyone kept it. Twenty-five." Orim read the roof beams, the rot in the thatch.

"The nests."

"Different question. Answer you won't like better than not having one." He crouched by the woman at the hearth, careful, not touching. "Some old. Some not old at all. Whatever's doing this hasn't stopped. It's thinned, out here — farther from wherever it runs thick. Edge of the wound. Not the wound."

Doyle hadn't gone into the house. He held the doorway, rifle at low ready, running the pattern. When Lyra came back out the receptor was fixed on the dead man — the readout had come again, unbidden, she read that off him before he spoke. He didn't offer it. She didn't ask. Something in the set of his shoulders — the new shell's, wider than the old, still not quite his — told her he'd carry this one a while before he set it down in front of anyone.

Not everything the Zone had put in front of them that day wanted them dead. An hour back, over something blind and thrashing in a ditch none of them had the will to name properly, Orim had said only, "Leave them. Nothing here to fight. Nothing here to save," and moved them on before she'd had to decide for herself. It hadn't prepared her for this.

They saw the first of them across the ditch line, upright among the lodged grain of the fourth farmhouse's outer field. Four full seconds, and nobody in the party said a word.

It stood at a man's approximate height and build, wrapped shoulder to boot in a suit sewn from hide — she made herself confirm that, because not looking would cost more later. Not one hide. Dozens, patched and re-patched, seams run in every direction a desperate hand could manage. Some plainly animal, coarse-haired, cured badly enough to still carry the shape of the flank it came from. Some — she held this the way Orim held the Still Faces, by fact rather than flinch — not animal at all. The stitching didn't discriminate. Neither, evidently, had whoever wore it.

The head told her this wasn't a person doing sensible things in a bad place. It rose from a collar too large for the shoulders under it, bulbous, studded with small wet gleams that took a full breath to read as eyes — not two, not four, a scattered handful with no symmetry to them, some blinking out of sequence with the rest, none obviously fixed on anything and all of them, somehow, giving the read of being watched from every angle at once.

Limbs hung from a rig lashed about the torso — dead limbs, human by the joint, animal by the length, strapped rather than worn, swaying loose with each step. Not weapons, so far as she could confirm. Not obviously anything. Tools, maybe. Trophies. Spares.

It worked at a collapsed section of fence with its own hands — the load-bearing pair at the ends of its own arms — with a patience that had nothing frantic in it. The motion of someone finishing a task already decided worth finishing.

"Doyle," she said, very quiet.

"Two more," he said. "East, working the tree line. Same gait."

"Weapons?"

"Tools. I think." A beat. "Can't tell the difference on these. Don't like that I can't."

Orim had gone very still — the specific stillness that came over him around readings that came back wrong. "No pattern for this. Not raiders. Not spawn. Gait's deliberate. Purposeful. Not a thing I've seen the zone produce on its own."

"Which means?"

"Means I don't know if I'm looking at someone who walked in here on purpose, in that suit, for reasons of their own." He didn't finish it the easy way. "Or something the zone built that learned to wear the walking-in as a shape."

The nearer figure straightened from the fence, unhurried, and turned its many-eyed head toward the ditch line. Toward them. Held there.

Nobody moved. Wren's hand had found a dagger hilt — reflex ahead of thought. Doyle's rifle stayed at low ready, the receptor running its pattern with none of the certainty it usually carried into a kill.

The figure held the look a four-count, five — longer than any animal spends confirming a threat, shorter than any person spends deciding whether to be afraid — then turned back to the fence and went on working. Unbothered. As if four people at the ditch's edge with weapons half-raised hadn't registered as worth revising a task over.

"Not coming for us," Orim said, low.

"No." Lyra didn't move yet either. "Doesn't mean I know what it is."

They backed off along the ditch line rather than the direct route. Unhurried. Nobody called it a retreat. Nobody called it anything else. The figures went on with their work behind them — tool-using, purposeful, unreadable — and Lyra carried the not-knowing the rest of the day with everything else Greymarch had put in front of her that she couldn't set down.

"Suits," Wren said, once the tree line had closed behind the last of them. "Someone made those. Sewed them. Takes hands. Time. A reason."

"Or something learned to look like it did," Doyle said.

Nobody had an answer for either read that made the other less likely. Nobody offered one.

The deer came out of the hedge line an hour before the light started to go. For the length of one held breath Lyra thought — with something close to relief — that it was simply a deer. The kind of ordinary living thing this farmland should have held in plenty, and conspicuously hadn't shown her until now.

Then it screamed.

Deer didn't scream. She knew that in the body, not the books. The sound coming off the animal crossing the field toward them wasn't the bleat or bark a startled deer sometimes made — higher, longer, a ragged edge at the top no deer's throat should produce, and it didn't stop. It screamed while it ran, as if the running and the screaming were two separate things happening to two separate wills sharing one body. Looking past the first, relieved misread, she understood why.

The deer's own head thrashed at the end of its own neck, eyes white-rimmed, legs driving in the rhythm of an animal discovering its own body wouldn't let it stop. Rising from its back, just behind the shoulder, where no deer ever grew anything, was a second head.

Small — a large dog's size — black, glossed with the same wet sheen as the nests and the beaks and the ditch water. Unfinished proportions, fetal, a face that hadn't decided its final shape and grown one anyway out of whatever the deer's own flesh had been repurposed to supply. It didn't scream. Its stillness against the animal's thrashing told her which will held control and which was riding as a passenger in its own nervous system.

"Lyra," Orim said, low, urgent in a register she'd rarely heard from him. "Deer isn't the threat. Whatever's riding it is using more than half the nervous system. Watch the gait. It's not choosing where it goes. It's being driven."

"Toward us."

"Toward something. Don't think it knows the difference anymore."

Doyle raised the rifle and didn't fire. She understood without asking: the second head sat close along the spine, angled so a shot that took it would likely take the deer's own skull with it. He was waiting for a shot he didn't have yet.

The deer screamed again, close now — under the scream she could hear the animal's own labored breathing, ordinary, terrified, nothing wrong in it at all, buried under the wrongness riding on top. Its eyes found hers. She'd think about that after: that whatever remained of its own mind spent its last purchase over its own eyes on looking at the thing that might end this. In that look, nothing she could call anything but a plea — wordless, no vocabulary to ask for what it wanted, entirely clear about wanting it anyway.

"Lyra-" Wren started.

"I see it."

She stepped into its path rather than away, shield up, and took the charge angled, turning rather than stopping. Except two different things drove this charge, and neither fully accounted for the other a half-second before it moved, so the impact came wrong, twisted: the deer's own legs trying, at the last instant, to shy from the shield — an animal instinct the rider hadn't suppressed fast enough. She felt both failures travel up through the shield at once. The deer's flinch. Under it, a half-beat later, the black thing's correction, forcing the flinch back into the line it wanted.

The Dissolution Blade went into the black head first — chosen deliberately, in the fraction of a second she had to choose anything. Whatever rode this animal was the thing doing violence. The animal underneath was the thing being murdered by degrees. The Catalyst compound in the blade's channels found the wound and wouldn't let it close. The black head made a short wet sound and went still.

The deer didn't go still.

It kept screaming — the driving will silenced, its own body released back to a nervous system too damaged, too overridden to survive alone — thrashing, legs finding no purchase, blood coming dark and wrong from where the black head had rooted into the spine over some span of time none of them wanted to guess at.

Lyra put the blade through its throat in one motion, low, fast — the mercy stroke she'd give a wounded warhorse on any battlefield she'd ever stood. The screaming stopped. The quiet after was the worst quiet she'd heard since the gate.

She stood over it a moment longer than the kill required.

"It didn't choose any of that," she said. To no one. Or to Orim. Or to the private ledger she kept of things she'd had to end that hadn't asked to be what they were.

"No," Orim said. "It didn't."

Doyle said nothing. The receptor stayed fixed on the black head a long moment. Whatever readout came behind the dead lens, he didn't offer it, and this time she didn't read that as a man carrying it alone. She read it as a man who'd found nothing in it that would have made this easier to have done.

They reached the barn an hour before full dark — the fourth farmstead's holding, the biggest of the four they'd passed: a house with two chimneys, outbuildings enough for a family that had done well before whatever ended them, and a barn set back on a rise that put its loft window above the tree line. A long room ran the ground floor's far end — a bar counter still standing against the wall among collapsed trestle tables. The district's tavern: the kind of barn-and-bar a commons built when it was too small to need separate buildings for harvest storage and harvest drinking, and had never planned on needing either abandoned.

"We shelter here," Lyra said. "Loft. One door up. Ladder we can pull."

"Agreed," Orim said. "Rather have height and one way in than ground level and four."

The ladder held. The loft floor held — tested board by board before anyone put full weight down, Wren going first with the method he brought to every unknown surface: contact, confirm, continue. The glassless loft window framed a darkening sky and, past the nearer tree line, a suggestion of something taller and darker that might have been distant hills, and might, Lyra thought, have been the walls themselves — patient the way the ground had been patient since the gate.

They ate cold rations. Nobody proposed a fire.

"Doyle," Lyra said, once the last light had gone the color it goes before it goes entirely, "the rifle. Show me the lead again."

He did, without asking why now — nothing else useful for the hour before full dark, and something ordinary to do with her hands was ballast against the day. "Not about the gun," he said, resetting her grip a half-inch back. "It's about where the thing's going to be. Not where it is." She'd spent seventeen years learning where a blade needed to be right now. This asked something else of her. She was slower at it than she wanted, and he told her so without unkindness, and she kept at it till the light failed entirely.

Wren took first watch at the ladder head, dagger loose in hand. Orim settled against the loft's back wall, the Rod's case beside him, unopened, and didn't sleep either — not at first, though Lyra noted the specific slowing of his breath sometime past full dark that told her he'd gone under, eventually.

Doyle did not sit.

He took the window — the one opening with a line on the yard below, the dead man's fields, the tree line past them — and stood there through the whole of what followed, the receptor running its low, middle, high, repeat, patient the exact way the ground itself was patient. Watching him in the last of the light before she made herself close her own eyes, Lyra understood he'd still be standing there when she woke. He didn't sleep. Hadn't slept once since Verlaine built the shell that carried whatever remained of the man he'd been. This — the standing, the watching, the pattern run through hours that asked nothing of him but to keep running it — was the closest thing to rest the trapped mind inside that borrowed steel was going to get.

She didn't know if that thought was meant to comfort her. It didn't, entirely. It also didn't leave her.

The loft held its silence the better part of three hours — a silence with texture to it: an old building settling, wind finding the gaps in the boards and singing through them low, the fields outside doing nothing at all, which after Greymarch's first farmhouse read less like peace than held breath.

Doyle spoke first, quiet, not turning from the window.

"Something's under the yard."

Lyra was awake before she'd finished deciding to be. Wren, at the ladder head, had already gone still in the way that meant he'd heard it before Doyle said it and had been waiting to see if anyone else had.

"Under."

"Not on it. Under it." The receptor held on one patch of yard, near the collapsed hay rick, ground that in the last grey light showed nothing different from any other patch in Greymarch. "Vibration in the boards. Regular. Something moving through soil. Not over it."

"How many?"

"No count for underground."

"Try."

Doyle went quiet a moment, the shell's stillness doing the work a held breath does in a body still made of meat. "More than one."

The first scorpion broke the yard's surface eleven seconds later — earth heaving up not in the ordinary scatter of a burrowing animal but in a clean cored punch, as if the ground had opened along a seam kept ready for it — and it cleared the hole moving, low, fast, segmented, black and slick with the same ichor sheen that coated everything else Greymarch had shown her that day.

Built along a scorpion's general architecture the way the hijacked deer had been built along a deer's — recognizable at the first glance, wrong in every particular the second glance found time for. The tail carried too many segments, curling in a slow double coil rather than the single clean arc a scorpion's tail describes — a thing that had grown one joint too many and simply gone on using all of them. The pincers were underdeveloped, folded close to a body that plainly didn't need them for its actual work. The whole of it draped — not stained, draped, the same wet hang the nest had worn over the dead man's ribs — in the same black vernix the creature had been grown in and never finished shedding.

"Two more," Doyle said, and fired, once, into the lead scorpion's forward segment before it had covered half the yard. The round went in. The creature kept coming. Whatever it had instead of a nervous system did not care about damage that would have stopped anything born in Entos.

"Ladder," she said. "Wren-"

"On it." Wren was already moving to the loft's edge, blades out, watching the ladder head the way he watched everything — economy first, commitment second.

The scorpions didn't come up the ladder. They came up the barn's own wall, through gaps in the old siding boards Lyra hadn't marked as gaps until something moved through one — segmented legs finding purchase on wood weathered soft enough to grip — and the first crested the loft floor's edge eight feet from where Orim stood, the Rod's case still shut in his hand.

"Orim!"

He turned too slowly — not fear, she understood after, but fifty years of reading threat through the Rod had built a reflex that reached, first, for the case, and the case had nothing in it to help him here. The half-second he spent learning that was the half-second the scorpion's tail needed.

It struck him low, along the outside of the thigh — one fast motion, none of the deliberate menace stories give a scorpion's sting, economical, almost incidental, the way a man swats an insect without breaking stride — and Orim made a sound she'd never heard from him in six years of knowing him: short, surprised, more confusion than pain.

His leg went out from under him and didn't answer when he tried to make it take his weight again. The confusion on his face turned, over three long seconds, into something close to the deer's own plea — wordless, no vocabulary built for asking.

"Paralytic," Lyra said, already moving. "Don't fight it — Wren, cover him, don't let anything close-"

"Moving."

Doyle put two rounds into the scorpion over Orim before it fully turned to finish what it started, and this time the shots found something that mattered — a seam in the segmented plating along the underside, exposed as it reared to strike again — and it folded sideways off the loft's edge with a sound like wet rope snapping.

The second and third came over the wall together. Lyra put the shield between them and Orim's body before either had cleared the boards, the impact traveling up through her shoulder in the same dense, wrong weight every Sinterspawn strike had carried since the deer — too much mass for the visible size, a process that had never learned to build a body fast and light both.

Orim's hand found her ankle. Weak grip, fingers not quite closing, but there. When she spared him a half-second's glance his eyes were open, tracking, entirely present behind a body that had stopped answering him.

"Can you speak?"

"-yes." Thick. Slurred at the edges the way a man's speech slurs with cold or drink, though this was neither. "Can't — feel the leg. Arm's going."

"Stay down. Stay still. We've got you."

"Wasn't planning-" He didn't finish it. Whatever wit he'd meant to close the line with, the paralytic took before he could spend it.

That was the night, then. Not whether they could kill what was coming over the wall. Whether they could kill enough of it, fast enough, to keep a man who couldn't move his own legs from becoming the easiest kill in the yard.

Wren took the third scorpion the way he'd taken the small kin-creatures three days back — not meeting it, arriving where it wasn't going to expect him, both daggers finding the seam behind the foreclaw where the plating hadn't finished closing — and it went down in two pieces and didn't reassemble the way, for one absurd half-second, some animal part of Lyra's mind had braced for it to.

Doyle fired again, into the yard below rather than the loft, where the ground was still moving in places that told her the count didn't have a ceiling any of them could see yet.

The corpse-fusion things came up from the tree line while the scorpions were still working the barn's edge - a wrongness of silhouette against the last grey band of sky, too tall, too wide, moving with a lurch that had none of a single body's rhythm to it.

"Two bodies," Orim said from the floor, thick-voiced, still tracking even flat on his back with a leg that wouldn't answer him. "Maybe three. Fused." He'd seen it before she had - watching from an angle low to the ground gave him, however useless the rest of him had gone in the last two minutes, a clearer read on the gait than her own upright vantage offered. "The Greymarch dead. Whatever does this doesn't need the chest cavity for everything."

The nearer of the two shambled into what light the loft's open window still gave the yard. Lyra made herself look at it the way she'd made herself look at everything in Greymarch that day - not away, not through - and confirmed what Orim had already named: two human frames grown together at the torso, the join a mass of the same black glossed tissue that filled the nests, four arms moving in an uncoordinated syncopation that suggested two separate wills, or half a will split between two bodies never built to share one. The faces - one slack, one twisted in an expression that might once have been terror, both long past anything called alive - hung at angles that put them looking two directions at once, tracking nothing, the aimless double gaze of a thing that moved because moving was what its combined mass had been repurposed to do.

It came at Doyle's flank, slow. He put a bayonet through the join where the black tissue ran thinnest, and it didn't fall so much as stop - the momentum going out of both halves at once, the ungainly structure settling to the loft floor's edge, the simple physical fact of a thing that had been moving and had, now, stopped.

The second one Wren took from the ladder head, low, before it had fully cleared the top rung - a dagger through what might have been a throat on either fused face - and it went back down the ladder the way it had come up, taking two scorpions with it in a tangle that ended, from the sound of it, somewhere in the yard below.

Three birds wheeled in last, drawn by whatever in the night carried the sound and smell of a kill site to wherever they'd been roosting - wings that shouldn't have held air and somehow did, membrane torn and healed wrong across every span, beaks hooked back on themselves in a sickle curve, wet black at the base of each skull where the same glossed sheen as the nests seeped steady and unminded. Ichor-birds, Orim called them, low, the name arriving the way his names always did - already finished, no visible work behind it. They didn't press the loft. They circled, patient, opportunist, waiting for whatever would be left when the fighting stopped. A quieter horror than the rest: scavengers who'd learned that farmland like this reliably produced something worth waiting for.

The last scorpion came up through a gap in the loft floor itself, where the old boards had rotted enough at one corner to let something patient find its way through, and it was on Doyle before the receptor's pattern caught the motion — low, middle, high, and this came from beneath, outside the pattern's design.

He took the strike on the shell's forearm rather than anywhere the paralytic could reach him through whatever his borrowed nervous system did with a sting, and the readout came again — mid-strike, unbidden, printing behind the dead lens the way it always did — and this time he spoke two words of it aloud, flat, before the rest of the fight swallowed the moment whole.

INTAKE — SUBJECT PARTIAL
MASS: est. 40-60 kg, distribution segmented, tail-heavy
LOCOMOTION: subterranean approach, no comparable entry vector in prior catalogue
ARMOR: chitin-analog, ichor-sheathed, seam density irregular
WEAK POINT: ventral seam, forward third
SPHERE-SOURCE: — SIGNAL DEGRADED -
CATALOGUE STATUS: UNRESOLVED. RE-SCAN ADVISED.

"Signal's bad," he said, and put the bayonet into the ventral seam the readout had found him before the thought had fully finished forming, and the scorpion folded around the blade and stopped moving.

He didn't say anything else about the readout. Some part of him — the part that was still a man from a coal town, not a war machine's clean accounting — had already decided the degraded signal was the barn's fault, or the night's, or the ichor fouling the lens, and not the first thread of a thing it would take a wider field and a bigger kill to make him stop being able to explain away.

Lyra didn't ask him what the readout said. She had Orim's weight against her side by then, dragging him back from the loft's open edge to the wall where the scorpions and the fused dead couldn't reach him without coming through the whole of the rest of them first, and there was nothing in the next several minutes that had room in it for anything but the fight in front of her.

It ended in degrees, not cleanly — a stretch of thirty seconds, then a minute, then five, in which nothing new came up out of the yard or over the wall or through the rotted floor. The ichor-birds, finding nothing yet worth the risk of landing, wheeled off toward the tree line and didn't come back.

Orim's leg came back to him first — feeling returning as a deep ache rather than pain, pins and needles run to the bone. The arm took longer. By the time the grey started to lift toward whatever passed for morning in the Sinter zone's filtered light, he could flex the fingers, slowly, watching his own hand do it with the clinical attention of a man reassuring himself an instrument still worked.

"I'm sorry," he said, to no one in particular, or to Lyra, or to the private ledger he kept the way she kept her own. "Fifty years, and I reached for the case."

"The case doesn't read this."

"No." He said it flatly, without self-punishment — the truest register he had for admitting a thing had cost him. "Doesn't read any of it. That's twice today the Rod's told me exactly nothing, and both times it was because there was nothing there for it to find. Don't know which is worse — a thing the Rod refuses to look at, or a thing it looks at and simply has no shape for."

Wren cleaned his blades in the grey light, the same unbothered economy he always brought to it, though Lyra noted he looked twice at the yard below before he started — at the collapsed shapes of the fused dead, the dark husks of the scorpions — longer than the cleaning strictly required.

"They were people," Wren said. Not a question. "The fused ones. Before."

"Yes."

"How many farms like this? Between here and the walls?"

Nobody answered. Not a question anyone in the loft was equipped to give a number to, and the number — whatever it turned out to be, whenever the commission's own surveys admitted to counting it — wasn't going to be small.

Doyle stood at the window through all of it, the receptor running its pattern, patient, unslept, the way he'd stood there since full dark and would go on standing until the party was ready to move. When Lyra caught his eye across the loft in the thin new light, there was nothing in the dead lens that told her what the night had cost him to watch alone. She thought, not for the first time, that this was a mercy and a theft in the same borrowed body, and that she'd stopped being able to tell the two apart.

"We move before full light," she said. "Orim, can you walk?"

"I can walk." He got his feet under him, slow, testing the leg the way Wren had tested the loft floor — contact, confirm, continue. "Rather not run for an hour or two. Past that, I'll manage."

"Then we walk an hour or two." She looked out past the yard, past the collapsed shapes the grey light was just starting to make ugly rather than strange, toward the tree line and whatever lay past it the walls had been patiently promising since the gate. "Greymarch's behind us either way. Whatever's ahead won't get gentler for our taking the morning slow."

She was right about that, though she wouldn't know how right until the rope.

The rope came first.

Strung between two dead trees at boot height, grey with age, slack in the middle where it had gone soft. A trip-line. Tensioned once to a bell — she found the bell four paces further on, half-buried in leaf litter, its clapper rusted solid. Somebody had built this line and walked it and stopped walking it, and the rope had stayed behind doing a job nobody serviced anymore.

She logged the span before she logged anything else — habit, seventeen years of habit, the kind of measuring that had nothing to do with this ground and everything to do with the one she'd trained on. Twelve paces between trees. A single-strand line, no redundancy, meant to be checked and reset by hand on a rotation somebody had stopped keeping. That was the whole report. She noted it and moved on to the next thing that needed noting.

Orim crouched at the knot without touching it.

"Vigil-line," he said. "Old pattern. Twenty years, maybe more."

He straightened slow — his knees allowed him nothing faster — and looked past it into the trees.

"They stopped maintaining this stretch."

"Why?" she asked.

"Because the thing it was meant to warn them about started coming from somewhere the rope wasn't."

She let that sit a moment and logged the ground instead of chasing the answer further. Three weeks she'd been walking country like this — packed earth, exposed root, standing water gone grey with autumn — and none of it read clean anymore. The trees held their shape. The moss didn't, not everywhere: patches of it had gone pale, faintly luminous, and climbed the root collar in a pattern that owed nothing to where the shade fell. She'd stopped cataloguing every wrongness at the two-hundred-meter mark. Too many to log individually. She'd need what attention she had left for whatever came next.

Doyle worked the pattern she'd learned to read as work and not wandering — low, middle, high, repeat, rifle at low ready, no strain on the wrist. The new shell ran a half-beat behind the old one on the turn from middle to high. A hitch in the shoulder actuator he'd never mentioned and she'd never asked about. He held at middle a fraction longer than the pattern called for.

"Doyle."

"Track." One word. He spent them like coin he wasn't sure would be honored.

She came up on his position and sighted along the oval receptor. Print pressed into the pale moss, three points of contact — she knew the shape from the patrol reports, the same contact Wren would log a day out from here, from a different bend of this same crossing. Six legs. A pack, moving at pace.

Wrong print, though. Deep on the outside edge, shallow on the inside — weight sitting somewhere a six-legged animal's weight shouldn't sit. Something in its build put more of itself on one side than the other and had simply gone on living that way.

"Fresh," Doyle said.

"How fresh?" she asked.

He crouched, the shell's knee joints folding with a small mechanical complaint that would've made him flinch, months back. Didn't now.
