Two fingers held an inch above the depression, no contact — she'd watched him read a boot print in mud at Schmalburg with the same patience he'd have spent on a shell crater.

"Ten minutes," he said. "No more."

Wren had gone still behind them — the particular stillness Orim called reading the room from the outside in, cataloguing before committing to react. One dagger half-drawn already. Not panic. The plain economy of someone who'd decided a long time ago that surprise cost more than readiness.

"How many, total?" Wren asked.

"More than the print shows," Orim said. Rod's case in his hand, unopened, held the way he'd held it since the gate. "There's a smell under the smell."

There was. Lyra had clocked it and set it aside, the way she set aside anything that wasn't immediately actionable — old iron, and under the iron something the iron was trying and failing to cover. A rot that hadn't finished rotting, like the process meant to finish it had been swapped out somewhere upstream for something else. Sat low in the chest. Didn't clear breathing through the mouth.

The old Vigil hands had a phrase for ground like this. Paying attention.

She'd carried that phrase for seventeen years at a desk in Ocipheus Station — soldier's shorthand, colorful, imprecise. Crossed the marker post three days back and stopped believing it was imprecise. Still didn't fully believe it was shorthand.

"Positions," she said, and didn't need to say anything else.

They came off the pale moss on both flanks at once — told her before she'd finished turning that whatever hunted here hunted smarter than the six-legged crawlers the reports had warned her about. Those moved single-file, at pace, feeding on momentum. These came in a pincer, deliberate — a unit's movement, from something that had already decided the pincer worked better than the file.

Three-quarters of a second of clean look before the first one closed distance. Small — dog-sized, bred too long and too hungry. Forelegs that didn't match each other. Left jointed twice, crawler-standard. Right jointed three times, ending in a hooked spade instead of a claw, moving wrong for its twin and compensating anyway. It had learned, or been built, or simply happened, to run crooked and land true. Its hide hadn't finished drying — an oil-black film sat in every joint hollow instead of running clear the way sweat or rain would, and under the film the skin looked thin, unfinished. Skin that hadn't earned the right to be tough yet.

She took it on the shield, angled, felt the impact travel up through her shoulder — heavier than its size should account for, dense and wrong in the hand the way everything out here was wrong in the hand. Put the Dissolution Blade in on the return stroke, low along the flank where the plating gapped. The Catalyst compound in the channels did its job and refused the wound a close. Short, wet sound. It folded into the moss and stayed down. What came out of it wasn't blood by the time it hit ground — black, thick, unhurried, sitting on the pale moss like oil on standing water. Didn't dry.

"Two, left flank," Doyle said, and fired before he'd finished the sentence. One round down clean, through what she took for a skull though it cost her half a second to find anything skull-shaped on the thing at all. The second shot took a furrow along the back instead of the vital mass, and it kept coming, and Wren was already there.

She'd watched Wren fight four times before this and each time refined the same read: Wren didn't close distance, he arrived at it. The fold spent like a good gambler spends a hand of cards — rarely, never as the whole play. No blink through this one. He simply wasn't where it expected to land, and then he was somewhere it hadn't accounted for at all, both daggers crossing in on the joint where a foreleg met the shoulder, reversed grip finding almost nothing where the muscle mass should've been thickest. This thing hadn't grown to be armored. It had grown fast and hoped fast would be enough.

It wasn't. Wren left it in three pieces and rolled clear of a fourth before Lyra had registered there was a fourth.

Six of the small ones, total. She counted the bodies the way she counted anything mid-fight, out of necessity, and stopped counting the moment the last one stopped moving — there was no report to file on rounds spent once the ground went quiet, only on the ground itself. Killing them cost less time than the last two hundred meters had. Clearing gone quiet after, the specific quiet that follows violence — not peaceful, spent — sword arm singing from six separate impacts, Wren wiping a blade clean on a fistful of pale moss like he was doing laundry.

"Kin," Orim said. He hadn't moved from his mark, Rod's case still shut against his ribs. "Testing pack. Same as the crawlers in your reports, except-" He stopped. Looking past the bodies, into the deeper trees, at something she hadn't turned to see yet, longer than a look he'd normally spend on anything. "Except crawlers breed true within a litter. These don't match each other."

"Meaning?" she asked.

"Meaning whatever's making these hasn't finished deciding what they're for."

Dry, unhurried — the way he reported weather. Worse for the dryness, not better. Six years she'd spent learning the difference between Orim's calm and Orim's fear, and this wasn't either. A third read she hadn't logged before. She set it aside under the same heading as everything else out here she had no heading for yet, and told herself she'd sort it out later, at the rim, when there was time to sort anything.

She checked her own position while there was still a lull to check it in. Blade clean enough to trust, shield sound, Wren and Doyle both upright and both reloading or resetting without being told to. No wounds on her side of the ledger. That was the whole of the report the lull gave her time to file.

The trees ahead of them moved. Not wind. Weight.

It came out of the stand at a height that made her recalculate every instinct three weeks of monster ground had built into her, in one held breath. Not fourteen feet at the shoulder like the harrower stories from the western garrisons had it — smaller than that, though still taller than a war-horse at the withers — and it didn't carry the ponderous weight the stories gave harrowers either. It moved like something still learning what its own mass was for. Three forelimbs where a harrower's stories gave it two, the third shorter, set higher on the chest, curled close — less a limb at rest than a limb still deciding what it would eventually be used for.

Hide wasn't membrane-grey like the western tales had it. Slick — wet in a way nothing living in dry autumn air had business staying wet, the same oil-black film caught in every seam. Mottled dark under it, shifting at the edges, seams of pale blue-white light running the plate joints, pulsing on a slow interval she caught herself starting to count and made herself stop counting. Counting implied she expected the number to mean something. She'd learned not to trust that instinct out here.

Eyes — two dark wet patches low on what worked as a face — didn't track her the way the kin's had tracked. Something else was doing the looking. The eyes were just where it had ended up putting them.

"Don't run," she said, low, mostly for her own benefit. The reflex was old and strong and dead wrong for the geometry in front of her.

It went for Doyle first — she'd turn that over later and not land on an answer that satisfied her — a long low charge that ate the twenty meters between treeline and clearing in under two seconds. Doyle read the geometry before it committed and put a fallen log between himself and the closing mass. Two rounds into the seam where the third limb met the chest.

The rounds did nothing she could see. It didn't slow.

"Lyra-"

She was already moving. Six meters to close, and she closed them at a flat run, shield leading, angled to turn a charge rather than stop one dead — stopping it dead was a fool's play against something that outweighed her by a factor she wasn't calculating mid-swing. Felt the impact through the shield's resin face in a shudder that told her nothing about where it was soft and everything about how little she understood its build. No reach problem like a harrower had a reach problem. No problem she recognized at all. Every instinct six weeks of monster corridors had honed put her where she should've been, and the geometry didn't reward her for it. She held her footing anyway. That was the whole of the report she'd have filed on it: held.

Behind her, small and cold and precise, Doyle went very still.

The oval receptor's lens stuttered behind his eyes — she'd learned to read that hitch as the intake routine working a thing it had no clean match for. When it settled he read it out flat, the shell's voice, not his:

"Mass, three-ten to three-fifty kilos, forward-heavy. Gait's asymmetric, three-point, no comparable pattern on file. Plating's chitin-analog, seam's non-repeating, luminescent. Weak point — insufficient data. Off-catalogue. No Sphere match. First one on record."

"No match," he said again, flat, the shell giving it no more weight than anything else. She'd learned by now the flatness was the tell, not the absence of one.

Every Sphere on record carried a number, that was Vigil doctrine, drilled into her the same intake week they'd drilled her the chain of command: the numbering was how the war kept track of what it spent. Thirty-one Spheres, last briefing she'd sat through. Higher ranges rumored, unconfirmed, dismissed as barracks talk and left there. A thing without a number wasn't a gap in the filing. It was a thing the filing had never been built to hold in the first place. She logged that distinction and did not care for it.

She didn't have time to ask him what it meant. The creature recovered from the shield strike faster than anything its size should, came around for a second pass, low — the short third limb unfolding from the chest for the first time, hooked terminus catching the grey light. Not decorative. Not vestigial. A weapon nobody had built into it on purpose, grown because growing it had worked, at some point in whatever process made things like it.

She took the strike on the shield again and felt something give — a crack running the resin face that hadn't been there a minute back — driven two full steps into ground that gave under her heel wrong.

"Orim!"

"Not yet," he said, and she believed him. She'd learned to trust the precision of Orim's *not yet* more than most people's *now*.

Wren found the seam. Quiet since the small ones died, watching this new thing with the same patient outside-in attention he gave everything, and when he moved it wasn't toward the head or the limbs. Toward the flank, low, where the plating running in overlapping courses down its side thinned and doubled back on itself just behind the third limb's socket — a place where the growth had run out of a clean pattern to follow and simply left a gap, the way a badly poured wall leaves a seam where two pours met and didn't fuse.

He didn't blink. Went in on his own legs, inside the reach — exactly where the harrower stories said a person had to go — drove both daggers into the seam to the guard.

No controlled fall like a harrower taking a joint strike. It reared, whole forward mass lifting, short limb whipping wide and catching nothing — Wren was already gone from where he'd struck — and in the gap that opened, Doyle fixed the bayonet, closed at a dead run on shell-legs that ate ground faster than the body under them was built for, and drove the blade into the seam Wren had already opened. Twisted it with everything the monster corridor had taught him three days back. Without grace. With everything he had.

The sound it made had no name. Old Watch shorthand for a thing nobody wanted to describe closer, and she understood now why nobody had ever tried harder than that. Not a scream. Not a roar. Closer to the sound stone makes giving way after years of pressure, and under it, buried, three or four notes that might have been a song if any throat built for singing had made them.

Then no sound at all. It folded into the pale moss and stayed down. The black film came off it in a wide stain that sat on the white moss instead of soaking in, and under it, for the moment before Doyle stepped back, the hide read less like armor than skin still waiting to be finished.

Three of them standing over it, none of them speaking. She checked each of them in turn, the old discipline of checking a line after contact — Wren upright, weight even, breathing hard but breathing even. Doyle upright, bayonet still fixed, weight favoring the new shell's off side by a margin she logged and didn't like. Herself last, shield cracked, arm singing, both feet under her. Line held. That was the whole of the assessment.

The quiet after had the same texture quiet always had here — spent, not peaceful — and it lasted exactly as long as it took her to place the second smell arriving under the first: woodsmoke, oiled leather, and blood already dried, carried in on somebody's clothing rather than freshly spilled.

Four of them came out of the treeline with the economy of people who'd done this enough times that caution had stopped being careless and become simple habit — leathers the same mottled grey-brown as everything out here, long-hafted pikes with barbed heads that told her, before any of them spoke, what those pikes were for and how often.

The one in front was a woman, fifty or so, weathered past any easy read on her age, a burn scar running jaw to collarbone, healed badly, long ago. She looked at the dead creature first — long look, professional, cataloguing — then at the party, and didn't look surprised to find a Templar standing over a kill that wasn't hers to make.

"You're off the reports." Not a question. Flat carry, a voice built to be heard over distance and wind. "Vigil-code on the shield. You crossed the Pass checkpoint."

"Three days ago." Lyra kept the blade low, not sheathed. "You've been tracking this?" she asked.

"Two days." Her eyes went back to the corpse. Something in her face recalibrated — not fear, the specific reset of a professional whose whole confidence rests on having seen everything the ground can produce, meeting something the ground hadn't shown her yet. "We've taken eleven off this stretch since spring. Six-legs, mostly. Couple long-necks, west garrison's problem more than ours." She crouched by the body, careful, nudged the flank plating with a pike butt rather than a hand. "Not this."

"You don't know it?"

The woman didn't answer that one herself. She let the silence sit a beat, no apology in it, the flat stance of a professional stating a fact about her own limits the way Lyra would have wanted any soldier under her to state one.

"Nobody knows it." A younger one — a boy, not past twenty, the same weathered economy but learned rather than earned yet — spoke without being asked, and the woman didn't correct him for it. That told Lyra something about how the unit ran. "We don't name what we haven't seen before. Naming it's a promise you'll get to tell somebody else about it."

"You'll want the biology," Lyra said. Not a question either. She'd read the patrol reports. Knew what the Eaters took and why — the arrangement the Liturgy's own filings called, when they called it anything, in language bloodless enough it had taken her three readings to parse: non-Liturgy Catalyst-adjacent compound, self-processed, unregulated. The institution's verdict on the people in front of her, best as seventeen years behind a desk had ever let her determine: tolerated, because they solved a problem the Liturgy made and declined to keep solving; unrecognized, because recognizing them meant explaining, in some sealed document, why eleven hundred conscripts had been left at this perimeter for three weeks on orders that amounted to survive if you can — and what had been done, after, to the ones who survived by methods the survey boards found distasteful to read about.

She didn't say any of that. Set it aside years ago, like everything else, and some fraction of it had lodged somewhere she couldn't fully name and stayed there since.

"We'll want the biology," the woman agreed. "You'll want to walk on before we start. It's not a clean process."

"We've seen worse."

The woman looked at her a moment — not unkind, just assessing. Something in the look might have been respect, or might only have been one professional clocking another doing different work on the same dying ground.

"Then you haven't seen this stretch in high summer." She turned back to the kill. That was the whole of the conversation the Eaters of Monsters were going to offer.

The boy and the other two moved in on the corpse with knives already out, no orders given that Lyra heard, which told her the same thing the woman's silence had — this crew ran on drill, not command. She'd have wanted that crew under her own roster, if she'd had a roster left to want anything for. She set the thought aside and left it there.

Doyle stood over the body a moment longer than the others, receptor tilted at the angle she'd learned meant he was looking hard rather than looking. When he straightened he didn't report it. She noted that too — Doyle always reported. This time he didn't, and the silence told her more than an out-loud reading would have.

"What's it tell you?" Orim asked.

"Not a mutation." Two words at a time, flat, spending them like always. "New line. Still being made."

He said no more than that. Whatever else the shell had given him, he kept behind the dead lens, in the tin voice that wasn't his and would never entirely be. Orim hadn't moved through any of it, Rod's case still shut in his hands.

"That's twice now," he said, to no one, or to her, or to whatever private count he'd been keeping since the gate. "Twice something out here's told me it doesn't fit anywhere I know to look."

He didn't say what the first time had been. She didn't ask. Some reports she'd learned to let a man file on his own schedule, not hers, and Orim had earned the right to keep his own schedule thirty years before she'd been assigned to this ground.

"The Rod?" she asked.

"Still nothing. I haven't raised it." He looked at the corpse, at the Eaters already working over it with knives that had done this before, unhurried and unspeaking. "I don't think I need the Rod to tell me what a thing this new means, this close to the edge. I need it to tell me how many more there'll be before we reach the rim."

Wren cleaned his blades again, same unbothered economy as before. His hands weren't quite steady doing it this time. Lyra logged that too — old habit, automatic. Four daggers, cleaned in the same order every time, edge then flat then grip. Wren had never once broken that order before today. He broke it now and started over halfway through.

"How many kinds of these are there?" Wren asked, "that nobody's catalogued?"

Nobody answered. Not a question anyone standing in that clearing was equipped to answer.

The boy spoke up anyway, wiping his own knife on his sleeve without looking away from the corpse. "You want farms too, while you're counting?" He didn't wait for anyone to say yes. "Nine, working this stretch. Maybe more we didn't walk close enough to count as farms instead of trees that used to have a fence around them." The woman didn't correct him this time, which told Lyra the number was one she'd already made her peace with, the way you make peace with a number you've stopped expecting to go down. "Wasn't a question anybody answered for us either. We just kept walking and counting."

Nobody said anything else to that. Wren finished his blades in the order he'd started them, and this time didn't need to start over.

They walked on before the Eaters finished their work — the woman with the burn scar had been right that it wasn't clean, and there was nothing further to gain by watching. Trees thinned ahead, pale moss giving way by degrees to bare stone scored across in a pattern weather hadn't made, and past that, past a distance her eyes kept refusing to resolve into a number that meant anything, the ground was going to stop being ground.

That was when she saw the shape standing at the edge of it.

For a long moment she took it for rock — an outcrop the scoured stone had thrown up along the rim, because nothing upright belonged at that height. Then it shifted its weight, unhurried, one side to the other, the way a man shifts standing in a doorway, and the outcrop became a thing with a posture. A hunched, elongated torso running up into shoulders that kept producing more shoulders, arm below arm below arm — six by her count, and she counted twice to be sure — thin as furnace-rakes and as gaunt, skin drawn tight enough over the framework under it that she could read the long bones the way she'd read them off a plate in an anatomy hall. No ichor-slicked bulk like the thing that had just gone for Doyle. Almost no bulk at all — stretched thin and impossibly far, like whatever built it had run out of material to make it broad and made it tall instead, because tall was cheaper. At the wrist of each of the six arms, a thread of the same black film clung and wouldn't dry. Same recipe as the small ones, twenty meters back. One recipe, used on everything it made, finished or not.

It wasn't moving toward them. Didn't seem to have noticed them at all, far as she could tell in the failing light. Stood at the rim like something that had always stood there, that measured its days in geology rather than hunts, one of the six arms lifting, slow, to touch something at its own feet she couldn't see from this distance and didn't want to.

She put a rough number on the range out of habit and distrusted the number the moment she had it. Two hundred meters, maybe less at that height — close enough that a rifle round could reach it in under a second, far enough that the reach meant nothing if the report she'd just heard held. She didn't order Doyle to raise his weapon. Some assessments didn't need saying out loud to be understood by everyone standing in the line.

"Don't," Orim said, before she'd so much as shifted weight toward it. One flat word carrying more warning than she'd heard from him in three weeks of warnings. "Not one you go looking at closer. Not today."

"Doyle." She kept her voice level, mostly for her own benefit.

Receptor already tilted at it, and for once the shell gave him nothing back — no stat-block, no cold cataloguing calm. Just a half-second stutter she'd learned to read as the intake routine reaching for a comparison and coming back empty even by its own low standard.

"Range exceeded."

Two words. He didn't elaborate. Watching the line of his jaw, she understood there was nothing to elaborate — whatever lived behind the dead lens had looked at the thing on the rim and declined to render a verdict, the way a man declines to guess the weight of a mountain.

Nobody moved toward it and nobody ran. Wren had gone still again, all four of his daggers doing nothing at all, because there was no play here four daggers were built for. Lyra wanted a number for the height of it, the same way she'd wanted a number for the distance to the crater a minute back, and got the same nothing back. Wanting didn't produce an answer that meant anything.

It lowered the arm. Didn't turn toward them. Some slow tide of attention that had nothing to do with sight passed over the rim, past the party, out across the scoured stone beyond — indifferent in a way worse than hunger would have been — and then it just went on standing, one shape among what she was starting to understand would be many, at the edge of a wound that had had fifty-nine years to decide what it wanted to grow.

They went around it. Not far around — no far enough at that height, not with that reach — angled their line to keep the fallen scoring of rock between the party and it, and nobody spoke above a working murmur until the shape had dropped behind a rise and out of sight. Even then the quiet after didn't read like distance. It read like permission, temporarily granted.

Lyra ran the range on it one more time, out of the same habit that had made her run it the first time, and got the same answer she distrusted the first time. No number that meant anything. She let the failure to get a number stand as the finding, and left it there.

"That," Wren said finally, "is not going on a rope-and-bell line."

"No," Orim agreed. "That's not for the Eaters either. Not for anyone carrying a pike." He didn't look back the way they'd come. "That's for whatever the crater's actually making, once it's had long enough to decide."

Nobody asked him what that meant to plan for. There was no plan yet that fit it, and she'd learned these last three weeks not to ask a question before she had some use for the answer.

Doyle walked the middle-height scan a fraction slower than before, the new shell's hitch worse now — whether from the fight or from something in the readout he hadn't voiced, she didn't ask. Bayonet stayed fixed. He didn't clean it. She understood, without either of them saying so, that he wasn't ready to yet.

Behind them, faint on the wind, a sound that might have been the Eaters at their work and might have been the ground itself, still paying the same slow, patient attention it had been paying since the marker post. The two things, she was starting to suspect, weren't as separable as the patrol reports had always made them out to be.

She counted it off while they walked, the way she would have at a desk in Ocipheus Station, if a desk in Ocipheus Station had ever once prepared her for a day like this one. Six small kin, killed clean, nobody hurt on her side. One unclassified, first of its kind on record, killed by seam and bayonet, not by anything the reports had told her to expect. One more standing at the rim that no weapon in the party's hands had a rating for, and no order given because there was no order that fit it. Three separate kinds of thing she had nowhere to put, all inside a single stretch of ground before full dark.

She did not like the count. She kept walking.

She didn't look back again.

Whatever the ground between the checkpoint and the rim had cost the party — and it had cost them, the farmstead and what had waited past it, the Eaters' line at the crater's outer perimeter and what it took to cross it — Orim let it fall behind him uncounted for now, the same as he let most things fall behind him: on the understanding that a debt not written down is not a debt forgiven, only a debt deferred to a better creditor. It would keep for a fire and a count of the packs. Most things kept. He had built a long life on the fact of it.

The crater's rim, when they reached it, did not resolve into the clean geological line the surveys had drawn. In places it was still stone. In places the stone had been consumed past the edge, so that what a boot found was not rim but the outward face of the layered growth itself, warm through the sole and faintly damp, giving very slightly before it held, the way skin gives before it doesn't.

Lyra tested it and moved on.

Wren came up on the near side and did the same — contact, confirm, continue, an unhurried method for unhurried unknowns — and said nothing about the warmth underfoot beyond noting it, once, with his eyes.

Doyle took the longer, more exposed arc around the far side, the habit of a man who had always rather see a thing coming than be comfortable while it arrived.

Orim came last, as he came last to most things now, the Rod's case still shut and useless against his ribs, carried the way a man carries a name he has stopped answering to but has not yet found the nerve to put down.

## The Crater Rim

Lyra stopped at the rim and did not look for anyone across the gap.

There was no one to look for. Orim had watched her do that before — check for a thing that was not going to be there, out of a habit older than the reason for it — and said nothing. He had learned, fifty years back, exactly how much good the saying of it ever did.

She had the letter instead. It had reached her at the checkpoint, handed across a low counter by a Templar archivist who volunteered nothing about how long it had been waiting there. Sealed twice: once under a Registry notary's press, once beneath it in her own sister's hand, in a script that broke form the moment procedure stopped requiring it. She had read it once, standing in the waystation's doorway, and had not read it again since, which told Orim more about what was in it than any question would have.

Vega. Twenty-four. A scribe by her own choosing, made because Lyra had gone into Liturgy service as a Templar and the Liturgy had been the world Lyra believed in, and Vega had believed in Lyra. Eight months copying an authorization chain that was individually routine and cumulatively a map of something with no public name yet. Sent north by a woman of seventy with no instruction beyond go, see what happens, write it down — except that Vega had not gone north at all, not the part of her that could be booked passage and counted against a muster roll. She had sent the going on ahead of her, in ink, the way the arithmetic of an island with every road ending at a quay required. Orim had known women like that. He had, once, been asked to be one, and had gone, and had not, quite, written it down. He offered no one that part.

She had already told him the shape of what mattered in it, in the flat cataloguing voice she kept for anything she needed him to carry as fact rather than feeling: Sanctorin's contingency reserve — the same reserve her own sister's notary seal had unsealed six months before anyone told Vega what it was for — was moving, and moving toward this ground. Not sent to help whoever reached it first. Sent to take charge of whatever they found, once somebody with the standing to matter finally arrived. Nobody at Ocipheus was coming to save them. Somebody was coming, eventually, to own the finding.

Who had gotten here first? The question answered itself before he finished asking it. The letter had.

The ground held. Wren tested it twice more and stopped testing it, satisfied. Orim followed at his own pace.

Lyra stood at the rim with the look of a woman who had spent eight months reading no action indicated in her sister's careful hand, and had crossed a continent to arrive at the place that hand had been describing the whole time, and had brought the last of its writing with her rather than leave it behind at a waystation counter. Orim read most of that before any of it was said. He had spent forty years reading exactly that look on exactly that kind of face, and the reading had never once been wrong.

Not fear, though there was some. Not relief, though there was that too. Mostly it was the look of someone who understood that the sister who had made the record true could not also be the one to make the truth official in person, and had done what the arithmetic allowed instead — and that a folded letter, carried two days against a body, was going to have to stand in for whatever a reunion would otherwise have looked like.

She did not take the letter out.

Then she looked at the crater, and — Orim watched this part closely, the part that mattered to him alone — at the warmth she could plainly feel now without needing to reach for it, through the case at her hip, through the leather, in the specific place on the wrist where the infusion membrane ran nearest the skin.

She did not open the case yet.

Lyra turned to the crater. Wren was already at her shoulder, watching the drop with the same patient, outside-in attention he had brought to everything since Caer Glas Moor. Orim stood a few paces back, the Rod's case still shut against his ribs. Doyle held the wider arc at the edge that he held at any ground he did not yet trust to bear his weight.

She unhooked the case from her own hip. She had kept it there the last two days rather than pass it into Wren's pack — not from distrust of herself, she had told him, but because the lens generated a low membrane warmth she could feel through the leather, and eighteen hours of proximity had produced a specific attentional drift she had noted and corrected three times the first day, then decided to manage by keeping the case at arm's length on her belt rather than against her spine. Research hygiene, she had told him, three nights back, at a fire that had mostly burned down to embarrassment. Not fear. He had said nothing to that at the time. He said nothing to it now. A man who keeps his own counsel does not spend it on corrections nobody has asked for.

She opened the case.

The first image was Year 630. Old country to him, though not in the way he had lived it — seven centuries before his own first breath, and still he knew the shape of the valley the way you know a face you have only ever seen in one photograph, kept long enough that the photograph becomes the memory in its own right.

The Relic did not replay recordings — it had been there, in proximity to what was being looked at, absorbing the membrane-impression of seven hundred and forty-one years of unbroken sight, in order, because the eye had never once blinked long enough to lose the thread. He had explained this to apprentices once, in words very like these.

Sinter in Year 630 was whole. The valley floor held the shape it had held since before anyone had thought to survey it — a hundred small Scrywell stations scattered across the basin the way a fisherman's floats scatter across a lake, each one tending its own patch of a membrane that never sat still long enough to be governed the ordinary way. Smoke from evening cook-fires. A caravan coming in off the eastern road, unhurried, the particular unhurried of people who had never once needed to be afraid of who might be waiting for them at the crossing. Sinter kept no wall and needed none. For three hundred years no House in Entos had required Sinter to be anything but exactly what it was: the one ground on which everyone's business could be spoken honestly, because no one standing on it could afford to lie and keep the privilege of standing there again.

He had grown up on the stories of it before he had grown up on the ruin of it, and it was strange now, worse than strange, to watch the stories simply be true.

Membrane density: distributed, stable. Scrywell installations operating within stated parameters. Conditions: ordinary. He had set that line down himself once, in a hand that no longer existed in any archive that would admit to holding it, describing a place he would not see whole in his own lifetime by six hundred and eighty-two years.

There was, on this image, nothing yet to feel underneath it. Not a wound. Not a crater waiting to happen. Just a valley doing what valleys full of people do, six hundred and eighty-two years still ahead of it before the morning that would end all of them, and none of it yet owed to anyone.

Year 833. Two hundred years on, the valley had only grown more itself. New installations threaded between the old ones, denser now — the practitioners of that generation had pushed the Scrywell array wider than their grandparents had thought wise, chasing membrane that kept surfacing in new places the way water finds new ground after enough seasons of rain. A dispute-hall stood where an open field had stood in Year 630, timber raised over the specific patch of ground where, if the old stories were reliable at all, the first two Houses to nearly go to war over a border had instead sat down and not gone to war over it. He had heard that story as a child, in a kitchen six hundred kilometers and five centuries removed from the kitchen it was actually about, and had believed it the way children believe anything told to them by someone who loves them enough to remember it correctly.

Membrane density: increased, distributed. Scrywell installations: forty-one, operational. Conditions: ordinary, expanding. He had never written that line himself. Someone else had, a stranger to him in every way except the shared trade, two hundred years before either of them existed to compare notes.

The warmth of the Relic, at that age, was pleasant. He knew this the way you know a room you used to live in — not from looking now, but from a memory the body kept without asking permission. He had noted the pleasantness once, decades ago, and noted the noting of it as a thing to monitor, right up until there was no longer a case in his hands to monitor it with.

Year 1133. Five hundred years in, the valley had become something no other territory in Entos had ever quite managed: a place where the membrane was worked, continuously, by so many hands in so many places that the practitioners no longer spoke of accessing it so much as tending it, the way a gardener tends a hedge that would otherwise simply keep growing into the road. Three hundred years of practice by then, though nobody standing in that image knew yet that they were only partway through a number that would end up mattering. The membrane at Sinter did not sit still. It had never sat still. That was the whole of what made the valley valuable, and it was not, on this particular afternoon in Year 1133, anybody's idea of a warning.

Scrywell installations: sixty-three, operational, continuous access confirmed at density unmatched anywhere else recorded. Conditions: ordinary.

He watched her go still at this one, as she had at each of the others, and understood exactly why: it was the last of them that would ever look like this. A hundred and seventy-nine years still stood between this afternoon and the morning that ended it, and not one soul in the image had the smallest reason to spend any of those years bracing for it.

Year 1312. He felt her go rigid before the image had fully resolved, and did not need it to resolve for himself. Every Templar with vigil training had seen the Liturgy's account: secondary geological event at Sinter basin interior, Year 1312, early spring, duration approximately seventy-two hours. Elevated monster emergence at the eastern and southern Vigil line sectors. Extraordinary Vigil line response. Mass casualties among patrol units. The origin of the modern Eaters of Monsters — the emergency-response conscripts the Liturgy raised, then abandoned, and then had to make a policy about. The standing internal wound of the past fifty-nine years, and older, in the part of him that had helped write the first draft of that policy and had told himself, at the time, that a policy was a kind of mercy too.

The record did not mention a city. It did not need to. By the time anyone outside the perimeter was told anything at all, there was no city left standing to dispute the telling, and an institution does not owe an accounting to a thing it has already outlived.

The Relic showed him Sinter.

Clear sky first, the ordinary business of a morning going on beneath it — a market square he had never stood in and knew anyway — a room known from a story told often enough that the story had worn its own path into him. Then the sky was not clear. No warning in it. No gathering weather, nothing building the way a storm builds toward what it means to do. Only a seam of white light opening straight down out of a blue morning, and then the ground where the seam ended.

He had heard the old men at the Pass describe the sound of it once, in his second year of contract, before he had learned to leave the room when the subject came up. He had assumed, at the time, that childhood had embellished it into something worth the telling. It had not been embellished.

Everything within perhaps two hundred paces of where the light met the ground went white and then went still, all at once, mid-motion — a woman's arm still raised to shade her eyes, a cart-horse still mid-stride, a row of shutters still swinging open under a hand that would never finish opening them — flashed to glass where it stood, flesh and timber and stone alike, and then, in the same half-second the flash allowed for nothing else, shattering under its own held weight into a field of jagged, cutting shards, the way a struck window keeps its shape for exactly as long as it takes gravity to notice it no longer has to. Nothing that had been standing there was a person anymore. Nothing that had been a street was a street. It was a field of edges now, glinting, silent, cooling toward something a boot would go on cutting itself open on for years without any of it once being swept away.

That had taken three seconds. The Liturgy's seventy-two hours started after.

Where the light had struck, the ground began almost at once to answer it — not fire, not settling, but something biological finding purchase in the wound the impact had opened: a slow dark bloom spreading outward from the new crater's lip, consuming the glassed stone and the raw rock beneath it in the same patient motion, building as it consumed — the same patient motion these walls would keep making for the fifty-nine years afterward, without once slowing down. Not an eruption answering the strike. A seed finding, for the first time in its existence, the room it had been waiting for. He recognized, watching it start, the same grammar he had spent fifty years reading off smaller wounds on smaller bodies — the same proliferation, the same patient hunger — scaled now to the width of a city, and understood — the recognition of a thing he had always half-known and never once let himself finish knowing — exactly what his own trade had been standing this close to his entire working life.

The rest of Sinter ran.

The vision spared them nothing of the running, as it had spared him nothing of the three seconds. People moving through streets that were no longer whole streets, over ground that was no longer entirely ground, past the glass-field and the men and women it held, not stopping for any of it because there was no longer a later in which stopping made sense. Structures coming down behind the ones still moving — not the bloom yet, not this early, only the ordinary collapse of buildings that had never been built to stand under a sky that opened like that. Someone screaming a name that went unanswered. Someone else not screaming at all, because screaming cost breath a person running for their life could not spare.

And then, all at once, the vision was not watching the running. It was running.

The frame lurched — hands, someone's hands, closing hard around a case and lifting it clear of a table Lyra had never been shown before and would never be shown again, and the world after that arrived the way a world arrives to something being carried at a dead run rather than something being watched: jolting, half-glimpsed, upended for one sick stretch and then righted, the glass-field flickering past close enough to nearly resolve into faces before the pace tore it away again, a wall coming down three strides behind, a shoulder, a collar, breath ragged enough to hear even through however this thing that was not an ear still managed to hear it. It went on longer than felt survivable, and ended the way all of it had started — without warning. Cloth came down over the lens, a coat or a wrap, someone's idea of care in the middle of the one unhurried decision anybody had left to make, and the light went out.

It did not come back for what the archive, much later, would file as an unaccounted interval. He understood now, watching it end, what that interval had actually been: the half-second the pair had come apart. The Orb, left somewhere in all that running, buried before the day was through. The sight, from that morning on, anchored to wherever the Orb had finally come to rest, and never again to whoever happened to be holding the Eye.

Every other year the Relic had shown them had watched from the rim — patient, fixed, indifferent to who stood where. This was the one morning it had not yet been fixed to anything, because on this one morning the two halves of it were still, for a few minutes longer, together.

"I was carried the same way," Orim said, low, not entirely aware he had decided to say it aloud. "Not this. Not exactly this. But a hand closing on you before you've understood there's a reason for it, and then a great deal of running you don't remember choosing to do." He did not look away from the frame going dark in her palm. "I have spent fifty years professionally certain that memory was the more reliable of the two records. I no longer feel that as strongly as I did an hour ago."

She said nothing. There was nothing small enough to say, and she had learned, watching him say it, that this was not a silence that wanted filling.

Year 1337. Wylla. He knew the name before the image arrived, the way you know a name spoken low at a fire you weren't invited to. The patrol records called it the Year 1337 incident — three Vigil line rotation soldiers and a Templar assessment team, a four-day unauthorized penetration of the zone interior before extraction, the official finding zone-induced cognitive compromise, perimeter breach, secondary biological encounter. Among veterans who had done more than five years of rotation, the word was Wylla, said — if it was said at all — like a thing you'd have preferred stayed unnamed. He had heard it said that way a hundred times and had never once, until this morning, had a face to put behind it. This part of the record had come after his own reading ended. He watched it now for the first time, same as she did.

The creature stood in the upper zone, three hundred meters inside the rim, where the organic architecture loosened from the densely structured walls into something more mobile — the way a nervous system loosens from axon into terminus. Large — not machine-large, nothing built, but large from twenty-five years of growing with no competition to stop it.

Fourteen meters, possibly more; the frame ran out before the creature did, its shape continuing downward past the edge of what the Relic's angle could show, down into the same dark that swallowed everything below the transition zone.

The upper structure was humanoid only in the sense of vertical orientation and bilateral symmetry — old evolutionary answers Entos's own biology had arrived at independently, answers something from far past the membrane might arrive at too, for the same mechanical reasons and none of the same history. The surface wore the same organic overlay as the walls, grown over and through a structure that might have been skeletal or might simply have been architecture wearing a body's shape. The face — a word that fit only in the mechanical sense, a region built to receive sensory information — was layered and pulsing at the Year 1133 frequency. Warm. Alive. Turned toward the four soldiers with an expression that was not human and was not threatening and was, precisely, attentive.

The patrol extracted. No casualties, the official record said. The unofficial record said the assessment-team member who had walked point was not entirely the same person afterward, had requested reassignment the following year, had not gone back to vigil work. Voluntary reassignment, personal grounds, the form read. He wondered, watching, whether anyone had ever asked that soldier what personal meant, and knew, without needing to check, that no one had.

Wylla. Origin: depth, lower levels, duration in zone in excess of two decades. Size: fourteen-plus meters. Behavior: non-aggressive, observational. The biology has been building things. This is one of them. He let that sentence sit exactly where it landed, and offered it no company.

Year 1371 — fifty-nine years into the Age of Vigil, 59 AoV in the archive's own shorthand. Now. As close to the present as accumulated membrane contact could offer, accurate, he judged along with her, to within several months. The organic architecture in the upper crater walls was complete — not growing, complete at this level, and continuing to develop below it, the way a building finishes one floor of itself and goes on building the next one down.

Neither of them could see the lower layers. Not because the image was too dim — the bioluminescence gave enough light. Not because the depth occluded the angle — a clean vertical sightline from the rim. The architecture in the middle and lower reaches was simply too dense to pass light through at all. A surface. The underside of a floor. Biological, structured, warm, pulsing at the frequency now catalogued three separate times over seven centuries, sitting some four hundred meters below the rim, and below the floor more, and below that more again, the depth continuing down to whatever waited at the bottom. Neither of them could see the bottom. He had never seen the bottom either.

But the walls could be seen, and the rate of change in them. Roughly three meters of organic overlay at the upper rim by Year 1337. Now, in Year 1371, eight meters of biological material on the same stretch of wall. Roughly twelve centimeters a year, the birth to Year 1337 — a figure he had done the arithmetic on himself, once, and had never once said aloud. He did not need the second calculation to know it came out worse. Neither, he saw, did she. You could see the shape of the progression without the number.

The rate was accelerating. Whatever was in the depth had been building something for fifty-nine years, and the rate at which it built had not peaked, and was not slowing, and was, in the most recent frames the Relic held, faster than any period that had come before it.

Upper architecture complete. Lower levels inaccessible. Rate of change: accelerating. Status -

She did not finish that field. He would not have finished it either.

This was not archive. The eye had not stopped at Year 1337 and waited politely for anyone to arrive with the case. It had kept looking the entire time — through her childhood, her first infusion, seventeen years of calibrating an apparatus that measured everything except the one thing that mattered, through the crossing itself, through last night's fire, through forty years of a Keeper's shame that had never once made it into a report. Whatever the wall was doing at this instant, under this sky, was being fed into the same unbroken sight she was borrowing through the lens. The thing she was watching grow was growing right now, under her own boots, while she stood on the rim and watched it.

"Lyra."

He heard Wren's voice go out across the ground before it reached her, and watched it fail to reach her, the first time.

The Year 1371 frame held steady in her hand: the pulse slow and deep, three seconds between peaks, warmth rising off the depth like heat off a buried hearth, unchanged, she would have found, across the eighteen months the Relic's most recent record represented. The pulse was not accelerating. The growth was. He recognized that she had not finished working through what that distinction meant, because he had not finished working through it either, in considerably longer than she had been alive.

"Lyra." Closer now. Wren's voice, a register he had learned to call careful-twenty-two — not alarmed, pitched at I have been saying your name for longer than I meant to.

Lyra kept looking. The pulse rate on the walls stayed consistent. But the thickness of the layer — eight meters at the upper rim — was pressing the original stone downward and inward. Not the walls widening into the crater. The walls growing into the stone from the outside face, consuming the rock beneath the surface and expressing what they took upward, course over course, the way a callus builds over a wound from the inside out. The crater was not getting wider. It was getting deeper, because the floor was feeding on itself. Down at the transition, where the architecture met the old stone, small dense structures sat fitted into the niches the rock used to shelter — built, organized, unnamed. Something down there was making things.

Radial growth: negative. Vertical growth: positive. Stone consumption at the floor: primary mechanism. The depth is not a feature of the impact. The depth is being made. He had come to a version of that sentence himself, forty years back, in the dark, alone with the case for longer than protocol allowed, and had never once written it down, on the grounds that a thing not written is a thing not yet true, which he had known even then to be a coward's arithmetic, and had used anyway.

Wren took the Relic from Lyra's hand.

He had carried this lens before — out of an archive, through a wall, into a night he had not chosen so much as inherited. Something in how he held it now — loose, unhidden, out where anyone could see — told him he had stopped thinking of this leg of the errand as theft. So had Lyra, plainly. Neither of them had discussed it. There had been nothing to discuss. He was, though he'd have said nothing about it, the only one here for whom the word theft still meant something specific, and old, and his.

Lyra's hand stayed curled around the shape the lens had left in it, unbending finger by finger, her eyes on the place where it had been. The cold that followed was not the zone's cold, constant since the marker post, but the absence of a particular warmth — the thing that had sat against her palm for forty minutes, saturated seven centuries deep, that she had stopped noticing ten minutes in and only now, with it gone, noticed she had stopped noticing. He recognized the shape of it. The same blind spot had once cost him the case entirely. He offered the comparison to no one.

She stood at the rim, hand still curled, and looked at the crater without the lens: the upper walls, the beginning of the depth, the pulse, slow and consistent, three seconds apart.

"Well," said Wren, looking at the lens in his hand, then at the crater, then back at Lyra. Pale — had been pale since the marker post, the good pallor of someone holding composure through an effort that had not yet run out but was working at it. "You're going to tell me what you saw?"

"Yes."

"Now, or -"

"Now." She turned from the rim. Her eyes took their time adjusting to any direction that was not the crater. She was going to carry the weight of fifty-nine years of something alive and building in the dark for a while yet, and the adjustment was not going to be quick. He knew that carrying from the inside.

"Come away from the edge," she said to Wren. "Far enough to signal the perimeter. I want Orim to hear this." She touched the letter at her own coat, out of habit more than need — still sealed, still waiting on its own reckoning. "And then we go further."

She came away from the edge. They walked back through the transition zone together, back through the pale overlay growth and the pulsing walls and air that was colder than it had any right to be, given what was breathing beneath it. Orim fell in behind them at the distance he kept from most things now, close enough to be called for, far enough not to be first.

He had not been told what she saw. He had not needed to be. He had read most of it himself, forty years and one theft ago, in a room with no window, holding a case that was not, technically, his to keep — a fact the Liturgy's own paperwork had never once disputed, and a fact he had spent forty years disputing anyway, in the only forum that had ever been available to him, which was his own silence. He understood, watching the case now hanging closed again at Wren's hip instead of Lyra's, what closing it had always actually done. It had never blinded the eye — only let an institution, and for a stretch of years he still declined to measure precisely, a man, call an open wound recovered, secured, safe in custody, while it went on staring into the dark, unwitnessed, the way it had for seven hundred and forty-one years.

He walked.

Lyra counted the spires before she let herself do anything else. Thirty of them, crystalline, bone-pale, spaced the way things space themselves when nothing tells them how to grow. Thirty feet tall at the crater's rim, standing like a ribcage that had been open a long time.

They were dead. The Sinter crawlers had stopped feeding here two years back — which was how the Descent Corps confirmed the spires had once been alive, in whatever sense counted as alive out here. Now the crawlers fed elsewhere. The spires stood.

What they still did: they vibrated. The spires hummed below hearing, a pressure in her back teeth she couldn't shake.

The ridge was the last solid ground. Past it, the crater's original rim — the one the founding surveys had measured and named — was long gone, eaten back until nothing remained to stand on. What was left: a shelf of stone cooled and re-cooled a hundred times, and past the shelf a floor that did not end so much as give way, the rot running down until distance swallowed it. She felt it through her boots. Down at the aperture, the ground was marked by nothing built. Only light. The Sinter light was wrong across the whole zone — atmospheric diffusion, the Descent Corps called it; wrong, her body called it — but at the aperture the light was wrong again, differently. Warmer. Directional, as if it rose as much as it fell. As if the stone had been breathing and this was the breath.

She did not write that down.

Orim Zebulun sat on a cooled lava shelf near the inner edge, the Rod across his knees, doing nothing with it. He had tried it once, coming up. Three seconds. Then he had lowered it and set it across his knees and told her: I came to see something. I am seeing it. That had been forty minutes ago. Fifty years he had carried that Rod to the edges of the membrane's secrets, and now it lay across his knees like a tool that had finally arrived somewhere it had no further use. He did not look diminished. He looked like a man reading a river junction — here is the situation, here are the exits, here is what will matter in the next hour.

Wren stood at the shelf's inner lip, where he had planted himself since the rise. Twenty-two years old, raised the same as every child near enough to Sinter to fear it — on the catastrophe, the cautionary reckoning, the shape of what the Liturgy had proven willing to do — and the place was not what the stories had built him to expect. He held his own reaction carefully, both hands, the way you hold something before you know its weight. He had followed Lyra this far because the thing he had been trying to understand since he read the transfer documentation on the moor was somewhere in this zone, and he had not finished understanding it, and he did not stop short of finishing things.

Doyle stood apart, bolt-action slung across his back, reading the crater as he read anything he lacked full language for — marking positions, inferring meaning from arrangement. He had done this since the first week in Verlaine barracks, before he had words for any of it. It had kept him alive.

At the far side of the crater, past the warm stone and the two dead spires flanking the aperture, there was no one standing. Only ground, and the aperture, and the forty minutes Lyra had already spent on it.

She had the letter still — the last of the three things her sister had ever managed to send her. She had read it twice more since the rim, once at the marker posts and once at the ridge before the descent, refolding it along the same crease each time before she put it away, a discipline that had less to do with care for the paper than with not yet being ready to have finished reading it. Traveling ink, a notary's economy in every line of it, dated weeks before this ground had a name any of them were using yet.

Lyra read the shape of what six months of Vega's work had resolved into — the last six of the eight, once the copying had stopped being routine and started repeating in a pattern only a sister would have caught — standing at last on the ground the work had been describing the whole time without either sister present to see it — fast, whole, no assembly required, the way she read tactical ground. Not the instruments one at a time. Not each authorization copied, each staging order renewed, each column movement filed into the sealed record. The shape of what had been built around her, through her sister's hands, before either of them understood what it was for. The senior Scribe who had sent Vega north with three words and no authorization but her own seal, knowing it would keep the body in Averlyne and send the ink on alone. And why.

Not relief. Not a younger sister's version of you made it — there was no younger sister standing across the gap to make it. Something quieter, in her own reading of her own sister's hand: I know what you are going to have to do. I have known since before I understood that was why I was sent.

That had been forty minutes ago.

"The thing you are carrying," Doyle said, not looking away from the crater floor. "It was used to take people."

Not a question. She had known, somewhere on the road north, that he had put it together. She had not known when.

"The Relic is a record of what the membrane has seen," she said. "What it has seen includes-" The notation broke down. The research language broke down. There was no way to finish the sentence without saying more than she was ready to say to him. "Yes."

He nodded. Not satisfied. Not forgiving anything. A fact set down in its correct place in his map of what had happened to him.

Orim had said nothing since the Rod came back empty at the rim. He sat with it across his knees now — a man with a tool that had just told him, as plainly as a tool can tell a man anything, that it had nothing further to offer.

Wren stood a little apart from the other two, watching the crater the way a man watches a debt he already knows he cannot pay on time.

There was no column of Vigil soldiers coming who knew this ground existed. There was no reinforcement three weeks and a war away that would arrive before whatever was down there finished becoming itself. There was only what was standing at this rim, and the one thing seventeen years of careful custody had never once required of her.

She took the Oculus from its case.

She had carried it since Caer Glas Moor without once raising it past the level of her own collarbone — the custodial grip, the way she had been trained to hold every Relic that had ever passed through her hands, close and low and unadmired. She had told herself, walking the whole width of Entos with it riding against her chest, that she was being careful. She understood now, standing at the one rim in the world where carefulness had run out of anything left to protect, that she had been afraid.

There was no one to countersign this. There was no writ that reached this ground, no Canon whose authority extended past the last waystation, no Vigil chamber sitting in judgment of what she was about to do. There was a crater going down in terraces that no one had quarried, and three living people who had walked here with her and one who hadn't lived to see it, and a thing weeping gold in her hand that had been waiting seven hundred and forty-one years for someone to stop being careful with it.

She raised it level with her eyes.

"Whatever this shows," she said, to no one in particular, or to all three of them, or to Vaen, who could not hear it, "we look at the whole of it. Not the part that's easiest."

Nobody answered. Nobody needed to.

She raised it higher, into the gray morning light coming off the crater, and looked through.

It had been hers to carry since Caer Glas Moor, since the heather above Twr Brennid where they had found it exactly where Esvane had set it down — careful even in her last unhurried minutes, the way a woman sets down a thing she still means to finish carrying. Palm-sized. Lens-shaped, slightly convex on both faces. The material matched nothing in Entos's catalogue — not glass, not polished stone, not any crystalline Catalyst mineral she had a name for. It was warm, always, regardless of the air around it. Slightly above body heat. Never higher. The warmth of something that had been working continuously for seven hundred and forty-one years.

And it wept. Always faintly wet — a slow golden bead gathering at the rim of the lens, warm as the lens itself. That was why it rode in a lined, sealed case and not a jeweler's box: the case was a dressing. Leave the seep to stand and the inner seam crusted pale — membrane-flesh proliferating at the lip the way it did at any aperture left open too long, straining to widen, trying to grow something in the wet. She had wiped it clean a dozen times since Caer Glas Moor. It had bled, patiently, the whole way here.

She did not look into it. She raised it.

Every other Scry she had made in seventeen years was a look taken and given back — the membrane parting to show something, healing shut behind the seeing, the give and close of a wound that always remembered how to seal itself. She had spent seventeen years treating the Oculus as the same act, only longer: a very good archive. Raising it now, she understood what the institutional language had never let her ask outright. The lens did not store what it had seen. It had never stopped seeing. Sinter's own Scriveners had bonded it to its paired Orb in Year 630, and the sight had run open ever since — first from inside Sinter itself, whole and unremarkable, for six hundred and eighty-two years, then from a crater that used to be Sinter, for fifty-nine more. In all that time, herself included, no one who sat the Ocipheus watch had raised the lens toward what it actually was.

She raised it. The curtain that had stayed drawn for seven hundred and forty-one years came back.

Holding the small wet window over the enormous one below, she understood: they were the same kind of thing. One palm-sized and warm in her hand. One miles deep, eating downward through rock. What stood on the other side of the curtain was not a memory conjured for her benefit. It was the crater's core, now, the same as it had been every hour since the morning it was born.

The window had already shown her this once, at the rim above the marker posts — the ordinary years of Year 630, Year 833, and Year 1133, whole and unwitting, Sinter simply being Sinter; the thing the Liturgy had logged as geology in Year 1312; and Wylla in Year 1337. It held all of it open at once, not a calendar but a single unbroken sight. What it gave her now was the part she had not yet been shown: not the wall. The desk.

Year 1312. Three months before the Event.

The archive room at Ocipheus Station. A woman at a desk in Canon's mantle, older than Sanctorin, considerably older. Writing. A sealed communication, the recipient designated only by the Quiet Mass's countersign. Lyra could not read what was written. She could read what the woman's posture said: I understand what I am confirming. I am confirming it anyway.

Lyra knew that posture. She had worn it herself, at smaller desks, on smaller mornings, filing a membrane flicker instead of chasing it — the specific stillness of someone certain that caution, recorded correctly and in the proper order, was its own kind of courage. The woman at the desk did not look like a person committing a crime. She looked like a person being careful. That was the whole of what the word had ever cost anyone, watching it now from the outside for the first time: it never announced itself as the worse choice. It only ever felt, from inside the moment, like the responsible one.

Then the valley floor, same period. The Scrywell array still running, still recording. Above it, in the upper atmosphere, something the same unbroken sight had been watching from an angle no apparatus had ever been built to ask about — watching long before any operator sat at that desk. It had communicated what it saw. Not to the instruments. To the operator at the desk. The operator had written her letter. The letter had been sealed.

Three million eight hundred thousand people in the valley had gone to sleep that night with no knowledge of what was coming. The woman at the desk had known. The Quiet Mass had countersigned the acknowledgment of received knowledge. The decision was never written anywhere, because the decisions that matter most never are. They live in the gap between the knowing and the response — in the silence after the letter is sealed, where we could warn them becomes something else, and then becomes nothing at all.

The Liturgy had gained, from Sinter's absence, every arbitration function Sinter had ever held. The Quiet Mass had gained, from one sealed letter, more institutional authority than any single act in Entos's recorded history had produced.

Year 1312, after. The window showed the Event the way it had actually happened, not the way the Liturgy logged it. Not an eruption. Not volcanic. Something falling out of a clear sky, with no warning any watchpost had been built to give, and the valley the Liturgy had known was coming and never once said so aloud. Not a catastrophe that ended when the ground stopped shaking. A birth — the first frame of the thing this same window had gone on watching grow, year over year, into whatever was assembling at the crater's bottom now. It had not recorded a birth and moved on. It had kept watching that same birth become an army, unbroken, every year since.

Year 1337. The Wylla incident, seen again, brief — where Wylla had come from, how far down. She already knew the shape of it. The window only confirmed it.

Year 1371 (59 AoV). Now — unchanged from what she had read at the rim above the zone: the architecture complete above, the depth still unresolved below, the rate of change faster than anything before it. It was still open. There was no present it stopped at.

The Relic grew warmer in her hand than it had been since the moor. Not uncomfortable. The warmth of a window that had waited seven hundred and forty-one years to be raised instead of lowered, and finally was.

She did not put it down when she should have.

She kept it raised.

The showing lasted a long time. She could not have said how long. The cold had stopped mattering. The chord of the Singing Spires was still in her chest, unchanged, as indifferent to what the lens had shown as it was to everything else.

Doyle had gone very still, in the particular register she now recognized - not the shell's stillness, the man's. Orim's face showed nothing it had not already decided to show. Wren had turned half away, toward the crater, as if the ground itself had asked him something he didn't yet have the words to refuse.

Nobody spoke. There was nothing small enough to say.

The Relic's temperature dropped back to its habitual warmth - slightly above body heat, the warmth of continuous work. The showing was done.

She should have lowered it there. Every year of training said so: a Scry concluded is a Scry put away, the vision received and recorded and reckoned with later, in daylight, at a desk, by people with the standing to reckon with it.

She did not lower it.

Her hand went, without her quite deciding to, past the case's open lid to the thing itself - past the plate of glass she had looked through for seventeen years and never once past, to the wet, weeping surface underneath. Custody had taught her exactly one rule about that surface: you did not touch it. Nobody touched it. The oldest notation in the archive said so in language too plain to misread, the kind of warning usually reserved for things somebody, once, had needed to write in blood rather than ink.

She touched it anyway. The old warnings were not wrong about what it would have done to an ordinary hand. Hers had not been an ordinary hand in seventeen years - not since three infusions had put something borrowed from the space between worlds into every vein she owned - and the surface that would have killed an unGifted woman before she'd finished the thought only weighed warm and heavy against her palm. Patient - finally asked for, instead of merely watched.

Wren made a sound low in his throat, the specific involuntary sound of a man watching someone do a thing he had spent months deciding never to try himself. He did not reach for her. There would have been no point reaching in time, and some part of him had already understood that the reaching wasn't really about stopping her - it was about not having to just stand there and watch.

The world lurched.

Not the crater. The lens. The view inside it swung, hard and sudden and entirely without her permission, the way a held breath swings when it finally lets go all at once, and for one ugly stretch of a second the floor of her own stomach went with it. She had to close her eyes against it - the particular nausea of a horizon moving faster than the body holding it - and when she opened them again the picture had found something to settle on and stopped. Not where it had been pointed a heartbeat before. Where it was pointed now, in her hand, out here, at the rim.

Not a fixed picture. Not a single showing, played once from one angle and closed. A window that turned with whoever was finally, actually holding it.

Seventeen years of custody, and every one of those years had held it exactly the way the Order had held it since Year 1330: behind glass, admired through the pane, never once lifted free of the case that kept its poison in and everyone's curiosity safely out. Nobody had ever tried moving it, because moving it meant touching it, and touching it meant a body built to survive the touching. In seven hundred and forty-one years, apparently, no one had happened to be the right person holding it - until a woman who had never once thought of her own blood as a kind of key found herself, at the one moment it mattered most, already holding one.

She turned it further, and what came into the frame emptied whatever calm the showing had left her.

The crater was festering. Not historically, not as a wound remembered - now, actively, the ichor at the bottom moving with a slow, wrong purpose, faster by any measure she had of it than what the vision itself had shown crawling toward this exact hour. Whatever the window had meant by faster than anything before it was not a fact about the past. It was a fact about this morning.

She lowered the Oculus at last, and looked at the three of them instead.

"There's no time to send for anyone," she said. "No column is coming that knows this ground exists, and if I wait for one to learn it exists, the learning alone will cost more time than we have."

Nobody argued. She had not expected anyone to.

"This is a wound," she said. "It needs cauterizing. Now. By whoever is standing here to do it."

She did not say it like an order. There was no rank left to give one from, out here, off every map her authority had ever been drawn on. She said it the way a person states a fact they have just finished checking twice.

They went down into the crater itself — Doyle first, reading the ground as he read anything he lacked the language for; Orim behind him, Rod slung and useless and carried anyway; Wren last, the Relic's case slung crosswise over his shoulder now that Lyra's hands were needed for the climb.

The glass started twenty feet down and did not stop. Not gravel, not scree — glass, black and sharp-edged, fused in sheets and shattered into drifts, the whole slope of it weeping a slow black ichor that pooled in the low places and found every crack uphill of it to keep weeping into. It cut through boot leather if you let your weight settle wrong. Doyle lost a strip of sole to it in the first fifty yards and said nothing about it — the same silence he kept about most of what this place cost him.

"Heat did this," Doyle said, at one point, crouching to look at a fused sheet of it without touching it. "Not fire. Fire chars. This melted and set." He looked up the slope, back toward the rim, gauging distance with the eye of a man who had once read blast radii for a living. "Whatever came down here came down hot enough to glass the ground for a long way out."

Nobody answered him. Nobody needed to.

The gear surfaced an hour past the rim, where the slope leveled into what had once, perhaps, been the crater's floor — not found so much as arrived at, a shape the glass simply stopped hiding once they'd walked far enough toward it: a Descent Corps recovery sled, half-swallowed, its runners black with the same ichor-glass that crusted everything down here, and lashed to its frame, still coiled, still ready, forty meters of cable and a portable winch housing stamped with a unit designation none of them recognized and one date, cut into the casing by hand, that all of them did.

1342.

"Three returned," Orim said, not a question, reading the same stamp Lyra was reading.

Doyle crouched at the winch housing longer than the winch warranted. When he stood again, something in the angle of him had changed - the particular stillness that meant he was somewhere else before he had said so.

The winch woke without asking anyone's permission first. Cable that had sat frozen for twenty-nine years paid out six feet before it found its own rust and stopped, groaning, and the housing's long-dead running lights came up dim and orange along its flank, the color of a thing remembering it used to have a purpose.

"There's a line down," Doyle said, from somewhere behind the sound of it, the shell standing empty-slack beside Lyra while whatever was left of him worked a machine four men had died bringing this far and never gotten to use. "Old rig. Whoever ran it meant to lower someone past this shelf, not climb it. I can still feel where the anchor's set."

He fed the cable out along the glass shelf ahead of them - not far, twenty feet, enough to bridge the stretch where the slope went from merely bad to the kind of bad that had, by the look of the drop past it, taken at least one of the four operators who never came back to report otherwise.

"It's not going to hold long," he said, the winch's old housing already ticking with a heat it hadn't produced in twenty-nine years. "Whoever built it built it to hold once. I don't think it cares that we're asking for more than that."

"Once is what we need," Lyra said.

They crossed on a dead man's cable, one at a time, Doyle timing the tension from a machine he was inhabiting the way he inhabited anything not built for him - carefully, and with the specific attention of someone who understood exactly how much it would cost everyone standing on it if his attention slipped even once. The housing gave out three seconds after Wren's boots found the far side, cable snapping back into its spool with a sound like something exhausted finally being allowed to stop, and the small black shell by the shelf's near edge came upright again, alone, its winch already going as still and as forgotten as it had been before anyone had asked anything of it.

Orim looked back at it once. He did not say anything about the one who never made it home carrying that rig into a place it had waited twenty-nine years to finally be useful. Some debts, Lyra was learning, you paid by using the thing rather than by naming what it cost to leave behind.

They found the hand not far onto the far shelf, where the glass leveled again into something closer to ground. It came up out of a drift of black shards the way a drowned thing comes up out of water — fingers first, curled, huge only because everything in this light looked huger than it was, glass gone milk-cloudy with fifty-nine years of ichor crusted into every seam of it.
