A hand. Not a statue's hand. A hand — knuckles, a lifeline crossing the palm, a hand that had once reached for something and never finished the motion, sealed mid-reach in the one second the world had to work with before it stopped being able to do anything at all.

"That's a person," Wren said, very quietly.

"Was," Orim said.

He did not move closer to look at it the way the others had. He was already looking at it the way a man looks at a photograph he has spent decades making certain never to find in a drawer — small, for what fifty-nine years of vitrified glass usually made a thing look, and a groove worn into the base of the third finger that had nothing to do with the disaster and everything to do with forty years of a ring worn before it, a ring he had not laid eyes on since he was a boy and had never once stopped being able to picture. He said nothing else. Nobody asked him to.

Lyra crouched beside it. Between two of the fingers — not gripped whole in a fist the way she'd expected, but wedged where the hand had closed a half-second too late to close all the way — a curve of something darker than the surrounding glass caught what little light the crater gave back. Round where the fingers weren't. Warm, when everything else down here had gone cold enough to ache.

And there, running the length of the smallest finger, hairline and new: a crack that hadn't been there an hour, or a day, or — she understood, looking at the milk-white age of everything around it — fifty-nine years.

"It's cracking," she said.

"It has to," Orim said. His voice had gone very level, the particular levelness of a man laying each word down with care because he did not trust the next one to come out steady if he didn't. "Everything down here is failing faster than it used to. Why would this be the exception."

Not far past where the hand had been, Orim stopped.

He knelt where the glass gave way, for a stride or two, to something closer to actual ground — a thin skin of ash-grey dirt caught in a fold of black glass that hadn't quite finished swallowing it — and worked a fistful of it loose with fingers that did not look, to Lyra, like they were asking permission from the rest of him first.

He let it fall through his hand slowly, grain by grain, the way a man tests whether a thing is still real by how long it takes to leave him.

"Home," he said. Not to her. Not to anyone standing close enough to have been meant to hear it.

She waited. She had learned, four hundred miles and one confession at a time, that Orim gave you the rest of it only once the first word had finished costing him what it was going to cost.

"That hand back there wore a ring on the third finger for forty years before this ground took the rest of him," he said, still looking at the dirt in his palm and not at her. "I was seven. I do not remember his face the way I remember his hands — a boy remembers what reaches for him, not what looks at him — but I would know that groove on that finger blind, in a room with no light in it at all, and there is no light down here at all, and I knew it the moment I saw it."

He closed his hand around what was left of the dirt.

"I carried the smaller half of what you're wearing against your chest out of this crater on a boy's legs, because he put it into my hands and told me to run before he had finished the sentence telling me why, and I ran, and I did not look back for the second telling, only the first — a child does what he is told exactly once before he starts deciding things for himself. I made it past the Pass with it still in my hands, and I was three days clear of this ground when a Calyx officer on the road stopped me, on a boy's belief that a Calyx uniform meant safety, and asked what I was carrying. I showed him. He decided a filthy Sinter orphan had no business owning anything worth that much attention, and I fought him for it the way a seven-year-old fights a grown man with a sword — badly, and for a long time, because it was the only thing of my father's I had left and I did not have the sense yet to know that losing does not stop mattering less for being certain from the start. He took it off me and sent me on my way with a boot for my trouble, and did not think enough of the encounter to remember my face, or he would have recognized it forty-one years later at Caer Glas Moor. I did not stay in Calyx after that. I did not trust the uniform anymore, and Calyx was too close to this ground for a boy who wanted never to think about it again. I went west, as far as my legs and other people's charity would carry a child with no name that meant anything to anyone, and Ocipheus is where I ran out of west to go."

He looked at her then, for the first time since he'd knelt.

"I always knew," he said. "Not the finding. Not the where. But that he had not run, and a man who does not run when he has just told a boy to does not fail to run — he decides not to, for a reason the boy is too young to be given. I have carried that knowing fifty-nine years without once being asked to set it down. You did not ask me to set it down now, either. The ground did that."

He did not say anything else. He got up, and did not brush the dirt from his palm before he closed it again, and kept walking, and Lyra understood, without being told, that fifty-nine years was not a length of time a person got to measure twice.

The hour had done what waiting usually did — settled the ground back under all of them a little — before she went back to the hand and let herself do what she'd been putting off since they'd found it. She worked her fingers into the crack the way you work a knife into a seam that wants to stay shut, patient, because glass this old broke wrong if you rushed it — a lesson from archive work, applied to something no archive had prepared her for.

It gave on the third try. Not a shatter — a release, the specific give of something that had been waiting fifty-nine years to stop holding on and had simply never been asked to. The fingers opened perhaps two inches, no more, glass grinding on glass, a sound she felt in her own jaw, and the thing they had been holding rolled free into her waiting palm.

It was heavier than the Oculus. Rounder, colder at first touch and then, within a breath, the same wrong-warm as the smaller lens, waking to her hand the way a banked fire wakes to a draft. Weeping the same amber-black seep at its seams. A larger, blinder twin to the thing already riding in its case against her chest.

She did not need Orim to tell her what it was. She had already stopped believing in giants.

Somewhere behind her, quiet, more reflex than commentary, she heard him say it anyway — the registry name for a relic nobody at Ocipheus had ever actually catalogued as separate from the eye that housed it. "Orbis Omnividens," he said. "The all-seeing orb." As if a name fixed anything.

He did not say anything else for a moment. Then, quieter, in the same register he'd used over the dirt an hour back: "Its smaller twin, I killed a man for. Once. Forty-one years ago, at Caer Glas Moor, over nine days that Calyx still tells stories about and I have never once corrected." He nodded, once, at the Oculus riding in its case against her chest. "The Champion who took it off a boy's hands on the road out of Calyx kept it eighteen years and never once thought to wonder whose it had really been. I took it out of his dead hand believing I was only recovering what was mine to begin with. I did not know I was only borrowing it back a second time — that the first hand it had ever left was my father's, not his." He did not turn to look at the vitrified hand behind them. He did not need to. "I gave it to Esvane, after. She knew how to keep a thing safer than I ever could. She carried it the rest of her life, and set it down gently, at the end, the way a person sets down something they mean to come back for. I have drawn Liturgy prestige for forty-one years on the strength of that day at Caer Glas Moor, Lieutenant. Nobody has ever once asked me what it actually cost. I have never once told them, because there was no honest telling that did not run through this crater, and I did not expect to stand in it again in this lifetime to make the telling necessary."

Behind her, the vitrified hand sat empty now, fingers still parted around the space where something had rested for fifty-nine years and would not rest there again. She found she could not look at it long. A hand that had reached for this and not made it the rest of the way was not a monument. It was just the last thing a person had ever managed to do.

"I'm sorry," she said, to no one who could hear it.

She took the Oculus from its case and, working by feel more than sight, fitted the two together.

They did not click. They did not need to. The moment the curved face of the smaller lens met the matching hollow in the larger, both of them went warm past anything she had felt from either alone, and the weeping stopped — not healed, not closed, simply satisfied, a held breath finally let go once the thing it was holding for arrived.

She raised the completed pair, and the crater turned to face her from every direction at once.

She did not raise it to her eye. She had learned in the last hour that the eye was not the part it needed.

She walked to where the crater floor stopped being floor. The shaft went down past anywhere daylight had reached. She held the completed pair out over it, opened her hand, and let it fall.

The completed pair did not need to land to work. It showed her the way down before it arrived — walls of the same black glass, narrowing, then not glass at all but something wetter, something that had never been stone, folding in on itself in slow deliberate pulses that had nothing to do with anything falling through it.

Then it showed her the bottom, and stopped showing her anything she could afterward pretend she hadn't seen.

There was no clean word for it. A womb was the nearest one she had, and even that fit badly — a wet, red-black hollow, walled in the same tissue the crater's whole throat was made of, and within it, filling most of what little room the eye's fall let her measure, something that moved. Not the slow drift of something merely alive down there in the dark. Limbs, if they were limbs, drew up and pushed out again. Drew up. Pushed out. Something in there was measuring a wall it had not yet grown big enough to come through.

She had watched what killed Vaen in three seconds, faster than her eye could properly follow.

Whatever this was made that look small.

Nobody spoke. Wren had both hands on his knees and had stopped looking down. Doyle's receptor, the shell's single dark eye, had not tracked once since the fall started. Orim kept looking. He did not lean in and he did not step back. Whatever his face was doing, it was not fear, and Lyra did not know him well enough to name it.

The Oculus reached the bottom and stopped falling, held — by what, she never learned, and never went back to ask — weeping steadily into the dark a few feet above the thing in the womb. Seeing it. That was the whole of what it had ever been able to do.

"We are not doing anything about that," Lyra said, and her voice came out steadier than she expected it to. "Not today. Not the four of us."

"No," Orim agreed, quietly. "Not the four of us."

"We get out," she said. "We get out, and we get this in front of someone who can."

Then, quieter, half to herself: "But not all of it goes with us."

She knelt at the shaft's lip and worked her fingers back into the seam she'd only just closed, patient the same way she'd been patient with the vitrified hand, until the smaller lens came free of the larger one with the same reluctant give as before — not a click, just a yielding, warmth going out of one half and staying in the other.

The Orb she let fall. Not far — it had nowhere far left to go — just back down into the dark it had already been watching for fifty-nine years, to keep doing the only thing it had ever been built to do, whether or not anyone was left to read what it saw.

"It stays," she said. "It's not a prize, it's a post. Somebody should still be standing it after we're gone."

Nobody argued. Orim looked at the shaft a while longer and then turned his back on it, which was answer enough.

She closed the Oculus back into its case against her chest — lighter now, alone again, but warm in a way it had not been before it had met its other half even once.

"Then let's go," Wren said.

The crater noticed.

She could not have said how else to put it. The glass had held still for fifty-nine years around a hand that had stopped moving and a thing that had never once been disturbed, and now the hand was open and the thing that had been sealed in it was gone, and whatever passed for attention down here turned, all at once, toward the four people standing in the middle of the change.

The ichor moved first — not toward them, not yet, just a general thickening of the black at the low points, the way water finds a new low after a shelf gives way somewhere upstream. Then the shapes came out of it.

Doyle saw them before anyone else did, which surprised no one. "Moving," he said, flat, already turning to put his back half toward the party and his front toward the glass. "Low. Coming fast."

They came low because they had four legs and had once, a long time ago, been something with a name — dogs, maybe, or whatever this world called the thing that filled a dog's role before the membrane got to it. Whatever they had been, the shape had gone wrong in the making: too many joints in the forelegs, hide the same glass-black as the ground they ran on, eyes that didn't reflect the light so much as fail to let any back out.

"Run," Lyra said, which was not a plan, only the truest thing available.

They ran.

The glass punished bad footing worse at speed than it had at a walk. Wren went down once, caught himself on a hand that came up bleeding, and did not slow down to look at it. Orim moved with the economy of a man who had run from worse things on worse ground and knew exactly how much speed his knees actually had left to spend. Doyle fired without stopping, over his shoulder, twice, and something behind them screamed in a register no living throat should have been able to make and then stopped screaming.

"How many," Lyra called.

"More than that," Doyle said, and put two more rounds into the dark behind them.

The rim was uphill the whole way, which meant the glass sloped against them exactly when they most needed it not to. Lyra's lungs burned with something that wasn't quite cold and wasn't quite the altitude. She did not look back to count what was gaining on them. She had already decided the number wouldn't change what she did next.

Doyle stopped running.

Not because his legs had given out. Because he had just finished the arithmetic Lyra hadn't had breath left to run herself: four people, one blade between them worth trusting, an Orb they'd sworn to leave sealed, and a well that was going to keep producing more of whatever was behind them for exactly as long as it stayed open. Getting the four of them to the rim didn't close the well. Nothing they'd agreed to twenty minutes ago had accounted for that, because none of them had known it yet when they'd agreed to it.

He gave up half a step of ground working that out. His receptor tipped up and back, past the rim, to the long shape still moored a mile off where they had left her two days ago.

"Go," he said. "I'll catch up."

"Doyle -"

"I'm not staying," he said. "I'm reaching."

His shell went slack, as it always did mid-Relay, the rest of him already somewhere else, and for three full strides Orim had to take him under one arm to keep the small black body from going down hard on the glass - dead weight, dark and empty, same as always when he was somewhere else wearing something larger.

Overhead, far off, a long low shape that had sat moored and patient for two days woke up.

Balthier did not fly toward them. She flew past them, low enough that the wash off her envelope flattened the black grass-that-wasn't-grass along the rim, and past the rim, and out over the crater itself, engines opening up to a note Lyra had only heard once before, at Sal Vento, the sound of a ship being asked for everything she had left to give in the time she had left to give it in.

She did not slow before the well.

She was forty yards out from the well and closing when the thing came up out of the ichor to meet her.

It rose crayfish-black and jointed, too much of it, the tail unspooling behind it the way a whip unspools before it's thrown - and it did not go for the hull. It went for the envelope, the soft gas-holding skin of her, the one part of Balthier a spar-gun could tear and a crash could not, and it wrapped, and it held, and thirty tons of ship that had been a heartbeat from throwing herself down a wound in the world instead began, very slowly, to come apart in the air above it.

The shell in Orim's arms jerked once, hard, the way a man jerks when he's kicked in his sleep. Out over the crater Balthier stopped going down and started clawing for height instead - not the crash he had planned, just away, just anything that was not straight into the thing they had come here to hurt. For three seconds it worked. Then the tail found a spar, and the spar gave, and she stopped climbing.

"Doyle!"

Nothing answered. There was no wheel to let go of, because there had never really been one - only the same kind of door that had opened once before at a turret ring a lifetime ago, the mechanism declining, at the last possible interval, to finish traveling into his hands. He went through it with half a second left before the rim did, and the small black shell in Orim's arms filled from the inside again, no longer empty, a beat before what was left of Balthier hit the ground without anyone flying her.

She came down the only way left that wasn't the well - hard, wing-first, along the near slope of the rim, close enough that the ground shook under all four of them and the impact threw the thing riding her clear, tumbling, already reorienting, already fast.

Doyle was up and moving before Orim had finished letting go of him, aperture fixed on the thing untangling itself from the wreck of the ship he'd nearly killed on purpose thirty seconds ago and hadn't, in the end, gotten the chance to.

"That's it," Wren said, very quietly, watching it come. "Same kind as the one that took the boat, maybe. Wrong color for the same one."

"That's the thing that took Vaen," Orim said, and did not sound afraid so much as certain - a debt two days overdue and about to be collected.

It came at Lyra first, fast and flat along the ground, the same charge it had used against the boat, betting speed over sense, and she gave it exactly the ground she wanted to give it - one step back, then none, blade already coming up into the line the tail would have to cross to reach her.

Wren was not where he had been standing. He had folded the four feet between himself and her shoulder and put himself in the tail's way instead, and the stinger caught only a shallow line across his forearm, because he was already folding again, out from under it, before it had finished arriving.

"Shallow," he said through his teeth. "I'll take shallow."

Orim's Rod took it across the eyes on its second pass - not a killing blow, just enough sudden black light to put it off its line by half a foot, and half a foot was all Doyle needed. He put two rounds into the joint where the tail met the body, the place he'd have gone for on anything built out of segments back on Sphere 31, and the tail's next strike came in slower, favoring the wound.

"Again," Lyra said, and this time when it came for her she did not step back at all. She let it close the whole distance and took the tail an inch off her own throat on her blade, wrist screaming, and held.

That was the half-second Wren needed. He folded in past the claws, past every part of it built to keep something from getting exactly where he got, and put the whole of Petra's second knife - carried and never once used since Caer Glas Moor - into the soft unarmored place low on its underside, where the shell gave way to something that had never needed armor because nothing had ever gotten close enough before to need it.

It went still the way the thing in the water had not had time to go: slow, all at once, the tail dropping to the glass with a sound like a dropped chain.

Nobody spoke for a moment. Lyra's sword hand would not open. She worked the fingers loose one at a time.

Behind them, what was left of Balthier sat canted hard on the slope, one wing low, an engine ticking as it cooled, envelope torn along a whole seam and sagging like something that had been badly hurt and was, for now, done arguing about it.

"Can she fly," Lyra said. It wasn't really a question.

Doyle looked at what was left of the ship he'd been thirty seconds from throwing away on purpose, and for a moment didn't answer.

"She can fly," he said finally. "Badly. Not far, and not fast, and somebody's going to have to hold that seam shut with their hands the whole way. But she can fly."

"Then that's better than the plan," Wren said.

"There was no plan," Doyle said. "There was a very short list of things I was willing to do, and that was the top of it, and I didn't even get to finish it."

"Then hold the seam," Wren said, and went up the ramp first.

Balthier came off the rim sideways, found the air, and took it. Wren had both hands in the torn seam, and blood on his forearm, and did not let go.

Balthier held the air for the better part of an hour past the rim — longer than Doyle had promised, and less than any of them would have liked — before the torn seam finally won its argument with what was holding it shut, and he put her down, gentler than the crater landing had been, on a stretch of broken high country that had never once been surveyed. East of it, by every account Lyra had ever been given, the maps simply stopped: the Untamed, where a person who wanted to disappear generally managed it, because nothing out there was interested enough in finding them to try.

Nobody stopped to ask whether the shapes that had been chasing them had followed past the rim. Orim had a guess, muttered once and not repeated — something about the crater's disturbance pulling their attention back the way a slammed door pulls a room's attention, however briefly — but nobody had the breath to discuss it, and it did not matter enough to spend the breath on.

They came down Balthier's ramp on legs that had briefly forgotten what solid ground was for, and did not go far from her — not because the ground demanded it, but because a wounded ship needed hands on her seam before hands on anything else, and none of them, in the end, were the kind of people who left a thing to fail of a wound they could still hold shut.

Wren was the one who finally sat down against the hull, hard, and put his bleeding hand against his chest, and said, "We're not going back the way we came."

It was not a question. Lyra understood it anyway.

"No," she said.

"Sanctorin's people are watching every road back to the Pass."

"Yes."

"So."

Orim, some distance off, had already turned east, toward the blank of it, the particular stillness of a man who had crossed unmapped country before and knew exactly what it cost to keep going that way. Nobody said the word Untamed. Nobody needed to. It was the one direction that solved everything and answered nothing.

Lyra thought of the letter before she thought of anything else — the line under the seal, and the line beneath that one Vega had trusted to ink rather than say aloud: look for me at Pallor before you look for me anywhere else. "Not east," she said. "Pallor. House Pallor answers to nobody's writ but its own, and a ship that can only just hold her seam needs a harbor more than she needs the kind of disappearing that ground out there is built for. My sister may have gone there too, if the worst I've feared ever caught up to her. I don't know that she has. I know it's the one door in this whole account I haven't tried yet."

Wren looked at her a long moment. "Pallor's not home," he said. "Nowhere is — I told Einmar as much. But no writ runs there, and a wounded ship could do worse than a harbor that takes your coin first and your story never."

Orim turned from the east without being asked to, the particular economy of a man setting down a direction he had already half-committed to, and did not comment on which way they were going instead.

"It's not sanctioned," Doyle said. It wasn't a question either.

"Nothing about today was sanctioned," Lyra said. "I don't have a command left to issue an order from. I have a direction, a wounded ship, and the people willing to fly her there with me."

She looked at each of them in turn — Doyle, standing on a shell that had just spent everything it had to spend and gotten nothing back for it but a maybe; Orim, already facing west instead of east; Wren, twenty-two years old and bleeding from a hand he hadn't looked at yet, sitting against the hull of a ship in a country that had every claim on him and, for the first time, none he hadn't chosen himself.

"Pallor, then," Wren said, and got up, and did not look back at the crater again.

Doyle didn't get up right away. He sat a moment longer with his hands loose between his knees, the way a man sits when he's finished a job and hasn't decided yet what to do with what the job cost him. Lyra didn't ask. She'd learned, somewhere between the dock at Sal Vento and tonight, that not everyone's ledger opened for inspection, and that the kindest thing she could do for a man carrying one was let him keep his own count.

They made camp that first night on the near side of a tree line that had no name on any chart at Ocipheus Station, and Lyra sat apart from the fire for a while, the way she always had, except that tonight the apartness meant something different than it had every other night of her life.

She had a report to write. Seventeen years of habit told her so, the same habit that had once made her log a membrane's idle movement at the correct hour whether or not anyone would ever read the entry. Recovery of Registered Relic O-001, she could have written. Completion of matched instrument confirmed. Threat assessment: catastrophic, location classified, response beyond present capability. She had the words for all of it. She had carried the discipline that produced those words for longer than she had done almost anything else.

She did not write it.

What she did instead was open the small private notebook she had carried since Ocipheus — the one no instrument required her to keep, the one that had never once carried a canonical seal — and wrote, for no office and no register, the things a formal account would never have made room for. The wall at Schmalburg, going up stone by stone under hands that were someone's, that nobody had asked about, least of all her. The laborers at the border checkpoint she'd looked at once and ridden past. She had told herself, both times, that she could not afford to pull on everything that unraveled, and she still believed that had been true. She no longer believed it excused her from writing down the names of the things she'd let fray, so that at least one page remembered she had seen them and chosen, deliberately, not to look twice. An accurate copy outlives the men who lied to fill it, she thought, and understood, for the first time, exactly which door that phrase was built to hold shut — and that a sister a continent away had reached the same understanding months before her, over a different desk, keeping a different copy for the same reason. Neither of them had known the other was doing it. It did not feel like a coincidence so much as a thing two people raised on the same discipline eventually did on their own, the way water finds the same low ground twice.

She turned the Oculus over once in her hands — warm, weeping faintly, patient — and understood that the report she wasn't writing was the last piece of the Vigil she was ever going to put down of her own accord, rather than have taken from her the way the rest of it already had been.

Nobody at Ocipheus would ever read an account of what happened at the crater. Nobody would learn whether she'd lived or died out here, or what had become of the Relic Sanctorin had built three years of ambition around recovering. The writ he'd left at the last waystation, countersigned by the Quiet Mass, would sit in whatever file it sat in, waiting for a response that was never going to come, and eventually somebody would mark it closed on a technicality, or simply stop looking at it, as institutions always eventually did with anything that had gone quiet long enough. *No action indicated* — she heard it this time in her own voice instead of Sanctorin's, the same rubber-stamped phrase she'd watched bury a border report and a dying man's warning both, hers to use on herself now. The difference, the only one that mattered, was that she knew exactly what it cost to say it, and said it anyway.

She did not owe them an ending.

Her hand found the clasp at her collar on its own. The Vigil's rank mark — a plain red circle, a Sphere, the same shape every practitioner learned before they learned to write their own name, a shape she had worn every day for seventeen years without once asking what it actually meant, until a soldier from another Sphere entirely told her, over a different fire, that nobody had ever needed to hide it from her. It had never meant anything but exactly what it said, worn openly: dominion. She had simply never looked long enough to see it. It did not seem to matter to the fire, which took it the same as it would have taken kindling.

She banked what was left of the flames lower, and did not build up a signal anyone might have seen from the road, and slept, for the first night in seventeen years, without anywhere she was due to report to in the morning, and without the mark that had told anyone, for seventeen years, what she was.

## Rennick

Vega reached Rennick, Pallor's harbor city, eleven days later, aboard the same low black two-master that had carried her out of Averlyne — Loera hulls did not change custody mid-crossing, whatever harbor they finally put in at, and the master took his second half-payment in the same silence he'd taken the first.

She had told herself, crossing the Inner Sea, that she was coming to close a file — the last waystation account, the last unanswered instrument, the loose thread of a sister who had gone into a quarantine zone and might not come back out of it. She understood, standing on the Rennick docks with salt drying stiff in her hair and the harbor watch marking her come ashore with the particular caution Pallor reserved for anyone arriving from Ocipheus asking questions, that she had actually come because eight months of copying other people's decisions had left her unable to sit at her own desk and copy one more.

The keeper of the harbor registry received her at a standing desk older than the pier it stood on. He was courteous. He was careful. He answered nothing directly, until he decided there was, for once, something worth answering plainly.

"No ship of that description has come through yet," he said, before Vega had finished asking. "A rider brought word four days back of a wounded hull crossing slow off the western capes, flying no colors anybody could put a name to. The harbor's held a berth since. There's a room above the registry; it's yours while you wait."

"You're certain it's her."

"I'm certain of a wounded ship and a direction." He looked at her the way a man looks at someone he has already decided not to lie to and also not to fully answer, and went back to his ledger.

Her sister had sent her witness ahead in ink once already, waystation by waystation, the whole width of Entos. It seemed, this time, Lyra had decided to come herself.

Vega sat with that a while, in a registry that smelled of salt and old stone, in a country that was not her own, holding a wait where a silence used to be.

She had spent eight months learning to read what the Liturgy would rather she didn't. She found, sitting there, that she had an instrument for this too, after all: hope, plain and unglossed — the kind a Scribe who wanted her instruments read accurately had spent eight months refusing to let herself keep in a desk drawer.

She did not go out looking for the ship. She understood, without needing to be told twice, that some arrivals you did not go out to meet — you let them come in on their own schedule, all at once, as a held breath finally does, and not a moment before.

She stayed in Pallor, settling what could be settled, and waited. She left the door to the room above the registry unbarred each night, the way you leave a door unbarred for someone you have already decided is coming home.
